papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) achieve remarkable success on diverse multimodal understanding and generation tasks, yet they still struggle to effectively leverage language-based chain-of-thought reasoning for image generation. As a result, existing reasoning-augmented UMMs often fail to inherit the test-time scaling and fine-grained controllability observed in large language models. We attribute this failure to a fundamental modality mismatch: reasoning is performed in a discrete token space, whereas image generation operates in a continuous space. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Latent Reasoning framework in Continuous space (LARC), which alleviates the token-level bottleneck by reasoning over continuous hidden states. Specifically, the training framework consists of two stages: (i) curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (ii) information-gain reinforcement learning (RL). First, the curriculum SFT stage gradually converts token-level reasoning into latent reasoning. Subsequently, the information-gain RL stage self-evolves latent reasoning without ground truth supervision. Experiments across diverse text-to-image generation benchmarks show that LARC consistently improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity. Notably, LARC achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval with a 7%p gain over BAGEL and demonstrates clear test-time scaling behavior, outperforming token-based generation under both parallel and sequential test-time scaling strategies.
authors: Byungwoo Jeon, Yoonwoo Jeong, Hyunseok Lee, Minsu Cho, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between discrete language reasoning and continuous image generation.
Uses curriculum supervised fine-tuning to transition from token-level to latent reasoning.
Applies information-gain reinforcement learning to develop latent reasoning without ground-truth supervision.
Improves generation quality, prompt following, and compositional fidelity across text-to-image benchmarks.
Achieves a 7-percentage-point GenEval gain over BAGEL and outperforms token-based reasoning under parallel and sequential test-time scaling.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant, Benjamin Hoover, Fraser Greenlee, Ruairidh M. Battleday, Radim Urban, Torsten Hoefler, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Targets the prohibitive cost and accuracy degradation of existing sparse attention beyond 1M tokens.
Organizes keys into a learned latent hierarchy, allowing queries to score clusters rather than all keys.
Introduces Distilled-LSA for adapting pretrained models and Native-LSA for native next-token-loss training.
At 10M tokens, D-LSA substantially accelerates prefill and decode while maintaining similar accuracy across evaluated tasks.
N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy and provides per-layer training speedups at 128k tokens.

papers.abstract: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io
authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Yvonne Wu, Zichen Jeff Cui, Nicolas Ballas, Mido Assran, Lerrel Pinto, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors and search complexity in long-horizon planning.
Uses a high-level model to sample feasible state transitions and a low-level inverse-dynamics model to realize them.
Enables fine-grained control without rigid macro-actions or fixed latent skills.
Synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, including in unseen configurations.
Improves performance by 38.5% over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion planners and by 135% over single-level world-model MPC across three navigation and manipulation suites.

papers.abstract: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.
authors: Kuankuan Cheng, Haocheng Yuan, Changjian Li
bullets: Introduces semantic-aware shape abstraction to avoid primitives crossing semantic boundaries.
Uses ellipsoidal primitives with semantic cues from large-scale foundation models.
Employs a differentiable projection–blending–evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence from input masks.
Alternates between semantic assignment and primitive optimization; the method is non-learning-based and needs no network training.
Supports user-controlled abstraction levels and generalizes across arbitrary shape categories, with experiments validating its effectiveness on several 3D shape collections.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Method Overview. Given an input mesh and multi-view semantic masks, we first estimate initial primitives using Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering. The label assignment and primitive optimization processes are then performed in an alternating manner to fit the primitives to the input mesh while adhering to semantic masks. An optional merging step can be applied to simplify the resulting abstraction.

Fig. 9. Semantic-aware abstraction with extra primitives.While our implementation utilizes ellipsoids with closed-form distance functions under projection, the semantically constrained primitive abstraction pipeline extends naturally to general support-function primitives, e.g. superellipsoids and zonotopes. Such primitives are more efficient when modeling shapes with angular features.

Fig. 5. Visual Comparison. We compare abstraction results across different methods, where colors indicate semantic labels. For semantically inconsistent primitives that are difficult to recognize, we highlight the conflict region with a transparent effect.

Fig. 1. Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction. Given a 3D shape from an arbitrary category, SemEllipsoid produces intuitive shape abstractions with a set of ellipsoids that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent. The gray mesh represents the input, while the adjacent models show different levels of abstraction. Each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part, avoiding any cross-semantic assignments.

(a) Existing shape abstraction methods (e.g., Marching-Primitives [Liu et al. 2023a]) consider shape geometry solely in their abstraction calculation, neglecting the importance of part semantics. papers.abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
authors: Shengguang Wu, Suning Huang, Cherie Ho, Ria Doshi, Hao Zhu, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Addresses the costly, manual redesign of agent harnesses for new robots and benchmarks.
A coding model observes rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness over optimization episodes.

Automatically discovers strategies such as clearing jammed arms, approaching obstacles horizontally, and reusing grasp-depth experience through persistent memory.
Benefits are strongest when the benchmark differs substantially from the policy’s training data; scope is demonstrated across multiple benchmarks and policies.

papers.abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.
authors: Assaf Singer, Maroun Khriesh, Noam Rotstein, Yoni Kasten, Or Litany
bullets: Addresses correspondence, depth, and occlusion errors inherited from lifting 2D tracks into 3D.
Uses a feed-forward trajectory corrector with attention along and across trajectories.
Trains only on geometric 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, independent of images, trackers, or geometry models.
Improves trajectories across different trackers and geometry providers without retraining.
Achieves state-of-the-art WorldTrack accuracy, with gains of 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 APD on dynamic points; faster variants remain competitive.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.
authors: Zongze Wu (Adobe), Xianbang Wang (MIT), Zhengyang Geng (Adobe), Mingdeng Cao (Adobe), Zhoutong Zhang (Adobe), Richard Zhang (Adobe), Eli Shechtman (Adobe), Ruiming Cao (Adobe)
bullets: Larger teachers can hurt student quality and trigger training collapse when the critic remains small.
Joint scaling—growing the critic alongside the teacher—prevents collapse in controlled ImageNet experiments.
STAC conditions the critic on the student’s generation step instead of modeling a step-agnostic output mixture.
Joint scaling and STAC improve few-step distillation for class-conditional images, text-to-image, and text-to-video generation.

papers.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
authors: Yuzhe Liu, Haolin Tian, Tonghan Wang
bullets: Addresses the cost of recomputing shared context when dynamically switching among heterogeneous LLMs.

Evaluated on five general-capability benchmarks and six context-dependent tasks.
Matches or exceeds original target-model performance with 75% less KV cache.
At roughly 19K-token contexts, KV conversion is 6.5–21.2× faster than target context prefill.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

papers.abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.
authors: Iulia Rusu, Anoop Praturu, Sergei Gepshtein, Tatyana Sharpee
bullets: Addresses IRL’s limited assumptions about the geometry underlying behavioral features.
Parameterizes rewards by hyperbolic distance between feature vectors and learned parameters, with a Euclidean-distance variant.
Evaluated against linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under deterministic and stochastic policies.
Performs comparably to state-of-the-art models on benchmarks and excels in low-data and dense environments.
Human museum-navigation data suggest rewards depend on non-separable conjunctions among exhibit-distance features.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.

Noise accelerated plasticity loss in harder tasks but could preserve plasticity as a regularizer in easier ones.
In the hardest stochastic settings, TD instability—not gradual plasticity loss—was the dominant failure mode.

papers.abstract: A fallen humanoid beneath an overhead obstacle faces a coupled recovery problem. It must create clearance while organizing support for a stable rise, since attempting to stand before making room can further increase obstruction. We introduce a reinforcement learning method with contact-supported geometric escape guidance, which rewards incremental reduction of robot-obstacle overlap without prescribing an escape path. To achieve this, a learned motion prior, together with posture-dependent support and joint-stall costs, is proposed to shape a single policy that learns when to clear the obstacle, how to establish support, and when to complete the rise, all using proprioception alone. In simulation, it recovers in 88.5% of trials beneath plates that can only be lifted, compared with 18.9% without geometric guidance, and in 98.6% of trials beneath free plates with randomized size, mass and placement. On a Unitree G1, the deployed policy recovered in 95 of 150 attempts across seven real-world obstacle scenes, including furniture and multi-object arrangements absent from training. Project page: https://lu-yidan.github.io/ROOF/
authors: Yidan Lu, Jiayuan Yu, Zongrui Cai, Jingwen Sun, Jinrui Han, Jing Wang, Ping Luo, Peng Lu
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenge of clearing an overhead obstruction while organizing a stable rise.

Combines a learned motion prior with posture-dependent support and joint-stall costs in a single policy.
Achieves 88.5% recovery under liftable plates with guidance versus 18.9% without, and 98.6% under free randomized plates in simulation.
On a Unitree G1, succeeds in 95/150 real-world attempts across seven unseen obstacle scenes, including furniture and multi-object setups.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
authors: Juntao Cheng, Jinzhou Tang, Fan Feng, Henrik I. Christensen, Yujia Zheng
bullets: WAMs may entangle action-relevant factors with nuisance variables when learning from demonstrations.
A sparsity constraint separates variables needed for action generation from those needed for full-scene prediction.
Under this constraint, action latents are identifiable up to permutation, without requiring sufficient temporal dependence or independent latent factors.
CWAM adds a sparse routing path to a pretrained WAM’s action head while leaving world modeling unchanged.
Synthetic and real-robot experiments support the theory and show improved closed-loop success efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Causal separation of action-relevant latents in world action models with robot validation; directly fits latent action and interactive world model interests.
papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
papers.tldr: CausalWAM identifies and uses only the latent factors that cause demonstrated actions, improving closed-loop action efficiency without changing the world-modeling objective.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.
authors: Gyeongjin Kang, Freeman Cheng, Botao Ye, Weijie Lyu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Eunbyung Park
bullets: Targets accurate depth and camera pose rather than rendering quality alone.
Uses all views for correspondence while excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed 3D scene.
Aligns features from sparse and dense observations to provide annotation-free geometric supervision.
Further aligns features with a frozen vision foundation model.
Reports improved depth and pose estimation over prior self-supervised methods, with benefits for later supervised training.

papers.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.
authors: Lidong Lu, Lidong Zou, Xinyi Mao, Jiaxin Lv, Zhenquan Li, Liangrui Dong, Tong Lu, Guo Chen
bullets: Introduces PanoVideoBench, a manually annotated benchmark with 1,000 questions across five categories and 15 types.
Evaluation of 11 models finds cross-view tracking and integrating evidence across space and time to be the main weaknesses.
Constructs PanoVideoCoT with 13,465 reasoning QA pairs from verified panoramic observations and agentic explorations.
Trains PanoVideoReasoner using Panoramic CoT SFT and evidence-privileged on-policy self-distillation.
Achieves 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving its backbone by 12.5 points and prior state of the art by 2.6 points.

papers.abstract: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.
bullets: Addresses rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions that limit observation-only DRL routing.
Uses per-satellite episodic memory, local and neighboring state, recent routing history, and a Transformer-based decision network.
Trains with Approximate Information State (AIS)-based auxiliary objectives.
In experiments, RAMA reduced mean and tail latency versus DDQN and achieved further gains with online updates across tested constellations.
Scope: results are reported for 140-satellite Kepler and 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1 networks.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.
authors: Pengfei Zhou, Yixing Ma, Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Zhenglin Wan, Hexin Wang, Wangbo Zhao, Yang You
bullets: Addresses the coordination and evaluation mismatch between deliberative foundation models and reactive policies.
Uses a System 2 brain, System 1 router, and System 0 policies under a rule that running policies never wait for the brain.
Combines route memory, a boundary-triggered judge gate, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery.
On 3,000 LIBERO-Pro episodes, reaches 95.9% success, with 25% fewer control steps and 17% lower control time than the cited baseline.
Also shows transfer to RoboTwin 2.0, BEHAVIOR-1K, and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, though the abstract does not detail limitations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs can improve the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by providing greater independence. However, reliable navigation especially in human environments is a major challenge due to factors such as dynamic obstacles, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, and the users' need to complete multiple stops along the way before reaching their final destination. This paper presents a hybrid path planning framework for multi-goal navigation in dynamic environments. The framework integrates the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for global task ordering with the Potential Field (PF) method and heuristic local planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) to achieve collision-free navigation. Within this hybrid framework, TSP determines the visiting order of intermediate stations, PF transfers global path information, and local planners avoid obstacles while guiding the robot to the stations. The local planners generate feasible paths that allow the robot to follow the global trajectory and reroute to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. For this purpose, two algorithms have been developed: (i) TSP-PF-RRT and (ii) TSP-PF-A*. The performance of the proposed algorithms are evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded scenarios that contain heterogeneous dynamic and static obstacles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid framework enables efficient multi-goal navigation while maintaining safe operation in dynamic environments with humans, with TSP-PF-RRT achieving fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances.

Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded environments evaluate performance with heterogeneous static and dynamic obstacles.
TSP-PF-RRT achieves fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances in the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.
authors: Amit Jain, Sergio Sanchez-Hurtado, Victor Rodriguez-Fernandez, Richard Linares
bullets: The method jointly proposes controller parameters and certificates while using certificate checks to guide black-box search.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation enables efficient inference through streaming prediction. However, existing methods are typically restricted to fixed sampling steps, limiting the flexibility to balance generation quality and efficiency, while one-step generation suffers from degraded visual quality and error accumulation over long sequences, leading to content drift and generation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Any Forcing, a unified framework for achieving Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability. Specifically, we introduce a unified adversarial discriminator that jointly performs real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency alignment, and first-frame quality enhancement, enabling flexible sampling while preserving one-step generation quality. Furthermore, we propose a training-free adaptive long-term memory selection mechanism that selects historical states based on global semantic relevance and local value contribution, while remapping their temporal positions to preserve temporal relationships within the memory cache, thereby enabling stable one-step long-video generation. Experiments demonstrate that Any Forcing achieves high-quality and stable one-step autoregressive video generation, achieving 20.9 FPS and 24.7 FPS for short and long video generation on a single H100 GPU, respectively.
authors: Jiahua Xu, Yijie Fang, Nannan Wang, Xunhao Lin, Li Cao, Lei Hao, Mingrui Zhu, Fei Gao, Xinbo Gao
bullets: Targets fixed-step sampling limitations and one-step quality degradation, error accumulation, content drift, and collapse.
Uses a unified adversarial discriminator for real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency, and first-frame quality enhancement.
Introduces training-free adaptive long-term memory selection based on semantic relevance and local contribution, with temporal-position remapping.
Reports stable one-step generation at 20.9 FPS for short videos and 24.7 FPS for long videos on a single H100 GPU.

papers.abstract: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.
bullets: Looping re-applies layers, preserving parameter count, storage, memory, and training cost but increasing per-token compute.
The study compares looped models against an identically trained unlooped model and the best unlooped model at equal inference FLOPs.
Experiments use Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models ranging from 0.8B to 9B parameters.
At 4B and 9B, looping did not outperform the same model trained without a loop.
The results suggest post-training loops pay off only for small models under a fixed parameter budget.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes inference-compute trade-offs of layer looping in pretrained LLMs; directly relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?
papers.tldr: Post-training loops rarely justify their extra per-token inference cost: across 0.8B–9B models, only the 0.8B looped model outperformed both equal-parameter and equal-FLOP baselines.

papers.abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.
authors: Jasmine Ratchford, Raffaele Romagnoli, Mark H. Klein
bullets: Uniform knot placement can waste control points or poorly capture rapidly varying trajectory regions.
The method learns local trajectory-variation characteristics directly from the system’s initial condition.
These predictions construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator.
The goal is to meet a prescribed approximation accuracy with fewer control points.
The abstract describes the approach and objective but does not report specific experimental results or limitations.

papers.selection_reason: Learning adaptive knot placement for quadrotor trajectory splines is transferable to efficient trajectory representation in robot planning.
papers.title: A Neural Network Approach towards Real-Time Knot Point Density Estimates for the Nonlinear Quadrotor
papers.tldr: A neural network predicts trajectory variation from initial conditions to enable real-time, adaptive knot placement for efficient B-spline approximations of nonlinear quadrotor dynamics.

papers.abstract: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.
bullets: Chaotic PDE forecast error combines unavoidable physical growth with amplification caused by the emulator’s dynamics.
The study introduces an amplification ratio by comparing model errors with a counterfactual propagated through the solver’s Jacobian.
Across 21 configurations spanning four PDEs, five architectures, and two model sizes, fine-tuning helped all seeds with amplification ratios of at least four, but few with ratios at most 1.25.
For strongly amplifying models, geometric-mean error decreased by factors of 8 for small models and 55 for larger models at one Lyapunov time.
Error-direction Jacobian matching generally beat random-direction matching, while input-noise injection performed comparably to error-direction matching.

papers.selection_reason: Jacobian-based regularization for stable autoregressive dynamics emulation; transferable to learned world models.
papers.title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
papers.tldr: Jacobian fine-tuning stabilizes neural PDE emulators mainly when their own dynamics strongly amplify prediction errors, while offering little benefit when amplification is weak.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
authors: Xiangyu Kong, Ruirui Yang, Xia Hou
bullets: Introduces a multi-country benchmark that converts dialogue into tariff and trade-share policies subject to capacity and network constraints.
Evaluates negotiated outcomes with an Economic Health Index (EHI), beyond agreement rates alone.
Proposes TACTIC, which adapts across episodes using prior experience, opponent behavior, and settlement outcomes without changing base LLM weights.
Across 20 episodes, TACTIC’s final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, outperforming its no-cross-episode-update ablation at 65.2.
TACTIC degrades less than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM under technology-control and energy-crisis shocks.

papers.title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but can they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry? We introduce GeoFlip, a video generation benchmark centered on physical outcome flips induced by geometry. With shared physical settings and textual prompts held fixed, GeoFlip applies controlled interventions to support extent, object placement, and mechanism configuration, constructing paired scenes with contrasting reference events, such as remaining stable versus falling or tipping. These pairs test whether models translate geometric differences in the first frame into correct physical evolution. The benchmark comprises 482 scene pairs and 964 reference videos across six physical categories, with reference outcomes established through procedural scene construction, physics simulation, and numerical validation and verification of physical events. We evaluate 16 models for image to video generation along three dimensions: event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos. We examine evaluation consistency with independent vision language judges. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest event correctness averaged across tasks is 27.98%, revealing substantial limitations in physical generation conditioned on geometry. Model strengths vary across physical mechanisms, and the three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity. By combining controlled geometric interventions, verifiable physical references, and multidimensional evaluation, GeoFlip assesses progress from visual realism toward physical consistency conditioned on geometry.
authors: Yuqi Li, Junming Liu, Bowen Hu, Ruize Niu, Huiran Duan, Yingli Tian, Hao Wu

Evaluates 16 image-to-video models on event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos.
Across 442 shared conditions, the best average event-correctness score is only 27.98%.
Common failures include ignoring geometry changes, incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and adding extra components.
Independent vision-language judges show high agreement for event correctness and structural integrity, with rank correlations of 0.906 and 0.929.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark testing geometry-conditioned physical consistency in video generation; directly relevant to video diffusion models.
papers.title: GeoFlip: Benchmarking Geometry-Sensitive Physics in Video Generation

papers.abstract: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.
bullets: Forgetting is evaluated as degraded prediction of standard web text after instruction tuning or subject-specific further pretraining.
The study fits a fixed vocabulary bias, alone or with a temperature, to correct final-token logits across 14 model pairs ranging from 1B to 7B parameters.
On held-out correction data, bias-only recovery is under 10%, while bias plus temperature recovers up to 36%.
Math further-pretrained models show the greatest loss and recover almost none of it with these corrections.
A controlled random-damage simulation recovers 29% despite having no planted bias or temperature shift, suggesting the method can capture spurious improvements.

papers.title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
papers.tldr: Fixed token-level logit corrections, especially when combined with temperature scaling, recover only part of the language-model performance lost through fine-tuning or further pretraining.

papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
authors: Zhangchi Feng, Harry Jiang, Yangyifei Luo, Ray Zhang, Richong Zhang
bullets: Finite-state memory and initialization can limit long-context retrieval in linear attention.
DAMI jointly configures gate parameters before training using geometric head-wise timescales and a low-high-low layer-wise sensitivity profile.
A small activation sample calibrates the implementation to these targets without adding trainable parameters.
Across five gated linear-attention families, DAMI raises average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29–16.71 percentage points over random initialization.
Language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval performance remains broadly comparable to baseline initialization.

papers.abstract: Modern visual tokenizers aim to preserve fine-grained visual details while learning high-level semantic representations for downstream generation and understanding. Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, yet how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information remains poorly understood. We reveal that these queries spontaneously develop complementary roles under semantic supervision: a small set of Content queries captures high-level semantic information, while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained visual details for reconstruction. To adapt token processing to these heterogeneous roles, we introduce MoETok, a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts. Jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, the router learns role-specialized processing paths adapted to each token's representation. Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently improves reconstruction, semantic representation, and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet, it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. We further validate MoETok at scale in a unified autoregressive model jointly trained for understanding and generation with a next-token cross-entropy objective. The resulting model combines competitive visual understanding with state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, matching or surpassing diffusion-based models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image on benchmarks including DPG-Bench (87.61), GenEval2 (40.04 GM), and WISE (0.49).
authors: Jiahao Guo, Bao Tang, Haoxiang Cao, Jingfeng Yao, Bo Li, Wenyu Liu, Kun Gai, Changqian Yu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Query tokens naturally separate into Content queries for high-level semantics and Detail queries for fine-grained reconstruction.
MoETok routes tokens through sparsely activated, role-specialized experts.
It consistently outperforms dense tokenizers across model scales and token budgets under matched supervision and active computation.
On ImageNet, it achieves strong reconstruction and semantic representation plus state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within 1D tokenizer methods.
At scale, its unified autoregressive model reaches competitive understanding and state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, with DPG-Bench 87.61, GenEval2 40.04 GM, and WISE 0.49.

papers.abstract: High accuracy on streaming video benchmarks does not establish whether a model uses visual history. Our review of OVO-Bench and StreamingBench finds that recent frames suffice for 32% of sampled historical questions, while models also answer many questions correctly from the question and options alone. We introduce TwinPast to test whether answers correctly follow changes in history, using 350 human-reviewed video pairs spanning five historical tasks. Each pair holds the recent video context, question, and ordered options fixed while changing critical historical evidence and the correct answer. Each video is evaluated independently, and PairAcc requires correct answers for both histories. We evaluate 34 model and input configurations. For Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-Flash, historical inputs improve performance on TwinPast, reversing the recent-frame advantage on existing benchmarks. The strongest evaluated streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, compared with 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models. This gap persists across all five tasks. Case studies further show that models select states from the wrong time or contradict recorded event order despite retaining the relevant evidence. These findings highlight the need to connect historical memory and retrieval with reasoning that uses evidence according to the question's temporal references and event relations.
authors: Haotian Yang, Yong Chen, Cheng Peng, Haobo Wang, Zhongle Xie, Xuanru Li, Gang Chen
bullets: Existing benchmarks can be solved using recent frames or the question and options alone in many cases, weakening claims of historical understanding.
TwinPast contains 350 human-reviewed video pairs across five historical tasks, changing critical past evidence while keeping recent context and questions fixed.
Its PairAcc metric requires a model to answer correctly under both histories, testing whether predictions follow historical changes.
Across 34 model/input configurations, the strongest streaming system achieved 49.14% PairAcc, below evaluated general-purpose models at 66.57–91.43%.
Failures include selecting states from the wrong time and contradicting the recorded order of events, motivating better temporal retrieval and evidence-based reasoning.

papers.abstract: Robotic Manipulation Surfaces (RMS) reposition objects by deforming the surface on which they rest. A recent class of RMS suspends a continuous fabric sheet from a sparse grid of vertical linear actuators lowering the actuator density of such surfaces but how to design such surfaces so that objects can be controlled everywhere on it, and how to extend it beyond a single module so that objects can pass between modules and achieve parallel, remain open. This paper presents a separable catenary model of the suspended sheet that is fast to compute and provides both the surface shape for given actuator heights and the actuator heights for a desired local slope. The closed form inverse lets a simple PID controller position objects on the sheet, and the model relates fabric length, module span and actuator stroke to the reachable workspace, yielding a minimum fabric length bound and design charts for these surfaces. The approach is then extended to a multimodular platform in which neighbouring modules share actuators. On a $2 \times 2$ prototype, we demonstrate that centimetre-scale objects are transferred between modules and positioned within 0.03 m over a $1 m^2$ workspace with only nine actuators, enabling multi-object manipulation and opening the way to parallel manipulation.
authors: Pratik Ingle, J{\o}rn Lambertsen, Kasper St{\o}y, Andres Fai\~na
bullets: Addresses how sparse-actuator fabric surfaces can provide controllable object motion throughout their workspace and connect across modules.
Introduces a separable catenary model that computes fabric shape from actuator heights and actuator settings for desired local slopes.
Uses a closed-form inverse with a simple PID controller for object positioning.
Derives relationships among fabric length, module span, actuator stroke, and reachable workspace, including a minimum fabric-length bound and design charts.
A 2×2 prototype transfers centimetre-scale objects between modules and positions them within 0.03 m over 1 m² using nine actuators.

papers.abstract: Data-driven controllers have enabled lower-limb robotic exoskeletons to adapt assistance to the user across many tasks. A leading example is biological torque control, which estimates the user's own joint moment from onboard sensors and assists in proportion to that estimate. However, its estimators are trained on data recorded with the target device, so deploying the controller on new hardware requires collecting new data. Existing open-source efforts release hardware, software, or controllers separately, so this data collection must still be repeated on the assembled device. Here, we present an open-source knee exoskeleton, built from off-the-shelf components and widely available fabrication tools, with a biological torque controller derived entirely from simulation. A muscle-driven imitation policy reproduces squatting motions from an open biomechanics dataset, and the resulting knee moments are distilled into an estimator that uses only onboard sensors, so no training data are recorded on the device. In seven able-bodied participants, assistance reduced peak biological knee extension moment by 21.5% and peak vastus medialis activation by 26.7% during squatting, relative to squatting without the exoskeleton (p<0.05). Our results demonstrate that a biological torque controller derived from simulation can transfer to physical hardware without device-specific data collection. Because the hardware and training pipeline are released together, research groups can train and compare knee exoskeleton controllers on shared hardware without additional data collection overhead.
authors: Rajiv V. Joshi, Jimin An, Ilseung Park, Dawit Lee, Inseung Kang
bullets: Addresses the need to recollect training data whenever biological torque control is deployed on new exoskeleton hardware.
Combines off-the-shelf hardware with a muscle-driven imitation policy and an onboard-sensor estimator derived entirely from simulation.
In seven able-bodied participants, assistance reduced peak biological knee extension moment by 21.5% and peak vastus medialis activation by 26.7% during squatting.
Releases the hardware and training pipeline together to support shared-hardware controller research without additional data-collection overhead.

papers.abstract: Automated endoscope guidance reduces the need for continuous manual camera control during minimally invasive surgery. However, the desired camera motion depends on the surgeon's immediate intentions and cannot always be inferred from the visual operative scene alone. We propose to automate the task using language-conditioned behavioral cloning; we define 6 clinically relevant guidance behaviors and collect 235 subtask demonstrations. In preliminary phantom experiments, our policy achieves 100% success on focus, overview, and stop, 80% on search-tip and follow-tip behaviors, and 50% on horizon leveling. These results demonstrate the feasibility of learning heterogeneous surgeon-requested camera behaviors with a single visuomotor policy, while the observed failure modes motivate future work on adding temporal context for more demanding guidance tasks.
authors: Ariel Rodriguez, Lorenzo Mazza, Ortrun Hellig, Alejandra Toscano, Rayan Younis, Stefanie Speidel
bullets: Endoscope motion depends on the surgeon’s immediate intentions, which may not be inferable from vision alone.
The study defines six clinically relevant guidance behaviors and collects 235 subtask demonstrations.
Preliminary phantom results show perfect success on focus, overview, and stop; lower success occurs for search-tip, follow-tip, and horizon leveling.
Failures suggest that temporal context may be needed for more demanding guidance tasks.

papers.abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.
authors: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong, Fan Yang, Wenbin Zhangg, Geng Yuan, Xue Lin, Yanzhi Wang, Dong Huang
bullets: On clean Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa data, a learned value selector underperforms random selection, while a hindsight oracle offers only limited, statistically uncertain gains.
Most states (82%) have identical candidate outcomes, leaving little headroom for candidate selection.
Token pruning reduces per-forward FLOPs by up to 47%, but achieves at most 1.15× measured end-to-end speedup on the deployed path; adaptive allocation remains inconclusive.
A silent rendering corruption increases on compute-heavy planning paths without affecting the official direct-policy result.
The authors release a corruption detector, fix, and scripts, and recommend auditing decision signal, realized efficiency, and evaluation integrity separately.

Limited variation in candidate outcomes constrains the headroom for selection, and the deployable value selector underperforms random selection, while the hindsight oracle provides only modest evidence of improvement. (2) Adaptive allocati n. Substantial nominal FLOPs reductions translate into modest end-to-end latency gains, while the joint allocation effect remains unresolved at the available noise and statistical power. (3) Evaluation reliability. Rendering corruption becomes much more frequent in the compute-intensive planning path than under directpolicy or best-of-N evaluation, while the official direct-policy result remains essentially unaffected. All findings are scoped to the tested Cosmos Policy–RoboCasa configuration.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical audit of test-time search for world action models; relevant to interactive world models and test-time learning.
papers.title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
papers.tldr: An audit finds that test-time search provides little reliable benefit for the tested world-action-model setup because candidate selection has weak signal, compute savings translate poorly to end-to-end speedups, and simulator corruption can undermine evaluation.

papers.abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.
authors: Jean Lucien Randrianantenaina, Hung Nguyen, Nasib Ullah, Jinbin Zhang, Nilesh Gupta, Inderjit S. Dhillon, Rohit Babbar
bullets: Targets the quality–cost trade-off of pruning LLMs at high sparsity, where one-shot pruning degrades sharply and end-to-end methods require large auxiliary state.
Progressively tightens a global sparsity constraint and trains a fixed-budget sparse delta to guide subsequent pruning decisions.
Evaluated on six models ranging from 125M to 13B parameters across 50%–90% sparsity.
Reports lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity, with reductions of up to 42%.
At 90% sparsity on LLaMA2-7B, uses one H200 instead of four, with 5.0× smaller persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours.
