papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.
authors: Abdul Fatir Ansari, Oleksandr Shchur, Jaris K\"uken, Andreas Auer, Boran Han, Pedro Mercado, Syama Sundar Rangapuram, Huibin Shen, Lorenzo Stella, Xiyuan Zhang, Mononito Goswami, Shubham Kapoor, Danielle C. Maddix, Pablo Guerron, Florian Saupe, Markus Reichstein, Tony Hu, Junming Yin, Nick Erickson, Prateek Mutalik Desai, Hao Wang, Huzefa Rangwala, George Karypis, Yuyang Wang, Michael Bohlke-Schneider
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing time-series foundation models that forecast each series independently.
Infers relationships among multivariate series directly from historical context without task-specific treatment.
Achieves strong average benchmark performance, improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points and win rates by 10 percentage points over the strongest baselines.
Produces forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU and is substantially faster than task-specific forecasters.
Performs competitively with specialized methods in infectious-disease, macroeconomic, carbon-flux, and runoff forecasting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The complete Chronos-2 pipeline. (a) Architecture overview: Input time series (targets and covariates) are first normalized (scaling) and then tokenized for downstream processing. The Transformer stack alternates between time and group attention layers. The output from the Transformer stack is mapped to quantile predictions through a neural network. The figure illustrates two time series tasks, the first (in cyan) with two targets and one known (future) covariate, and the second (in pink) with one target and two known covariates. (b) Tokenization: Meta features are appended to the time series which indicate the position of an observation (time index) and whether it is missing (mask). Time series and meta features are split into non-overlapping patches and mapped to high-dimensional embeddings via a neural network. (c) Attention layers: Each Transformer block alternates between time and group attention layers: the time attention layer aggregates information across patches within a single time series, and the group attention layer aggregates information across all series within a group at each patch index. The groups corresponding to the two time series tasks are highlighted in cyan and pink. A group is a flexible notion of relatedness and may correspond to a single time series, multiple series sharing a source or metadata, variates of a multivariate series, or targets along with associated covariates. The group attention layer enables the model to infer relationships between different time series in the group based on the available context at inference time (in-context learning).

Figure 5: Zero-shot forecasting of complex human-centric systems. (a) Forecasting incidence of Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) and Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) across 31 European countries. Performance is evaluated using the Weighted Interval Score (WIS) relative to a simple quantile baseline provided by RespiCast (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2026), calculated as log2(WISbaseline/WISmodel); values greater than 0 indicate improvement over the baseline. Plots show the median relative WIS (solid lines) and 95% confidence intervals (shaded bands) over 67 rolling evaluation windows (Oct 2024–Jan 2026). In univariate mode (U), Chronos-2 is competitive at short horizons (1 week) against the operational RespiCast Hub-Ensemble (a consensus of mechanistic and statistical models). At longer horizons (> 1 week), Chronos-2 significantly outperforms the ensemble, with in-context learning yielding further gains by exploiting cross-country correlations (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p < 0.001). (b) Joint forecasting of German Consumer Price Index (CPI) components (2021–2025). Performance is measured by the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) relative to a Seasonal Naive baseline, log2(RMSEbaseline/RMSEmodel). While univariate inference (U) performs comparably to robust statistical baselines, enabling in-context learning significantly improves accuracy by leveraging shared structural patterns within CPI groups. Pairwise comparisons (right) confirm that Chronos-2 outperforms the strongest baseline (AutoETS) on the majority of item-window pairs (Wilcoxon signed-rank test p < 0.001 for both 3-month and 12-month horizons).

Figure 3: Evaluation of Chronos-2 on time series forecasting benchmarks (best viewed in color on a screen). Performance is evaluated using the Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) and Scaled/Weighted Quantile Loss (SQL/WQL) for point and probabilistic forecasts, respectively. The Win Rate measures the proportion of pairwise comparisons where a model outperforms competitors, while the Skill Score reflects the average percentage improvement over a Seasonal Naive baseline. Dark purple bars denote Chronos-2 in univariate mode (group attention disabled); light purple segments highlight the performance gain attributed to in-context learning (ICL) via group attention. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals obtained through bootstrapping. (a) Results on fev-bench (n = 100 tasks), a rigorous benchmark where 68 tasks involve multivariate dependencies. Chronos-2 outperforms all baselines, including statistical ensembles, tree-based methods, task-specific deep learning models, and existing foundation models, while maintaining fast inference speed; Wilcoxon signed-rank test p < 10−6 against all baselines (see Tables S4 and S5 in the Appendix for results in tabular format and Table S6 for the p-values). (b) Results on Chronos-Bench-II (n = 27 tasks) and GIFT-Eval (n = 97 tasks), which focus primarily on univariate forecasting. Chronos-2 outperforms or ties state-of-the-art methods; notably, enabling ICL yields performance improvements even in these univariate settings by retrieving patterns across related series. n.s. indicates that the performance difference relative to Chronos-2 is not statistically significant (p ≥ 0.05) based on the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; see Tables S7, S8, S10 and S11 in the Appendix for results in tabular format and Tables S9 and S12 for the p-values.

Box plots show the median (center line), interquartile range (box limits), and 1.5× interquartile range (whiskers); points denote outliers. (b) Representative summer time series at the Monte Bondone site in Italy (IT-MBo), showing observed fluxes (black) and Chronos-2 predictions from the meteorological covariates with 10–90% prediction intervals (red shaded); the corresponding covariates (TA, SW_IN and VPD) are shown below. (c) Rolling one-month-ahead forecasting over the full year 2020. For each evaluation month, models condition on the preceding 12 months of context and predict the subsequent month (step size: 1 month). Bars report normalized RMSE (RMSE divided by the target standard deviation) stratified by prediction month for Chronos-2 and XGBoost, highlighting seasonal variations in predictability across NEE, LE, and H.

Figure 8: Hierarchical forecasting with Chronos-2. (a) Mean and maximum coherence error on the Tourism-Q and Tourism-M datasets for Chronos-2 (U) and Chronos-2 (ICL). Enabling ICL reduces the coherence error on both datasets. (b) Root-level forecasts on Tourism-Q. Solid red line shows the direct forecast generated by the respective models for the root level, while the dashed blue line shows the bottom-up aggregated forecasts. The shaded region shows the coherence gap. Chronos-2 (ICL) produces a narrower gap than Chronos-2 (U) indicating that group attention implicitly learns the aggregation structure. (c) Distribution of per-series scaled quantile loss (SQL) with bottom-up reconciliation on Tourism-Q (left) and Tourism-M (right). Chronos-2 (ICL) achieves the lowest median SQL on both datasets (0.56 and 0.60, respectively), outperforming the end-to-end HierE2E model trained specifically for hierarchical coherence as well as ETS and ARIMA statistical baselines. Methods are ordered by median SQL.

Figure 4: Qualitative analysis of in-context learning (best viewed in color on a screen). Probabilistic forecasts show the 10% to 90% quantile interval; bar charts show SQL forecast errors per time step. (a) Retail sales forecasting: univariate inference versus in-context learning with covariates including promotions, customer traffic, and holiday indicators. Covariates are shown in the lower panels. (b) Regime change: store closure at different positions relative to the forecast horizon. The top and bottom rows show the same series with different forecast origins, so that the closure falls within the forecast horizon (top) or entirely within the historical context (bottom). (c) Scenario analysis with simulated future covariates: promotion intensity (top four panels) and customer count trajectories (bottom panel) varied across hypothetical trajectories. (d) Energy load forecasting: univariate, past-only covariates, and full covariates (air temperature, dew temperature, sea-level pressure). The three rows show progressively more covariate information available to the model.

Figure 2: Generation of multivariate synthetic training data. We generate multivariate synthetic time series by applying random transformation functions to time series sampled from univariate generators. Univariate generators produce diverse temporal patterns to serve as the building blocks for multivariate data. These include: (a.1) KernelSynth (Ansari et al., 2024a), which draws samples from Gaussian processes defined by the random composition of basic kernels (e.g., linear, periodic); (a.2) Trend-Seasonality-Irregularity (TSI), which stochastically combines structural components; and parametric simulations using random (a.3) Autoregressive (AR) and (a.4) Exponential Smoothing (ETS) processes. (b.1) Instantaneous transformations impose coupling between variables without time delays. A mixing function transforms univariate samples at each time step. We employ (b.2) random linear operators (e.g., random dense, sparse, sign or aggregation matrices) and (b.3) non-linear mappings via random Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to simulate complex static dependencies. (c.1) Sequential transformations introduce time-delayed relationships between time series. A random function maps a look-back window of univariate series to multivariate outputs. We generate (c.2) linear lead-lag relationships via a Temporal Causal Model, which samples sparse directed edges across time and variates (simulating Vector Autoregression), while (c.3) non-linear dynamic correlations are introduced via random Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

Figure 7: Rainfall-runoff simulation using Chronos-2. Performance is evaluated using the Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), where a score of 1.0 represents perfect correspondence between simulated and observed discharge. (a) Top: Distribution of NSE scores across 1,582 catchments in the CAMELS-DE dataset. The zero-shot Chronos-2 (ICL) model achieves a median NSE of 0.68, significantly outperforming univariate inference (Chronos-2 (U), NSE=0.15) by leveraging meteorological covariates. While the domain-specific LSTM ensemble achieves higher performance (NSE=0.90), fine-tuning Chronos-2 (FT) bridges this gap, matching state-of-the-art performance without ensembling, access to static attributes, or training on the NSE metric. Box plots show the median (center line), interquartile range (box limits), and 1.5× interquartile range (whiskers). Bottom: Exceedance probability curves showing the cumulative proportion of basins (y-axis) achieving an NSE score greater than or equal to a specific threshold (x-axis). The fine-tuned model closely tracks the reliability profile of the LSTM ensemble. (b) Hydrograph for a single catchment (DE110180) over one year. The zero-shot prediction (top) captures the relationship between rainfall and runoff but exhibits high uncertainty (shaded region denotes 10-90% prediction interval). Fine-tuning (bottom) tightens the predictive distribution, accurately modeling the discharge.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.
authors: Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu, Huiguang He
bullets: Targets the unclear correspondence between MLLM internal criteria and the latent structure of human cognition.
Uses a 66-dimensional semantic space derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out judgments.
Trains models to predict both triplet choices and linguistic rationales grounded in the inferred salient dimension.
Improves consistency with human similarity judgments while retaining competitive multimodal benchmark performance.
Searchlight RSA on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset shows increased model–human representational alignment.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Cortical projection of representational alignment improvements across subjects. The heatmaps visualize the voxel-wise difference in ∆̃RSA(c) scores between the aligned and baseline Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct model. Darker colors indicate better representational alignment between models and human brain. Consistent positive shifts are observed, demonstrating that our alignment framework robustly shifts the MLLMs internal representational geometry to be more human-like.

Figure 1: Overview of triplet-level semantic dimension attribution. (a) Human similarity judgements are collected via crowdsourcing. Then learning a representational embedding space via SPoSE yields the multidimensional mental representations of natural objects. (b) For one triplet, we compute the original softmax probability based on the entire representational embedding for all pairs. We then iteratively prune each dimension from the representational embedding space and compute the changes in softmax probabilities relative to those obtained with the full embedding as the relevance score for that dimension. By sorting these relevance scores in descending order, we establish a hierarchical ranking of dimensional importance. The top-1 dimension yielding the maximum probability change is regarded as the most salient semantic dimension driving the human decision-making.

Figure 3: (a) Overview of hybrid dataset. The total dataset includes three subsets: Single-image (126K samples), Multi-image (102K samples), and Cognitive-Alignment (80K samples). (b) Examples. The examples include Spot the Difference, Image Edit Instruction, Visual Storytelling, LLaVAR, COCO Caption, and Odd-One-Out tasks.

Figure 2: Pipeline for dimension-grounded reasoning enhancement. This pipeline illustrates the process of reasoning enhancement via LLM. For one triplet with their textual descriptions and the most salient semantic dimension d∗ driving human decision-making, we integrate them into the structured prompt Prompt(T , cap(T ), d∗). LLM is then utilized exclusively to enhance reasoning. By injecting the dimension d∗, we guide the LLM to perform targeted reasoning enhancement. This effectively converts discrete cognitive criteria for decision-making into explicit CoT rationale r(d∗).

Figure 5: Stability of alignment shifts across different extraction depths. The cortical projections display the alignment improvements ∆̃RSA(c) of subject 1 computed using features from the last layer, the second-to-last layer, and the concatenation of the last four layers. Darker regions reflect better alignment improvement. The spatial distribution of these positive shifts remains consistent regardless of the extraction depth, confirming that the achieved representational alignment with human cognition is robust and not a selective layer choice.
Figure 6: Comparison of choicebased RSMs between Qwen2.5-VL7B and human.

papers.abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl
authors: Zhuguanyu Wu, Congjia Chen, Ruihao Gong, Yang Yong, Shiqiao Gu, Yi Xu, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Few-step flow models require stochastic denoising transitions for policy optimization, but existing coefficient-preserving constructions do not specify which policy to choose.
Geo-FSRL selects the admissible isotropic Gaussian policy minimizing conditional KL divergence under velocity-output updates.
This criterion reduces to a scalar geometry factor that also controls velocity-space Fisher information and transition log-likelihood-ratio variance.
The method derives a unique closed-form transition optimizer and timestep-dependent policy-gradient and KL weights through gradient-scale matching.
Experiments report higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image and video generation models in the 4-step setting; inference retains the deterministic solver.

papers.abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.
authors: Lorenzo Mazza, Ariel Rodriguez, Stefanie Speidel
bullets: Addresses the costly, hard-to-repeat, and hardware-dependent nature of surgical data collection.
Supports configurable robot and sensor streams through ROS and ROS2 middleware.
Combines operator-facing acquisition, processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation.
Evaluated across 1,516 recordings spanning phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments, with preliminary usability feedback.

papers.abstract: This paper extends an existing framework for the coordination of mobile agents in unknown worlds, by considering the possibility of dynamic instability. In the original problem, known as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) (arXiv:2512.09495), the multi-agent system must establish a communication network which completely covers an initially unknown constrained space. However, the POCGAGP fails to account for the unpredictability often seen in real-world deployment. To address this, the dynamic case (DPOCGAGP) introduces two settings which can influence the mobile network during deployment: Agent Loss and World Change, which represent dynamic changes to the world. Within this study, we present advancements to two state-of-the-art algorithms, the Centralized Agent-Directed Exploration for Network Coverage (CADENCE), and its decentralized analogue, DADENCE, to provide solutions in these cases. We then compare their performance against another state-of-the-art benchmark algorithm, and show that the adapted algorithms outperform across our benchmark test set, which comprises over 4500 test cases of varied size and structure.
authors: Hugo Gandhi, Edwin Meriaux, Antonio Lor\'ia
bullets: Extends the POCGAGP framework to dynamic settings called DPOCGAGP.
Models two disruptions: Agent Loss and World Change.
Adapts CADENCE and DADENCE for dynamic network coverage.
Evaluates the methods on more than 4,500 varied benchmark cases.
Reports that both adapted algorithms outperform a state-of-the-art benchmark across the test set.

papers.abstract: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.
authors: Jose Miguel Ramos, Luis SaCouto, Andreas Wichert
bullets: Binary sparse representations aim to combine biological energy efficiency with useful information retention.
Existing approaches span efficient-coding theory, backpropagation-trained deep models, and local Hebbian methods.
The proposed metrics treat information preservation as similarity preservation: how well codes retain the input data’s relational geometry.
Across four methods under matched conditions, greater information preservation generally comes with reduced sparsity.
Competitive Sparse Codes uniquely achieve near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information, though balancing both goals remains unresolved.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Conceptual framework for the results that follow, sparsity and information preservation define two axes along which each method’s codes can be positioned. The high-sparsity, high-information quadrant (top right) is the desired outcome the central hypothesis holds is difficult to reach; the low-sparsity, low-information quadrant (bottom left) is trivial and uninteresting. The two off-diagonal quadrants represent the trade-off itself, sparsity gained at the cost of information, or information retained at the cost of sparsity.

Figure 8: Entropy versus the average of the two Structure Preservation variants shown above. The dashed lines mark example thresholds for what counts as sufficiently high sparsity and information preservation, added to make the comparison with the quadrant framework introduced above easier to see. Under this choice of thresholds, only CSC reaches the desired quadrant, and only at the highest entropy values within its range.

Figure 2: Entropy achieved by each method, against the random-sparse-code reference ceiling (RSC). CSC-G reaches entropy close to the RSC ceiling both consistently and tightly, while CSC-R reaches a similar ceiling only in its best configurations, with substantially more variation across the rest of its range. Dictionary Learning, GAE, and Random Projections all trail behind the ceiling, with different levels of deviation: Dictionary Learning is consistently high with little variation, while Random Projections shows much higher variation, and GAE displays a bimodal spread.

Figure 6: Entropy versus kNN Accuracy (K = 30), across all evaluated configurations. CSC-G is the strongest performer overall, consistently at or above the pixel-space baseline. Contrary to expectation, kNN Accuracy appears to increase with entropy across most methods rather than decline.

Figure 1: Per-neuron average activation fraction across 1000 samples with 1024-bit code and 16 active bits, for three example codes at increasing entropy. At low entropy (0.601), a small number of neurons fire far more often than the rest, producing sharp spikes against an otherwise near-silent population. At high entropy (0.899), this unevenness is much reduced. At entropy close to the ceiling (0.998), activation is almost perfectly flat across the entire population, closely matching what uniform usage of the code space looks like in practice.

Figure 3: Per-model distribution of Class Overlap Separation, Nearest-Class Impostor Margin, Structure Preservation (Euclidean and Cosine), and kNN Accuracy, summarising the results above independently of entropy.

Figure 5: Entropy versus Class Overlap Separation and Nearest-Class Impostor Margin, across all evaluated configurations. GAE achieves the highest values on both metrics overall, though its configurations split into two clusters reflecting its bimodal entropy distribution, with the lower-entropy cluster reaching higher values on both similarity preservation metrics. DL and RP remain confined to comparatively low bands with little apparent dependence on entropy within their own ranges. Within the same entropy values, CSC-R and GAE perform relatively similarly on both COS and NIM, contrary to what the univariable analysis suggested, with CSC remaining able to push further beyond the 0.9 entropy threshold at a slight cost to similarity preservation.
Figure 7: Structure Preservation against Entropy, computed separately using Euclidean (left) and Cosine (right) pixel-space distance.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates energy-efficient binary sparse representations and information preservation, relevant to the broad efficient-AI interest in reducing energy and computational cost.
papers.title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
papers.tldr: The paper introduces metrics for evaluating binary sparse codes by jointly measuring sparsity and preservation of input-space relationships, revealing a persistent trade-off between the two.

papers.abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.
authors: Jie Liu, Nicola Bastianello, Wenying Xu, Daniel W. C. Ho
bullets: Addresses neighborhood convergence caused by stochastic-gradient noise in decentralized optimization with local updates.
Uses variance reduction in a primal-dual framework with stepsizes independent of network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates.
Provides the first expected linear-convergence guarantee for strongly convex decentralized optimization with multiple stochastic-gradient updates, according to the authors.
Communicates only one variable per round, halving communication relative to gradient-tracking methods.
Experiments show faster convergence and higher accuracy, though the stated guarantee is for the strongly convex setting.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) embodies a foundational paradigm for sequential decision-making in the face of uncertainty. The rapid growth of model complexity in emerging applications has significantly amplified the challenges of achieving data-efficient RL, particularly in sample-starved scenarios where data collection may be costly, time-consuming, or even high-stakes. Consequently, understanding and improving the data efficiency of RL algorithms has become a central problem of both fundamental theoretical interest and practical importance. Despite decades of research, the statistical underpinnings of RL remained remarkably underdeveloped until relatively recently, particularly in the finite-sample regimes most relevant to modern practice. Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.
authors: Yuxin Chen, Yuejie Chi, Jianqing Fan, Gen Li, Yuting Wei, Yuling Yan
bullets: Focuses on sample-starved RL, where data collection is costly, time-consuming, or high-stakes.
Studies tabular Markov decision processes under generative-model, online, and offline sampling.
Covers both model-based and model-free approaches through non-asymptotic sample-complexity analysis.
Emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithms, including methods designed to avoid substantial burn-in costs.
Also discusses extensions including robust, multi-agent, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

papers.abstract: How to reuse a pretrained locomotion policy for precise loco-manipulation is still an open problem. We propose an online method to learn the closed-loop dynamics under a frozen locomotion policy. The learned model predicts floating-base motion and improves loco-manipulation accuracy. However, unobserved latent conditions of the policy introduce heterogeneous responses, meaning that the same observed state will lead to different motions. Direct learning without accounting for this heterogeneity introduces bias and fluctuations into dynamics estimates, degrading floating-base prediction and end-effector tracking. To address this problem, a contaminated Gaussian model is proposed to approximate the effects of latent conditions. The model uses two Gaussian components to approximate predictable and unpredictable responses under the same observed state. Then, the contaminated Gaussian model is combined with a Gaussian process to construct an online learner using random Fourier features (RFFs). The learner estimates each response's probability of belonging to the predictable component and uses it to weight online updates, capturing predictable responses while reducing bias and fluctuations caused by heterogeneous observations. With consistent and unbiased dynamics estimates, model predictive control (MPC) predicts floating-base motion accurately and enables precise loco-manipulation. A finite-sample error bound is established to ensure uniform convergence in online learning. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate consistent end-effector tracking across different manipulator configurations and tasks, with errors of 0.01 m.
authors: Tianlin Zhang, Weipeng Xia, Lingwei Zhang, Yiyang Shao, Zhongyu Li, Yun-Hui Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reusing pretrained locomotion policies for accurate loco-manipulation.
Uses a contaminated Gaussian model to separate predictable and unpredictable responses caused by unobserved policy conditions.
Combines this model with a Gaussian process and random Fourier features for online, probability-weighted dynamics updates.
Integrates the learned dynamics with model predictive control to improve floating-base and end-effector tracking.
Simulation and hardware experiments achieve consistent tracking across manipulator configurations and tasks, with 0.01 m errors; a finite-sample error bound supports uniform convergence.

papers.abstract: Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by the scarcity of diverse, robot-executable data and by the difficulty of jointly learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control. We present Movens-5M, constructed from raw Internet videos through clip generation, quality filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery, and physical refinement with humanoid retargeting and execution verification. It contains 15 million human-motion sequences and 5 million physically executable humanoid-motion sequences spanning over 10,000 hours, aligned with text, RGB video, speech, and music. Building on this data, we introduce Movens-Zero, a scalable understanding-generation-execution architecture that supports joint learning across modalities and real-time closed-loop execution. Task-mixed flow-matching training jointly optimizes a single action expert across seven generation tasks, enabling direct motion generation from text, speech, music, and video. Multimodal Real-Time Chunking connects overlapping chunks under continuously updated instructions and robot states for continuous closed-loop execution. We further introduce Movens-Intent, a four-track benchmark with 8,192 expert-verified condition-motion pairs across text, speech, music, and video. Experiments show consistent gains across all four modalities when scaling execution-verified data from 1% to 100% and action-expert capacity from 64M to 911M parameters, while demonstrating that data quality and cross-modal supervision improve generation and execution.
authors: Wendong Bu, Tinghong Ye, Qizhou Wang, Jiacheng Li, Zhiqi Ge, Yuze Lin, Zhongqi Yue, Yi Su, Jingyu Wang, Kai Shen, Jingdong Liu, Chengyuan Deng, Xiaoxuan Chen, Xin Tan, Jiaming Ji, Wenqiao Zhang, Chenghong Jiang, Tuoyu Li, Siliang Tang, Jun Xiao, Tat-Seng Chua, Yueting Zhuang, Xingxing Wang, Juncheng Li

Enables continuous control through Multimodal Real-Time Chunking, which adapts overlapping motion chunks to updated instructions and robot states.
Results show improved generation and execution as verified data and action-expert capacity scale; Movens-Intent provides a four-track benchmark across text, speech, music, and video.

papers.abstract: LLM-based robotic agent systems can generate programs for robot control, yet their generalization to new tasks often depends on elaborate scaffolding. Expanding their skill repertoires alone offers limited guidance on how to assess new capabilities or identify what remains beyond their reach. We introduce META-Robot, a framework that couples self cognition with capability scaling by expanding the criteria through which an agent evaluates and develops its skills. At its core, action-level predicates make execution outcomes explicit and available for LLM reasoning. The agent uses these assessments to identify its own limitations, extend relevant evaluation criteria, and guide the structured expansion of its skills. Proprioceptive feedback further grounds this process in the robot's physical state, enriching the evidence available for self-cognition. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate stronger overall task performance, generalization to new tasks, continued expansion of skills and evaluation criteria, and effective use of non-visual proprioceptive signals.
authors: Xuanzhi Feng, Zeyu Liu, Weiheng Gao, Xinchen Li, Jiankun Tang, Fangqi Zhu, Quanxin Shou, Hao Chen, Zhengyang Yan, Hualei Zhang, Junhao Li, Zhiyao Wu, Jie Zhang, Song Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generalizing to new tasks without relying on elaborate scaffolding.

Experiments in simulation and on real robots show improved task performance, task generalization, skill and criterion expansion, and effective use of non-visual signals.

figures.caption: Figure 1: META-Robot starts from a task description. Its framework consists of three components: (1) Loop Execution Agent, which generates programs and predicates, evaluates execution evidence, and repairs failures; (2) Proprioceptive Signal Orchestration, which supplements insufficient visual observations with physical feedback; and (3) coupled Predicate and Skill Libraries, which consolidate validated criteria and repairs for cognitive and capability scaling.

Figure 2: META-Robot Loop Execution Agent. Given a task description, the agent (1) decomposes it into executable subtasks and initial conditions; (2) jointly generates the task program and action-level predicates; (3) executes each skill while collecting task-relevant evidence; (4) evaluates predicate transitions to determine whether execution should continue or be repaired; (5) locally corrects and re-executes the failed skill, missing evidence routine, or verification check; and (6) performs system-level repair and full-task validation, consolidating validated predicates and skills for reuse. This procedure is repeated to form a closed execution–evaluation–repair loop.

Figure 3: Proprioceptive Signal Orchestration Mechanism Example: in thin-towel grasping, torque change provides a contact cue, while gripper feedback and a lift check verify successful acquisition to complement insufficient visual evidence during execution and verification. Validated signal usage is then consolidated into a reusable skill together with corresponding action predicates, jointly expanding sensing, execution, and verification capabilities

papers.abstract: Simulation benchmarks score robot policies by success rate, and every failed episode counts against the policy. Many of these failures are the simulator's fault, not the policy's; we find the cause and fix it. Testing a vision language action model and a world action model in simulation, we find that the policy often places the object and the simulator then ejects it, and that the benchmark's own scripted demonstrations fail the same way. We present SimuGuard, an auditing plugin for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa and RoboDojo. It leaves the evaluation unchanged. At every physics step, it records the state and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and it reruns the episode with one simulation parameter changed. With it we trace these episodes on RoboTwin to the collision detection of the physics engine: for geometry one to two centimeters apart, the engine reports a penetration of about two centimeters, and the solver throws the object out at several meters per second. The cause is one constant: the distance algorithm discards triangles below a fixed area threshold, which valid triangles fall below at the centimeter scale. With that constant changed and nothing else, episodes with an artifact fall from 12 in 100 to none, and the success rate on five container tasks rises from 89% to 98%. Success rates in simulation thus count failures that the simulator causes. Benchmarks on PhysX 5.3.1 or earlier should rerun in a repaired engine. Where the engine cannot change, they should report the success rate together with the range it spans when every flagged episode fails or passes: 75.8% to 98.5% around a reported 83.1% for LingBot-VA.
authors: Alex Zhou, Junhao Wu, Xueyang Zhou, Yixiao Huo, Hongcheng Gao, Di Zhu, Zhenghao Zhang, Yongchao Chen

On RoboTwin, the artifact traces to a physics-engine distance algorithm that discards valid small triangles, producing false penetrations and high-speed object ejection.
Changing this constant alone reduced artifact episodes from 12/100 to 0 and raised success on five container tasks from 89% to 98%.
Benchmarks using PhysX 5.3.1 or earlier should be rerun; otherwise, report success-rate ranges reflecting flagged episodes that could either fail or pass.

papers.selection_reason: Auditing contact artifacts in simulated robot benchmarks; technically meaningful for evaluating robot policies and improving simulation reliability.
papers.title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks
papers.tldr: SimuGuard shows that contact-detection artifacts can cause simulated robot failures and provides an audit-and-repair workflow that substantially improves reported benchmark success rates.

papers.abstract: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.
bullets: Addresses Transformer KV-cache growth and the limited addressability of fixed-state State Space Models.
Uses multiple complex-diagonal dynamical memory units with input-dependent leak rates to encode sequences.
A decoder attends to memory outputs rather than the full token history; recurrence supports O(T) work and O(log T) parallel depth.
Matches Transformer closely in language modeling, outperforms both baselines on several cognitive tasks, and remains behind Mamba on language modeling.
Shows stronger selective-copy length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer; performance has task-dependent limitations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture combining dynamical systems with attention to achieve constant cost attention and efficient memory retention.
papers.title: Dynamical Memory Transformer: Selective Recurrent Memories with Constant Cost Attention
papers.tldr: Dynamical Memory Transformer combines selective recurrent memories with attention-based reading to provide fixed-size inference state and efficient long-context processing.

papers.abstract: Inserting an unseen part requires sub-millimetre precision and the correct orientation of keyed features. Current zero-shot agentic manipulation methods built on vision-language models (VLMs) produce spatial outputs that are far too coarse for this. We propose to let a VLM build a sketch model of the task, i.e., a few geometric primitives and two mate frames, which a VLM agent measures with geometric tools in multi-view depth and which a standard planner and compliant controller execute. Because a sketch describes the parts independently of their placement, the robot needs to build it only once per task. A sketch memory stores each agent run and transfers the stored sketch to later placements by point-cloud registration, so that the VLM is called only for unfamiliar parts. After grasping the part, the robot inspects both mating faces at close range and corrects the sketch by shape matching. On 69 simulated insertion episodes, our method inserts 88% of the parts at the assembled pose in a strict kinematic test, while ReKep and MOKA with the same VLM insert none. On new placements of eight tasks, reusing one stored run inserts as many parts as calling the agent in each episode, and it produces the sketch in 3.4 s instead of about 90 s.
bullets: Targets sub-millimetre insertion of keyed parts, where existing VLM-based agents produce overly coarse spatial outputs.
A VLM builds a task sketch with geometric primitives and mate frames; geometric tools, a standard planner, and compliant control execute it.
The robot refines the sketch by inspecting mating faces at close range and shape-matching them after grasping.
A sketch memory transfers prior sketches to new placements via point-cloud registration, invoking the VLM only for unfamiliar parts.
In 69 simulated episodes, SketchMate achieved 88% strict-kinematic insertion versus 0% for ReKep and MOKA; reuse matched fresh agent calls while reducing sketch creation from about 90 s to 3.4 s.

papers.title: SketchMate: Agentic Geometric Reasoning for Zero-Shot Precision Insertion
papers.tldr: SketchMate uses VLM-generated geometric sketches, tool-based measurement, and sketch reuse to enable fast, zero-shot precision insertion of unseen parts.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly capable of understanding images and performing complex visual reasoning, suggesting the possibility of using them to automate biological image analysis. This need is becoming increasingly urgent as advances in technology continue to generate ever larger and more diverse microscopy datasets, already exceeding the scale at which manual visual analysis is feasible. With the final aim to use MLLMs for visual comparison of complex phenotypes, we investigate a very simple baseline: comparison of the size of body parts in synthetic images of ants. We find that state-of-the-art open-weight MLLMs fail for some body parts, but not for others, even though the comparison itself is visually trivial for all of them. We evaluate different in-context learning strategies and analyze performance on the related object recognition task. Our results suggest a recognition-driven grounding failure: structures that the models cannot recognize are instead associated with a recognizable semantic concept, impairing the grounding and comparison of both. Further analysis of the vision encoder is consistent with the hypothesis that fine-grained visual structure may be less well preserved without semantic support. Together, our results reveal a surprising limitation of current MLLMs: semantic recognition can gate simple visual comparisons that do not intrinsically require semantic understanding. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/kreshuklab/Open-Weight-MLLMs-Cannot-Compare-What-They-Cannot-Name
bullets: The study tests MLLM comparison of ant body-part sizes in synthetic images, motivated by scalable biological image analysis.
Models succeed on some parts but fail on others despite equivalent visual comparison difficulty.
In-context learning strategies and a related object-recognition task are evaluated.
Results suggest recognition-driven grounding failure: unrecognized structures are mapped to familiar concepts, impairing comparison.
Vision-encoder analysis supports the possibility that fine-grained structure is poorly preserved without semantic support.

papers.abstract: Accurate BEV map prediction is a critical component of autonomous driving systems, enabling downstream planning and control. Recent approaches such as Mask2Map achieve strong performance by predicting vectorized, instance-level map elements directly from multi-view images. However, existing BEV map prediction models operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, despite the fact that traffic participants frequently occlude or implicitly encode information about road geometry. In this work, we propose a multitask architecture that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects, explicitly enabling information exchange between the two tasks. Building upon Mask2Map, we introduce an object detection branch and incorporate cross-task feature fusion at both the BEV feature level and the instance-query level via deformable attention and cross-attention mechanisms. This design allows map instances to leverage object context while remaining robust to occlusions caused by traffic participants. Experimental results on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with particularly significant gains of 21% mAP in scenes containing heavy object occlusion.

papers.abstract: Camera localization methods are mostly multi-stage pipelines relying on dedicated and complex maps that are costly to construct, store, and maintain over time. Alternatively, well-structured maps that organize scenes with compact yet expressive primitives are often readily available, providing rich structural and semantic cues that humans can interpret. However, their potential for direct camera localization remains largely unexplored due to the significant modality gap between map primitives and visual observations. This motivates a new concept for localization, which estimates camera poses by grounding query observations to map primitives. In this paper, we instantiate the concept in the context of planar primitives with PGGT, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer network. Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the network is trained to predict multiple localization targets for feed-forward 6-DoF camera localization that generalizes to unseen environments. With this straightforward and scalable architecture, our method pushes the state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models. The code and models are available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/PGGT-Loc
authors: Hanqiao Ye, Yuzhou Liu, Mengqi Rong, Jian Liu, Yangdong Liu, Shuhan Shen
bullets: Addresses the cost and maintenance burden of dedicated, complex localization maps.
Uses a Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer to bridge visual observations and planar map primitives.
Predicts multiple localization targets in a feed-forward architecture that generalizes to unseen environments.
Reports state-of-the-art localization performance on dense surface maps and minimal layout models.
Code and models are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.
authors: Anastasiia Prutianova, Alina Bogdanova, Mikhail Shutov, Dmitrii Poimanov, Anatoly Gorkov, Ilia Zharikov
bullets: Addresses performance degradation from aggressive VQ compression and the limits of training-free, layer-wise reconstruction.
Uses straight-through estimation with trainable latent weights to support gradient-based optimization under discrete quantization.
Applies block-wise knowledge distillation to balance quantization quality and training efficiency, with practical training accelerations.
Is compatible with modern VQ schemes and achieves strong low-bit post-training quantization quality with a modest budget.
Reports near-lossless 2-bit quantization of LLaMA2-70B, with a 1% accuracy drop on popular question-answering benchmarks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. This figure illustrates the proposed TVQ method, applied to a single linear layer with the weight matrix W . During optimization, these matrices are updated: the indices matrix I, the weight matrix W , and (optionally) the codebook C. TVQ involves three main operations: I is calculated according to (3); The dequantized weight matrix W q is gathered from C and I according to (2) and used to calculate the loss function; The gradients of the loss are propagated from W q to W and C, W (and optionally C) is updated with gradient descent. After training, only the compressed representation consisting of C and I is stored and used for inference instead of the original weight matrix.

papers.abstract: Tabular transformer models such as TabPFN achieve strong predictive performance but incur substantial inference costs, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained settings. While looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing, they can lose significant predictive power when stopped early. To address this challenge, we introduce the Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer (ElTab), a single model trained to operate across different computational budgets through supervision at randomly sampled early exits. Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, a single ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs. These results show that elastic-depth training yields a single model that adapts to the deployment budget at hand, offering a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computational cost.
authors: Mieszko Komisarczyk, Saurabh Mathur, Maurice Kraus, Sriraam Natarajan, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of tabular transformers in resource-constrained deployments.
Uses shared weights with supervision at randomly sampled early exits to support multiple computational depths.
Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half.
Matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs.
Provides a deployment-flexible trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computation.

Averaging over budgets reflects deploying one model at every budget, including those it was not trained for. Datasets are sorted by ElTab’s gain over the mean of the six fixed-depth models. ElTab matches or outperforms all six fixed-depth models on 28 of 30 datasets. Its gains are largest where the fixed-depth models depend most on their training depth, such as mfeat-fourier and MiceProtein.

Each fixed-depth model comes close to TabPFN at its own budget, even below TabPFN’s compute, but drops sharply when run at any other budget. A single ElTab model (blue) stays close to TabPFN across budgets, matching it to within 0.27 points while using 25% fewer FLOPs.

Figure 2: ElTab architecture. ElTab predicts the labels of query rows from a labeled context using three components. An embedder (Eψ) turns the table into token representations. A shared stack of Transformer blocks (Fθ) then refines these representations and can be applied repeatedly, up to L times. Finally, a decoder (gϕ) turns the refined query representations into class probabilities. Because ElTab is trained to predict after every loop, it can stop after any loop M ≤ L, letting the deployment choose how much compute to spend. All loops share the same weights and decoder.

papers.abstract: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. We reproduce three representative state-of-the-art extraction methods and find that, on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 accessed through the standard chat-completions interface, all three return zero CoT tokens. The failure is structural rather than a bug: the reasoning field is absent, named tool selection is rejected, free-text scratchpad arguments are filtered, and no replayable reasoning block is exposed. We therefore take a different route. We present RECAST, a reconstruction-based framework that conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer, reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, cleans it, and builds SFT-ready data. To the best of our knowledge, RECAST is the first system to reconstruct CoT from frontier closed models such as Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 without using hidden reasoning channels. We instantiate RECAST on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 and additionally obtain successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3 with the same answer-only protocol. The system is open-source and packaged as an agent skill: one prompt deploys it and runs the complete pipeline to produce SFT-ready CoT data. This preprint describes the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation; it does not claim large-scale benchmark improvements.
authors: Qi Wang, Kang Xu, Chengcheng Wan, Jiangtao Wang
bullets: Existing CoT extraction methods fail on Claude-Sonnet-5.5’s standard chat interface because reasoning fields, tool calls, scratchpads, and replayable blocks are inaccessible or filtered.
RECAST conditions a decoder on the original question and target model answer to generate and clean a first-person structured rationale.
The framework produces SFT-ready CoT data and is packaged as an open-source agent skill with an end-to-end deployment prompt.
The authors report successful qualitative reconstructions on Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 using an answer-only protocol.
The preprint presents controlled artifact validation and does not claim large-scale benchmark gains.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an opinionated set of ten desiderata intended to inform the design and evaluation of reinforcement-learning agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime. We use these desiderata to examine a representative selection of existing approaches. Progress on individual desiderata is valuable, but the longer-term aim should be to integrate all ten within a single agent. To our knowledge, no published evaluation has yet provided evidence for such an integration. Likewise, the representative benchmarks we review probe different parts of this target, but separate evaluations do not establish that the corresponding properties coexist within one agent throughout a continuing lifetime. As a secondary contribution, we therefore present a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion to the desiderata and outline a proposed benchmark that examines a broad range of associated behavioral capabilities together within one such lifetime.
authors: Nis Meinert, Jakob Gawlikowski, Edward Grant, Max Cyprys, Nathan Schurr, Neil Boston, Alfredo Ibias, Milind Tambe, Janusz Marecki
bullets: Proposes ten desiderata for designing and evaluating agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime.
Reviews representative approaches and benchmarks, finding that they typically address only subsets of the desiderata.
Emphasizes that progress on individual properties does not show they coexist within a single agent over time.
Introduces a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion and outlines a broader integrated benchmark.
No published evaluation is identified as demonstrating all ten desiderata together in one agent.

For the behavioral columns, indicates that a dedicated protocol or readout directly probes the property; indicates incomplete component coverage or indirect or confounded evidence; indicates that the property is not probed. The system-level desiderata D3–D5 are omitted.

The mapping is not one-to-one: D6 and D7 overlap in the same lifetime situation, while the salty-bean situations couple retention and credit under D6, prediction under D8, and evaluation under D9. These proposed readouts provide the basis for the companion’s coverage ratings in Table 1.

papers.tldr: Continual reinforcement learning should be evaluated as an integrated lifelong-agent problem rather than as a collection of isolated capabilities.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $\rho$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.
authors: Miha Kap\v{s}, Bla\v{z} Bertalani\v{c}, Carolina Fortuna
bullets: DFA, DRTP, and NoProp were adapted to 1D convolutional architectures and systematically evaluated across 112 UCR datasets.
Their mean F1 scores were 0.76–0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84).
Intra-class temporal variability was the property most consistently linked to the performance gap versus InceptionTime.
Pooling results suggest near-random convolutional features for DFA and DRTP, while NoProp preserved feature learning more effectively.
DRTP cut training FLOPs by 33% and helped mainly on series longer than about 700 steps; NoProp cut peak memory by 38% but took 48% longer to train.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Architectures of models used in this study. (a) Architecture shared by BP, DFA, and DRTP, consisting of convolutional modules followed by fully connected layers. (b) Architecture of a NoProp block, in which the input X is processed through a convolutional stream, while the previous latent state zt−1 is processed through a residual fully connected stream. The two streams are concatenated and passed through shared layers.

papers.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.
authors: Markus Gallacher, Vu Anh Minh Le, Matteo Trobinger, Davide Vecchia, Carlo Alberto Boano, Gian Pietro Picco
bullets: Wearer-induced NLOS from the human body can substantially degrade UWB ranging but remains understudied.
The work evaluates machine-learning and lightweight radio link-indicator classifiers, and proposes hybrid methods combining both.
Performance—including ranging impact from misclassification—varies substantially across channels and PHY settings.
Energy costs differ sharply: some methods provide only marginal accuracy gains while using up to 39.6× more energy.
A recommender tool helps select classifiers under user-defined accuracy, runtime, and energy constraints; the dataset and tool are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Cultural value alignment requires not only model optimization but also a well-specified target grounded in real-human evidence. Yet how such targets should be grounded in human data remains largely unexplored, raising three fundamental questions: (1) whose values should be represented? (2) where should cultural values be observed? and (3) what signals reveal underlying values? We investigate these questions through Re3Culture, a large-scale dataset linking (i) Representative communities: 700+ human participants across four cultures recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling; (ii) Realistic scenario: culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, e.g., family and kinship; and (iii) Revealed value signals: 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioral principles and explicit value priorities with responses for 6,000+ situated questions. Our analysis shows why these choices matter for defining the target, with three implications. First, estimating cultural values requires both community affiliation and broad internal coverage. Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates. LLM simulations also disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Second, values must be observed in concrete, community-guided situations. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and communities differ in which scenarios they identify as culturally value-revealing. Third, value priorities should be elicited explicitly, not learned from response preferences or bottom-line answers alone. Preferences conflate value agreement with other response-level qualities, and similar answers can be derived from different value priorities. By addressing these requirements, Re3Culture provides the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.
authors: Jing Yao, Hyunjin Hwang, Weihua Zheng, Bryan Chen Zhengyu Tan, Jia Wang Peh, Dylan Raharja, JinYeong Bak, Roy Ka-Wei Lee, Rui Cao, Yuki Arase, Jacki O'Neill, Zhicheng Dou, Xing Xie, Xiaoyuan Yi, Furu Wei
bullets: Studies three target-definition questions: whose values to represent, where to observe them, and which signals reveal them.

Finds that community affiliation and broad subgroup coverage affect estimated cultural values; LLM simulations can overrepresent specific subgroups.
Shows that concrete, community-guided scenarios reveal situated priorities better than abstract profiles.
Argues that explicit value elicitation is necessary because response preferences and similar answers can mask different underlying priorities.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.
authors: Kathrin Korte, Christian Metzner, Akshay Bedhotiya, Viet Anh Khoa Tran, Eleni Nisioti, Sebastian Risi
bullets: Task similarity, data-change rate, and presentation order can refer to different levels of the learning setup.
Partitioning the same data trajectory at different granularities changes measured continual-learning outcomes.
Changing presentation order or the underlying data’s similarity structure also affects results.
A review of representative benchmarks finds that these properties are often not fully specified.
For models with undisclosed pretraining data, underlying-data properties are embedded in the model’s initial state.

Its lifetime scope is the breadth of experience the stream covers as a whole, of which only the past is available to it and the future is unobserved. (b) The same stream under a single partition. Similarity is defined for every pair of tasks and computable from the data once the boundaries are fixed. What a learner retains of each task is a separate quantity (Sec. 2.3). (c–e) A teacher–student stream in which the teacher’s weights follow a fixed trajectory, with the student trained on tasks sampled along it. Reversing the stream reverses the profile of retained error across it, and shuffling removes its structure. papers.abstract: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360{\deg} multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360{\deg} multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Resources: https://github.com/cvims/WorkIng
authors: Xujun Xie, Dominik R\"o{\ss}le, Adithya Mohan, Daniel Cremers, Torsten Sch\"on

Evaluations span 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning architectures.
Results indicate real-world data is the main performance driver, while scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves performance across tasks.
The benchmark targets work-zone geometry and regulatory diversity missing from existing datasets.
