papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal in-context learning (MICL) arises from tasks that are ill-defined without context and require uncovering the underlying rules from demonstrations. Existing methods predominantly treat MICL as direct input-output mapping, overlooking the importance of explicitly inducing and reasoning over such rules, limiting both performance and interpretability. We propose ERIM, Explicit Rule-Induction for Multimodal In-Context Learning, a unified framework that enhances MICL by explicitly inducing the latent rules governing demonstration samples. Leveraging the reasoning ability of multi-modal large language model (MLLM), ERIM constructs rule-centric MICL datasets, introduces explicit supervision for rule induction, and fine-tunes MLLM to perform explicit rule-induction via a two-stage training strategy that combines mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show consistent performance improvements across diverse MICL settings and demonstrate that correctly inducing underlying rules directly leads to stronger and more stable performance.
authors: Yuquan Li, Xinyang Jiang, Yuhao Xue, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Addresses ill-defined MICL tasks whose solutions depend on uncovering rules from examples.
Uses multimodal large language models to construct rule-centric data and provide explicit rule-induction supervision.
Trains models in two stages with mixed cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Experiments across diverse MICL settings show consistent gains and more stable performance.
The approach focuses on settings where latent rules can be inferred from demonstrations.

The model is trained with a two-stage strategy that combines mixed supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, enabling robust induction and application of underlying rules from context.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ERIM, a framework for multimodal in-context learning that explicitly induces and reasons over latent rules using MLLMs.
papers.title: Multimodal In-Context Learning with Explicit Rule Induction
papers.tldr: ERIM improves multimodal in-context learning by explicitly inducing the hidden rules behind demonstrations rather than relying only on input-output matching.

papers.abstract: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.
authors: Mo Shahdloo, Faegheh Sardari, Mathew Salvaris
bullets: Addresses the loss of spatial and fine-grained visual information caused by text-only communication between modular VLMs and SLMs.
Uses a lightweight codec with a domain encoder mapping VLM states into the SLM embedding space and a LoRA-based attention decoder for visual prefixes.
Trains only about 1.6M parameters, or 0.2% of the combined model size, while keeping both models frozen.
Reports higher performance than matched text-communication baselines on CLEVR, GQA, and Flickr8k.
Demonstrates compatibility across models with different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

papers.selection_reason: Latent-space communication between VLM and SLM for visual perception, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
papers.tldr: Latent-Lens enables a frozen vision-language model and frozen small language model to exchange visual information through latent states rather than lossy text, substantially improving visual task performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.
authors: Matthias Busch, Marius Tacke, Tamadur Albaraghtheh, Sviatlana V. Lamaka, Mikhail L. Zheludkevich, Roland C. Aydin, Christian Feiler, Christian J. Cyron
bullets: Seven frontier LLMs were evaluated on four molecular-property datasets against classical baselines trained on the same molecules.
After contamination screening, three datasets were clean; ESOL was largely memorized by the models and used for comparison.
On clean datasets, all LLMs improved with more context, and the best model surpassed every baseline with 30 examples.
Self-reported uncertainty weakly ranked errors, reaching Spearman correlations of up to 0.46—similar to baseline uncertainty.
On memorized ESOL, context brought no improvement and models reported lower uncertainty for molecules whose values they recalled.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs for molecular property prediction and uncertainty estimation, demonstrating in-context learning capabilities.
papers.title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
papers.tldr: LLMs can predict molecular properties effectively from in-context examples, but their self-reported uncertainty only weakly indicates when they are wrong.

papers.abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.
authors: Yukiya Horiba, Hakaze Cho, Takahiro Yakoh
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding of task vectors as seemingly atomized steering directions.
Uses candidate-label unembeddings to formulate a TR/TL/residual decomposition and Bayesian optimization of component coefficients.
Evaluates the approach across multiple model families, classification tasks, and instruction- or demonstration-based task vectors.
The optimized TR/TL interventions outperform original task vectors, with especially reliable gains for instruction-based vectors.
Component-specific interventions produce distinct logit effects consistent with their intended functional roles.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our approach. (a) TR and TL capture complementary aspects of in-context learning. In a narrow sense, TR processing finds the label candidates like “Positive” and “Negative”, and TL find which label should be output in the candidates. (b) We decompose a TV into TR, TL, and residual components. (c) Optimizing the TR/TL coefficients improves task performance.
Figure 3: Effects of isolated TR and TL component interventions on the TR- and TL-related logit metrics.

Figure 2: Accuracy gain over the original TV on the optimization set across Transformer layers. Each cell shows the change in accuracy (percentage points) after TR/TL-based optimization; red and blue indicate improvement and degradation, respectively. All Transformer layers are shown.
Figure 5: Accuracy gains over original TV on JF-ICR.
Figure 4: Accuracy gains over the original TV using TR/TL and random search axes.

papers.selection_reason: Decomposes task vectors into interpretable components for LLM steering, offering a method for controllable intervention.
papers.title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
papers.tldr: Task vectors can be decomposed into task-recognition, task-learning, and residual components that enable more interpretable and effective model steering.

papers.abstract: Looped language models can strengthen reasoning through repeated computation with shared weights, increasing execution depth without adding independent parameters. However, each additional pass increases training floating-point operations (FLOPs), making these gains more expensive to obtain. To address this cost, we propose UpLoop, a pretraining schedule that uses upcycling to train looped Transformers while exactly matching a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, total training tokens, and training FLOPs. Specifically, UpLoop begins with a shallow Transformer, progressively grows its depth by copying learned layers, and uses the computation saved early to support repeated execution of a shared middle block later in training. Experiments across model scales show improvements in language modeling and downstream performance, with the average score across 22 downstream tasks increasing from 22.99 to 27.52 at 1.3B parameters. These gains also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.
authors: Cheng Liang, Tengfei Zhang, Ya Zhang, Yanfeng Wang, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped models can improve reasoning through shared-weight repeated computation, but normally require more training FLOPs.
UpLoop starts with a shallow Transformer, copies learned layers to grow depth, and later repeats a shared middle block.
It exactly matches a standard dense baseline in final parameter count, training tokens, and total training FLOPs.
Across model scales, it improves language modeling and downstream performance; at 1.3B parameters, the 22-task average rises from 22.99 to 27.52.
Benefits also extend to mathematical reasoning after supervised fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes UpLoop, a method to train looped Transformers efficiently via upcycling, matching dense baseline FLOPs.
papers.title: UpLoop: Training Looped Transformers via Upcycling at No Extra Pretraining Compute
papers.tldr: UpLoop trains looped Transformers within the same parameter, token, and FLOP budget as dense baselines by progressively upcycling layers and reallocating saved computation to repeated execution.

papers.abstract: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.
authors: Ziteng Wang, Jianqiao Lu, Xinyu Ma, Jintao Zhang, Jun Zhu, Yiyuan Ma, Jianfei Chen
bullets: Problem: Standard residuals force the state width carried through depth to match each layer’s compute width.
Method: Group layers into blocks with d-dimensional PreNorm layers and a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual, linked by learned projections.
Contribution: Makes residual width an independent scaling variable using only dense projections and normalizations.
Results: Reports 1.30× better FLOPs efficiency, 0.0208 lower training loss, and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy in the stated experiments.
Scope: Designed to reduce activation memory and I/O relative to other residual-expansion methods without specialized kernels or infrastructure changes.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), an architectural efficiency improvement for Transformers that decouples residual width from compute width.
papers.title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width
papers.tldr: HiRes decouples residual width from per-layer compute width, improving scaling efficiency with a simple Transformer modification.

papers.abstract: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.
authors: Burak Bakkar, Hana Moalla, Mohamed Salem Jedidi, Haifa Ben Messaoud, Nicolas Lopez Carranza
bullets: Clinical-trial failure motivates better phase-level outcome prediction using information in registration text.
BioBERT and BioMistral represented trials as text from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields and were evaluated with fine-tuning or frozen-embedding probing.
All four variants exceeded published HINT results in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, with reported relative PR-AUC gains of 10–20%.
Fine-tuning was strongest in Phases I–II, while frozen BioMistral embeddings performed best in Phase III; most variant differences were small and untested for significance.
F1 gains were limited: no approach clearly surpassed the trivial always-success classifier on F1.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Clinical trial outcome prediction pipeline. Trial records are parsed from ClinicalTrials.gov, cleaned and tokenized, and then used either to train a classifier on frozen language-model embeddings (probing, top) or to fine-tune the language model end to end (bottom). Orange components are trained; blue components are frozen. Abbreviations: LoRA, low-rank adaptation; MLP, multi-layer perceptron; PR-AUC, area under the precision–recall curve; ROC-AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; XML, Extensible Markup Language.

Figure 4: Training strategies. (a) Full fine-tuning updates all transformer weights and the classification head. (b) LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and trains low-rank adapters (∆W = (α/r)BA) inserted into the attention projections, together with the classification head. (c) Probing uses the frozen model only as a feature extractor; token embeddings are mean-pooled and only the MLP classifier is trained. Abbreviations: LoRA, low-rank adaptation; MLP, multi-layer perceptron.

Figure 5: Test-set F1 (left), ROC-AUC (middle) and PR-AUC (right) by phase for HINT and the four language-model variants (values from Table 2). Colour indicates the model and marker shape the training strategy. Dashed grey lines show the trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial (for ROC-AUC, chance level 0.5). Abbreviations: HINT, Hierarchical Interaction Network; PR-AUC, area under the precision–recall curve; ROC-AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.

Figure 3: Input representation. For fine-tuning, the ten fields are concatenated into one sequence that is passed through the trainable language model. For probing, each field is encoded separately by the frozen model, token embeddings are mean-pooled per field and averaged across fields, and the result is passed to an MLP classifier. papers.abstract: Training interactive language agents from terminal outcomes poses three coupled problems: which task and state continuations to sample, how to assign delayed feedback to decisions, and how to aggregate token losses for multi-token actions. We present TSBPO, a tree-structured sampling-to-update paradigm that addresses these problems within one training loop. A likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator uses retained task and state evidence to target continuations likely to produce contrasting terminal outcomes under fixed rollout budgets. On the resulting replayed physical trees, trajectory advantages compare immediate sibling segments, while observation-group step advantages compare outcomes at matched task/observation states. The actor then sums clipped token surrogates over each complete response and normalizes across active turns, avoiding response-length averaging in the policy-gradient term. With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, fixed checkpoints obtain 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for each of the 500 WebShop test goals. A WebShop step-term ablation yields 75.93% at the same update-100 evaluation; an ALFWorld aggregation comparison shows higher observed command validity with complete-turn weighting. These results support the evaluated training configuration on two interactive benchmarks.
authors: Rui Yu, Chong Mu, Jinchuan Zhang
bullets: Targets task and state continuations likely to produce contrasting terminal outcomes under fixed rollout budgets.
Uses sibling-segment trajectory advantages and matched observation-group step advantages to address delayed feedback.
Sums clipped token objectives over complete responses and normalizes across active turns rather than averaging by response length.
With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, reports 97.79%/96.64% seen/unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and 81.07% per-episode success across six stochastic episodes on 500 WebShop goals.
Scope: results support the evaluated configuration on ALFWorld and WebShop; a WebShop step-term ablation reached 75.93%.

papers.abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.
bullets: Pooled coverage can appear near nominal while individual-cell coverage is extremely poor, motivating fleet, batch, and cell-level reporting.
A residual-free weighting scheme uses frozen signature features, batch labels, and cycle indices to partially close this gap.
The 10th-percentile cell coverage improves from 0.750 to 0.830, while worst-cell coverage rises from 0.642 to 0.694, with no deferrals.
Weights can worsen performance under protocol drift, and limited battery diversity bounds repair capacity.
Within-domain behavior replicates, but intervals collapse on a cross-chemistry external set.

papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.
authors: Miguel Andrade, Jos\'e Almeida, Carlos Santiago, Catarina Barata
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of high-resolution spatial and single-cell transcriptomics by leveraging widely available WSIs and bulk RNA-seq.
Extracts morphology with the UNI2-h pathology foundation model and builds hierarchical patch- and cell-level spatial graphs.
Trains with direct supervision and weakly supervised consistency losses across bulk, spatial, and single-cell biological scales.
Evaluated on TCGA, Visium, and Xenium samples from lung, kidney, and breast tissues.
Predictions support survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification using molecular signatures.

papers.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.
bullets: The study addresses the tension between correlated model errors (monoculture) and conflicting decisions among similarly accurate models (multiplicity).
It separates reasoning as a controlled intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior.
Across nine models, two developers, and three classification tasks, increased reasoning effort raises agreement on the same individuals.
Individuals producing longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models.
Both effects remain after accounting for model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.
authors: Siqi Li, Ziyi Bai, Xinrun Xu, Tinglei Huang, B\"orje F. Karlsson
bullets: Defines six requirements for embodied memory, including world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning.
Categorizes methods into eight architectural families, such as recurrent states, fast weights, visual/symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems.
Reviews benchmark practices for distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task-solving ability.
Highlights open challenges in retrieving relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs, and consolidating knowledge across episodes.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for image recognition are typically trained using mini-batches, with a forward pass to compute predictions and losses followed by a more computationally expensive backward pass to update model parameters. However, not all training samples contribute equally to learning, suggesting that computation can be reduced by performing backward passes only on informative samples. The challenge is that sample informativeness changes throughout training: difficult samples may be valuable early on, improving samples become important later, and class diversity becomes increasingly relevant toward the end. Existing methods often rely on fixed selection rules or computationally expensive per-sample gradient calculations. We propose OT-CAL, an adaptive data selection method that automatically adjusts its sampling preferences during training. OT-CAL represents each sample using five informativeness features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty. A curriculum vector describes the currently preferred sample characteristics, and optimal-transport-based matching assigns selection weights according to how closely samples match this target. The curriculum vector is then updated using the selected samples, forming a feedback loop that adapts without a manually defined schedule. Experiments on three standard visual learning benchmarks show that, when selecting 50% of each mini-batch, OT-CAL improves performance by 1.3--2.1 points over AdaSelection while achieving 1.18--1.24 times faster training than full-data training.
bullets: Targets the unequal informativeness of samples during mini-batch training to reduce costly backward passes.
Represents samples with five features, including difficulty, learnability, and uncertainty.
Uses an optimal-transport curriculum to match samples to evolving training preferences.
Updates the curriculum from selected samples, enabling feedback-driven adaptation without a manual schedule.
Selecting 50% of each mini-batch improves performance by 1.3–2.1 points over AdaSelection and trains 1.18–1.24× faster than full-data training on three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.
authors: Wenbo Fu, Chenghui Mao, Chengwen Hu, Haifeng Lv, Zhou Lv
bullets: Addresses the tension between local neighbor graphs that miss long-range interactions and quadratic-cost all-pair attention.
Maps centroid-relative atomic distances to learned radial features and combines them with content-dependent queries and keys.
Uses factorized aggregation and readout for linear scaling with atom count at fixed feature dimensions.
Inserted between EquiformerV3 local blocks, with conservative forces obtained by differentiating the energy.
On OPoly26 polymer-derived clusters, matched 5M models reduce per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%; the 20M model achieves 15.81 meV total-energy MAE and 2.619 meV/angstrom force MAE.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RKA in an equivariant atomic potential. Each local block updates the geometric representation. RKA reads its scalar channels and positions, and writes a scalar residual before the next block. The final scalar readout gives atomic energies. Shared elemental references and screened repulsion complete the total energy, whose coordinate derivative defines the forces. Charge/spin conditioning and repulsion are present in both 5M models.

Figure 1: Radial Kernel Attention. A finite structure defines a centroid and node radii. Learned radial features organize content-dependent key–value statistics over the entire structure. Each node reads the shared statistics through its radial features and query, and receives a scalar residual update. The basis curves are schematic, rather than fitted checkpoint values.

papers.abstract: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. Limited or uneven connectivity in this support may isolate subsets of feature dimensions, forming information islands that restrict direct task-specific interactions through the trainable update. To address this issue, we propose Small-World Induced Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a sparse tuning framework inspired by small-world connectivity. SWIFT combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic scattering permutation that routes the mixed outputs across feature groups without additional trainable parameters. We further show theoretically that certain random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can exhibit information islands, whereas a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the trainable block-diagonal factor consists of equal-sized, structurally dense square blocks. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification demonstrate that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning. Implementation is available at https://github.com/xianchaoguan/SWIFT
authors: Xianchao Guan, Zijun Xiong, Yifeng Wang, Yubo Cui, Yaowei Wang, Guo-Sen Xie, Xin Li, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Sparse tuning can suffer from limited feature connectivity, creating information islands in the update structure.
SWIFT uses block-diagonal updates for local feature mixing and a fixed scattering permutation to route information across feature groups without extra trainable parameters.
Theoretical analysis shows block-diagonal and some random sparse updates can form islands, while sufficient scattering provides positive block-level expansion under stated conditions.
Experiments across commonsense reasoning, text generation, and image classification show SWIFT outperforms evaluated PEFT baselines on average and can match or exceed full fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Continual adaptation to new tasks is essential for robots deployed in the real world, but adapting pre-trained policies remains challenging due to parameter growth and the need for continual demonstration collection. Parameter-Efficient Continual Fine-Tuning (PECFT) isolates task-specific updates, but adapter-per-task designs require demonstrations and grow with the task set. We propose ResMerge, a two-stage framework that learns mergeable residual policies atop a frozen pre-trained policy: residual reinforcement learning (RL) acquires task-specific corrections without additional expert demonstrations during adaptation, and parameter-space merging consolidates compatible residuals to reduce stored parameters. We introduce Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a simple, bounded, and interpretable metric that assesses compatibility in residual action-field space by comparing correction direction and magnitude. Experiments on LIBERO across two backbones and on a real-world Franka robot show improved continual learning performance over strong PECFT baselines, while selective merging reduces the residual-parameter footprint. Project website: https://resmerge.github.io/.
authors: Kefei Zhu, Lingyun Xu, Yue Xin, Xiaoqi Li, Caixin Guo, Xincheng Du, Yuanpei Chen, Yaodong Yang, Hao Dong
bullets: Addresses the need to adapt pre-trained robot policies without continually collecting expert demonstrations or storing one adapter per task.
Uses a frozen base policy with residual reinforcement learning to learn task-specific corrections.
Merges compatible residual policies in parameter space to reduce the stored residual footprint.
Introduces Residual-Field Consistency (RFC), a bounded and interpretable metric based on correction direction and magnitude.
Shows improved continual-learning performance on LIBERO and a real Franka robot, with selective merging reducing residual parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Residual policy learning with parameter merging directly addresses continual adaptation of robot policies and fits both robot learning and continual learning.

papers.tldr: ResMerge enables continual robot-policy adaptation by learning demonstration-free residual corrections and merging compatible task updates to limit parameter growth.

papers.abstract:
Robot policy learning is dominated by zeroth-order methods such as PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box and pay for it with enormous sample counts. First-order policy learning differentiates through the dynamics, but on contact-rich whole-body control it has rarely worked: its gradients explode. A recent world-model method showed that derivative information can make humanoid motion tracking far more efficient, using surrogate gradients of a learned model. We show that exact gradients of the simulator itself do better, once two obstacles are removed. Exact gradients contain rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges near some events; and they are expensive, because the simulator's adjoint has to replay the contact solve. $
abla$Mimic bounds these samples with median-relative per-sample gradient clipping at every step of the backward pass, and reuses each costly simulated window by multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets, which bounds every action target independently of the gradient scale. NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulation engine for the Unitree G1, removes the cost: it computes MuJoCo's full contact dynamics with fused per-world kernels and the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel, with analytic gradients that match float64 finite differences, $11.5	imes$ faster than the available MuJoCo Warp adjoint. On whole-body tracking of all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, $
abla$Mimic reaches the score reported by the state-of-the-art world-model method, 0.82, in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. SHAC, the standard first-order baseline, stops on exploding gradients within minutes. We release NablaEngine and $
abla$Mimic as open-source infrastructure for first-order humanoid policy learning.
bullets: Addresses the sample inefficiency of zeroth-order methods and instability of first-order learning in contact-rich humanoid control.
Clips rare, unbounded gradients during backpropagation and reuses simulated windows through multistep regression to control action-target scale.
Introduces NablaEngine, a GPU differentiable simulator for the Unitree G1 with analytic whole-step adjoints and fused contact-dynamics kernels.
On 40 LAFAN1 tracking clips, reaches score 0.82 in 20 minutes and 0.874 in 1.8 hours; SHAC fails from exploding gradients.
Releases NablaEngine and ∇Mimic as open-source infrastructure.

papers.abstract: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.
bullets: Addresses rare-pathology annotation scarcity, morphological distortion, catastrophic forgetting, and siloed task development.
DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling improves differentiable topology and boundary continuity.
3D Group Prompt extracts shared domain knowledge from volumetric image-mask alignment and text prompts.
Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head supports fast addition of new categories with negligible computational cost while retaining prior-task performance.
Ablations on abdominal and extra-abdominal organ and lesion datasets support the effectiveness of the proposed modules.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of DT-MorphLoss. The overall pipeline proceeds as follows: 1) a Sigmoid activation and Otsu binarization convert the prediction map into a binary mask; 2) the mask is fed in parallel into two branches, where the morphological-loss branch applies erosion and dilation to compute Lmorph, while the distance-transform branch extracts an edge mask to produce a distance field for Ldt.; 3) the two terms are weighted and combined with the standard Dice loss (Ldice) and cross-entropy loss (Lce) to obtain the total loss.

Fig. 3. Overview of Many-to-one-CSH. Visual queries are encoded into multi-level features, while the text branch uses a Hash function to map various input texts into corresponding targets within a vocabulary registry and generate specific prompts. These prompts are transformed into distinctive text embeddings ωi, which are sequentially combined with the visual features and fed into a parameter generator composed of multiple specialized MLP heads. This module dynamically generates prompt-conditioned weight parameters θi that directly modulate the layers within the segment head, allowing the decoded query features to be processed into final masks.

Fig. 2. Overview of GroupPrompt3D. A 2D Swin encoder extracts features from both a support volume and a query volume. The support path processes features through a concept filter, while the query path extracts multi-scale representations via a decoder. Crucially, since the target labels in the support and query volumes do not perfectly match during training, a Conv3D block is required to map the conditional prompt knowledge and predict the final mask.

Fig. 5. Unified axial-space mapping of the discrete slice distributions across 6 test cases with 5 lesion categories. The horizontal axis indicates the actual slice index, while the dual-axis aligns the lesion labels and the case identifiers.

Fig. 6. Hierarchical expansion of the medical vocabulary registry for the MSWAL dataset. Semantic relevance to the core concept weakens moving outward: the innermost circle is the baseline VOCAB with 7 core medical categories, while the middle and outermost circles include extended clinical and anatomical variants.

Fig. 4. Segmentation predictions versus the weight of DT-Morph Combined Loss for the identical liver tumor slice. The results reveal the nonlinear morphological evolution of the prediction, demonstrating the transition from over-segmentation to undersegmentation as ω increases.

papers.title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made significant progress in spatial reasoning, particularly by integrating RGB images with depth data, which is often assumed to faithfully reflect physical distances. However, mirrors violate this assumption: they distort depth readings while reproducing object appearances, making reflections difficult to distinguish from real objects. As existing benchmarks rarely consider such reflective scenarios, VLM performance in mirror scenes remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset from reflective scenes to evaluate the spatial reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art VLMs in these scenarios. Specifically, we collect 1,011 RGB-D images from 525 real-world scenes, spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, six reflective surface types, and both daytime and nighttime conditions. All images are annotated with reflective surface region masks and mask annotations for both directly observed and mirror-reflected objects. Then, we curate a benchmark named MIRA-Bench (Mirror-Induced Reasoning Ambiguity Benchmark), comprising 14,140 QA pairs across eight sub-tasks organized into three cognitive levels: Reflection-aware Perception, Spatial Reasoning, and Scene-level Decision-making. We evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on MIRA-Bench and find consistent failures across tasks: models misclassify whether objects are directly observed or reflected, fail to match reflected instances to their real-world counterparts, and produce erroneous spatial inferences. Remarkably, providing depth data actually degrades reasoning performance, implying that VLMs cannot identify incorrect depth in mirror scenes. The code and data are available at https://github.com/EvaYin-cloud/MIRA-Bench
authors: Hao Yin, Tianchen Guo, Heming Du, Yan Ke, Yanbin Liu, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset of 1,011 images from 525 real-world scenes across varied environments, reflective surfaces, and lighting conditions.
Provides annotations for reflective regions, directly observed objects, and mirror-reflected objects.
Builds MIRA-Bench with 14,140 QA pairs spanning eight tasks and three levels: reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and scene-level decision-making.
State-of-the-art VLMs often confuse reflections with real objects, fail to associate reflections with their sources, and make incorrect spatial inferences.
Depth input degrades performance, suggesting models do not recognize unreliable depth measurements in mirror scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks spatial reasoning of VLMs with RGB-D mirror ambiguity, directly fitting multimodal spatial intelligence.
papers.title: When Depth Lies: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Mirror-Induced RGB-D Ambiguity
papers.tldr: MIRA-Bench shows that vision-language models struggle with mirror-induced RGB-D ambiguity, and added depth can worsen their spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multi-target on-orbit servicing missions require planning tools that can adapt to evolving operational conditions while accounting for the outcome variability inherent to safety-critical spaceflight. This paper presents an adaptive planning approach for multi-target servicing campaigns in low Earth orbit and applies it to inspection missions flown by a low-thrust servicer. The approach is based on Distributional Reinforcement Learning, which learns the full distribution of mission returns and thereby supports explicit risk-sensitive decision-making at each planning step. Specifically, a Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN) agent selects which target to inspect next by jointly considering the expectation and the variance of the predicted return through a mean-variance criterion. The mission environment models circular orbits with a spread in inclination and uses Edelbaum's combined-manoeuvre low-thrust transfer estimates. The observation comprises the orbital elements, the visit history, the observed risk state of each target and the remaining mission-time budget. The risk state of each target changes stochastically during the campaign, making the outcome of an inspection uncertain and creating operationally meaningful distinctions between risk-neutral and risk-averse planning strategies. Because the mission-time budget generally admits only a subset of the candidate targets, the planner must also select which targets to inspect. Numerical experiments on scenarios with five target satellites show that one risk-aversion weight moves the policy across a range of mean return and return variance, over an unchanged environment and reward. Risk-averse agents reduce the variance of the episodic return by approximately one half relative to risk-neutral agents and lower the probability of a mission loss, at a cost in mean return. To validate the learned policies, the efficient frontier, which gives the highest mean return attainable at each level of return variance, is computed exactly by enumerating the admissible visit orders. At equal variance, the learned policies lie close to this frontier in mean return, and the risk-averse policies have a lower probability of a mission loss than the frontier policies.
bullets: Addresses adaptive planning for low-thrust, multi-target inspection missions with stochastic target risks and limited mission time.
Uses Distributional Reinforcement Learning with QR-DQN to estimate return distributions and select targets via a mean–variance criterion.
Represents orbital conditions, visit history, target risk states, and remaining time in the planning state.
In five-target scenarios, risk-averse policies reduce episodic-return variance by about half and lower mission-loss probability, sacrificing mean return.
Learned policies approach the exact efficient frontier; risk-averse policies can outperform frontier policies in mission-loss probability at equal variance.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Solution architecture. The observation 𝑠𝑡 is formed in the mission environment. The quantile network (inverse cumulative distribution) returns 𝐾 quantiles per action, and the next inspection is selected from them using the mean–variance score under the feasibility mask. The same masked score is applied to the bootstrap action during training.

Fig. 1: Mission concept overview. A low-thrust servicer transfers between circular orbits with varying semi-major axes and inclinations to inspect multiple targets within a set mission-time limit. Each target 𝑗 , marked 𝑇𝑗 , has a value 𝑣 𝑗 and might enter a high-risk state with a failure probability 𝑝 𝑗 > 0 (indicated by a filled marker). Numbered arrows illustrate a sample visit sequence.

Fig. 4: Mean return against return variance on the same 4000 test instances. The solid line is the efficient frontier, obtained by enumeration. Filled circles are the mean–variance policies for 𝜆 = 0, 0.1 and 0.3, with error bars showing the standard deviation across three training seeds.

Fig. 5: Return distributions for the risk-neutral and mean–variance (𝜆 = 0.3) policies, combined across three training seeds, with 12 000 evaluations each. Dashed and dotted verticals mark the lower decile (𝑞0.1) of each distribution. The shaded region marks mission losses (𝑍 < 0).

Fig. 3: Cost of traversing the sampled orbital bands, starting from the orbit at 500 km and 85.75◦, calculated using Eq. (1). The right axis indicates the equivalent thrusting time. A transfer across both bands exceeds the mission budget.
Table 1: Environment and training parameters for the five-target scenario.

Values for the learned policies are means over three training seeds, with standard deviations no more than 0.05 for the mean of 𝑍 and 0.42 for the variance of 𝑍 . papers.selection_reason: Presents a risk-sensitive mission planning approach for multi-target on-orbit inspection using distributional reinforcement learning, applicable to robotic servicing tasks.
papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Mission Planning for Multi-Target On-Orbit Inspection via Distributional Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: A QR-DQN planner enables risk-sensitive selection of inspection targets in uncertain multi-target orbital missions, substantially reducing return variability and mission-loss risk at the cost of mean return.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching visuomotor policies require iterative denoising or numerical integration for multimodal action generation, introducing latency and execution mismatch. We instead consider a different formulation: conditioned on vision and proprioception, demonstrated bimanual action chunks concentrate in a structured observation-dependent region of joint-action space, making the action target more direct to model than the generative process. Based on this view, we propose the Direct Manifold Action Transformer (DMAT), which reformulates action generation as the direct modeling of clean, observation-conditioned joint-space action chunks from stochastic interpolants, thereby enabling single-step inference without relying on iterative generative inference or auxiliary trajectory-straightening procedures. Within DMAT, local 3D geometry anchors predictions to spatial structure, while State-Consistent Spectral-Time Refinement (STR) reconciles predicted chunks with proprioception and suppresses high-frequency residuals. Across 567 standard and out-of-distribution (OOD) trials per method, DMAT outperformed Improved 3D Diffusion Policy (IDP3) and DiTFlow3D in aggregate success rate, achieving relative improvements of 129.1% and 95.7%, respectively, while generating action chunks 2.06x and 1.34x faster and remaining robust under repeated 50 N interventions. These results pave the way for a novel generative paradigm for efficient and robust bimanual manipulation.
authors: Hongren Wang, Mingyu You, Zihan Li, Zhipeng Wang, Shuo Jiang, Bin He
bullets: Targets the latency and execution mismatch caused by iterative denoising or numerical integration in diffusion and flow-matching policies.

papers.abstract: Autonomous inspection of a target spacecraft is typically the initial step in on-orbit servicing. Planning close-proximity observation viewpoints involves a complex combinatorial problem constrained by coverage, fuel, and safety considerations. This paper models the viewpoint selection as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and applies Proximal Policy Optimization with Lagrangian relaxation to solve it. The system combines a high-level planner, which sequences camera viewpoints on an observation sphere around the target, with a low-level model that assesses each transfer using the Clohessy--Wiltshire (CW) equations for relative motion. The deterministic constraints on single-impulse reachability and $\Delta v$ cap are enforced directly on the action set. Safety margins are affected by navigation and manoeuvre errors, making the actual clearance stochastic. To address this, a chance constraint on the realised trajectory is implemented, with a Lagrangian multiplier governed by PID control to adapt the penalty during training. The approach is tested on a Galileo-class navigation satellite in medium Earth orbit, modelled as a point cloud where visibility from each viewpoint considers field-of-view and line-of-sight occlusion. Across various risk budgets, the trained policy maintains the keep-out violation rate within the specified limit, achieving coverage close to its maximum and staying within the mission $\Delta v$ budget. Compared to the usual practice of applying a fixed margin to the keep-out radius and planning deterministically, the chance-constrained policy attains less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage. This makes the collision risk an explicit design parameter, eliminating the need for re-tuning per case. The learned policy selects a viewpoint without the repeated Monte Carlo risk estimates required by a greedy, chance-constrained planner at every decision point.
bullets: Models viewpoint sequencing as a constrained Markov decision process with coverage, reachability, safety, and Δv constraints.
Uses PPO with Lagrangian relaxation and PID-controlled penalties for trajectory-level chance constraints.
Combines a high-level viewpoint planner with low-level Clohessy–Wiltshire relative-motion transfer assessment.
On a Galileo-class navigation satellite scenario, the policy respects risk and Δv budgets while achieving near-maximum coverage.
Compared with fixed keep-out margins, it achieves less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage and avoids repeated Monte Carlo risk estimation during decisions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently been extended to vision-language models (VLMs), yet its effectiveness remains limited for text-rich reasoning tasks. We highlight a key factor contributing to this limitation: models frequently arrive at correct final answers despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate steps. We define this phenomenon as Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR). Because standard RLVR rewards only final-answer correctness, it fails to differentiate between properly grounded and misgrounded reasoning, reinforcing both equally. Through token-level analysis, we reveal that CVMR tokens exhibit distinct attention patterns that differ systematically from well-grounded ones. Based on this observation, we propose GRIT, a training framework that incorporates visual grounding into RLVR to mitigate the impact of CVMR. Furthermore, to address the lack of text-rich reasoning benchmarks that allow for systematic evaluation across text length and reasoning depth, we introduce GRIT-Bench. Experiments demonstrate that GRIT significantly improves both reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Noori Bae, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Identifies Correct-but-Visually-Misgrounded Reasoning (CVMR), where models answer correctly despite misperceiving visual information during intermediate reasoning.
Shows that CVMR tokens have distinct attention patterns from well-grounded tokens.
Introduces GRIT, which uses gradient masking to incorporate visual grounding into RLVR training.
Introduces GRIT-Bench for evaluating text-rich reasoning across text length and reasoning depth.
Experiments report improved reasoning accuracy and grounding fidelity over existing RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: Low inference latency is critical for closed-loop robotic manipulation, especially under asynchronous inference, where action chunks must be updated promptly to correct accumulated deviations. However, existing visuomotor policies rely on computationally expensive visual backbones, resulting in high inference latency and deployment overhead. In this paper, we propose RTPolicy, a multi-view visuomotor policy that attains accurate manipulation with high inference efficiency. Its core design combines view-aware feature fusion with visual compression to aggregate complementary information across camera views into a compact token representation. The representation conditions a flow-matching action generator with the robot state and flow time, reducing the cost of action generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this design reduces the computational cost of visual representation and action generation while preserving visual information required for manipulation. On the RoboTwin~2.0 single-task clean evaluation across 50 tasks, RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 52.26\%, outperforming the strongest leaderboard baseline $\pi_0$ (46.4\%). We further evaluate RTPolicy under asynchronous streaming inference on a real bimanual platform, where RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 72.0\% and sustains real-time inference at 30.35 ms (32.9 Hz) on the RDK S600 and 149.72 ms (6.7 Hz) on the RDK S100, both in INT16. Project Page: https://d-robotics-ai-lab.github.io/RTPolicy.project.
authors: Xianbao Hou, Zehao Ni, Yonghao He, Lingfeng Qian, Xin Shi, Hu Su, Wei Sui, Cong Yang
bullets: Targets high inference latency in closed-loop manipulation, particularly asynchronous settings requiring prompt action updates.
Uses view-aware feature fusion and visual compression to combine multi-camera information into compact tokens.
Conditions a flow-matching action generator on the compressed visual representation, robot state, and flow time to reduce action-generation cost.
Achieves a 52.26% mean success rate across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 single-task clean evaluations, exceeding the reported π₀ baseline of 46.4%.
On a real bimanual platform, reaches 72.0% mean success with 32.9 Hz inference on the RDK S600 and 6.7 Hz on the RDK S100, using INT16.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
authors: Chanseul Cho, Jaesung Jun, Dongheon Lee, Youngmin Ro
bullets: Problem: Always-on CoT can cause overthinking, misaligning visual grounding with the query.
Method: Estimate input difficulty from attention-map entropy; high entropy triggers CoT, while low entropy skips it.
Robustness: Bidirectional Rethinking reverses the initial reasoning choice when the output fails.
Results: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on reasoning segmentation benchmarks and improves inference efficiency.
Scope: Training-free adaptive inference for multimodal reasoning segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of the proposed DA-CoT framework during inference. The aggregated attention entropy Hagg, computed over the pre-identified layers L, is used to adaptively decide whether to trigger CoT reasoning. If Hagg ≥ τ , the model follows the Difficulty-Aware Prompting Path with CoT for structured reasoning; otherwise, it takes the direct path without CoT for efficient inference. When the initial reasoning path fails to produce a valid output, a discrete flipping signal activates the Bidirectional Rethinking Path, enabling re-evaluation and recovery from overthinking or underthinking. The final bounding boxes or point prompts are then passed to the segmentation head to produce the reasoningaware segmentation result.

Left: CoT-detrimental cases, where CoT leads to misgrounding by overthinking spatial reasoning; without CoT, the model correctly identifies the target with concentrated attention and low entropy. Right: CoT-beneficial cases, where CoT enhances performance in ambiguous scenarios by guiding reasoning towards the correct region, as reflected in high-entropy attention maps. The visualized attention entropy (bottom right of each map) provides an intrinsic signal that distinguishes when CoT is helpful or harmful.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.
authors: Wutong Xu, Yun Qu, Haiyan Feng, Qi Wang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Existing unlearning methods can forget coarsely because they optimize complete responses without isolating the knowledge to remove.
The paper defines Knowledge Association (KA) as the conditional predictive distribution linking a query context to target knowledge.
KARU uses reinforcement learning with token-level rewards, distribution-level suppression, and proximity-aware sampling of retained knowledge.
Experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks show improved forgetting effectiveness with comparable retention and general utility.
The method targets selective knowledge removal, with scope determined by the identified knowledge associations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a framework for selectively removing specific knowledge associations from LLMs while preserving general capabilities.
papers.title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
papers.tldr: KARU treats context–knowledge associations—not whole responses—as the target of LLM unlearning, enabling more precise forgetting while preserving retained knowledge and general utility.

papers.abstract: A robot should act only on an instruction from a person or on an intent that the robot explicitly represents and generates. Unintended actions taken without such an instruction can cause risk or inconvenience to people and the environment. We examine how recent vision-language-action (VLA) policies respond when the instruction is missing or meaningless. We apply a paired protocol with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, and wrong-task instructions to six model checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation. Holding the initial state fixed and varying only the instruction, we ask three questions: whether the robot starts to move, which task it completes, and what the instruction determines. Even when the instruction was empty, the robot started moving in every episode with all six checkpoints, and with five of them it often completed a task that the instruction had not specified. On two GR00T checkpoints, the instruction determined which task was executed but not whether the robot started moving; the robot moved even on infeasible instructions. We then tested three methods for suppressing the start: prepending "if no task is given do not move" to the instruction; a gate that holds the robot when the first action chunk for the given instruction nearly equals that for an empty instruction; and fine-tuning the policy to hold still on non-task inputs. The prefix stopped the robot in none of the six checkpoints, and the gate held it on non-task inputs in five of the six checkpoints. The fine-tuned policy never completed a task on non-task inputs, but it did not reliably keep the robot still, and it failed to suppress the start on infeasible instructions.
authors: Minsu Jang, Jae-Woo Choi, Youngwoo Yoon, Dohyung Kim
bullets: Across six checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation, robots moved in every episode with empty instructions.
Five checkpoints often completed tasks not specified by the instruction, including under meaningless or wrong-task inputs.
On two GR00T checkpoints, instructions selected the executed task but did not determine whether motion began.
A textual prefix failed to suppress starts; an action-chunk similarity gate succeeded on non-task inputs in five of six checkpoints.
Fine-tuning prevented task completion on non-task inputs but did not reliably suppress motion or handle infeasible instructions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and suppresses unintended starts in VLA policies, directly relevant to vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: VLA Policies Do Not Know When Not to Act: Unintended Task Execution and Start Suppression
papers.tldr: VLA policies may start and execute tasks even without a valid instruction, while a simple action-similarity gate suppresses starts more reliably than prompting or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Ying Xu, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: Audits 25 claimed cognitive-architecture mechanisms using static code tracing, falsifiable predictions, interventions, replication, and repair controls.
In 18 of 25 modules, computed values never reached production outputs; three previously undescribed idle-wiring patterns were identified.
Across 12 interventions and 61 frozen criteria, 53 were confirmed, five falsified, two partially adjudicated, and one remained ambiguous.
Repair experiments improved planner task success and reduced state-controller error, showing that implementation defects can materially affect behavior.
Findings are case-level across two systems; the authors argue module names and actual computations must be evaluated independently.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a transferable verification protocol to audit whether LLM-based agents actually implement claimed cognitive mechanisms (e.g., Theory of Mind), addressing the claim-implementation gap.
papers.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
papers.tldr: A pre-registered audit finds that many named cognitive modules in LLM agents do not perform meaningful computation, and offers a reusable method for verifying implementation claims.

papers.abstract: RGB-D SLAM requires accurate online tracking, high-quality rendering, and geometrically consistent reconstruction. Existing Gaussian SLAM methods mainly optimize Gaussian primitives with photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints, which are often insufficient in indoor scenes with weak textures, large planar structures, noisy depth, and long trajectories. The resulting maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred structural boundaries. We propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a drawing-like process: explicit point-line geometry first sketches the structural layout, and implicit neural Gaussians then fill in high-fidelity appearance and continuous geometric details. It estimates camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction through point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and converts them into differentiable regularization terms on Gaussian centers and normals. To improve compactness and efficiency, DrawSplat further combines an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling, which allocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DrawSplat achieves robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian-based SLAM systems, while maintaining a practical balance among quality, efficiency, and model size.
authors: Fan Zhu, Zhisong Xu, Ziyu Chen, Zhenjun Zhao, Takayuki Okatani
bullets: Targets pose drift, surface artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred boundaries in weak-texture indoor scenes.
Jointly tracks points and lines to estimate camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction.
Uses Atlanta World plane priors to regularize Gaussian centers and normals.
Combines anchor-based implicit neural Gaussians with adaptive sampling for compact, efficient reconstruction.
Experiments across multiple datasets report robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometry with a practical quality–efficiency–size trade-off.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of DrawSplat. DrawSplat follows a hybrid Gaussian SLAM paradigm [36]: explicit point-line geometry provides stable tracking and structural cues, while the implicit Gaussian map is incrementally updated online for compact, photorealistic, and geometryconsistent reconstruction. Given an online RGB-D stream, the tracking front-end jointly estimates camera poses, selects keyframes, and builds a sparse 3D geometry map from point and line features. The mapping back-end converts tracked 3D points into a sparse feature grid and decodes implicit Gaussian primitives through lightweight MLPs. Structural 3D lines further induce structural planes constrained by the shared-gravity Atlanta World prior, which regularize Gaussian centers and normals during joint map optimization. The final system produces compact, photorealistic, and structurally consistent indoor reconstructions.
