papers.selection_reason: Gaussian SLAM for indoor geometric reconstruction is directly relevant to 3D vision and embodied perception.
papers.title: DrawSplat: Atlanta World-Guided Implicit Gaussian SLAM for Indoor Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DrawSplat improves indoor RGB-D Gaussian SLAM by using Atlanta World-guided structural geometry to achieve more robust tracking and consistent, detailed reconstruction.

papers.abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Nekruz Maxudov, Bedil Karimov, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: The model is adapted from LFM2.5-2.6B-Base for Tajik tool calling on modest hardware.
LoRA continued pretraining uses 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents, followed by SFT on translated Tajik tool calls, English replay data, and Tajik instructions.
Strict Tajik full-call accuracy increases from 20.69 to 64.14, while English performance remains essentially unchanged.
All continued-pretraining checkpoints score zero on tool calling, indicating loss of the native format and some underlying skill—not just formatting mismatch.
Knowledge accuracy improves, but English MMLU declines; the model is weak at refusals and multi-turn calls, so generated calls require validation.

papers.selection_reason: Details the adaptation of a hybrid model to Tajik for tool calling using LoRA continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, analyzing the effects of CPT on model capabilities.
papers.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
papers.tldr: A two-stage LoRA adaptation substantially improves Tajik tool calling, but continued pretraining erases the base model’s native tool-call format and harms several broader capabilities.

papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
authors: Ruurd J. A. Kuiper, Robert A. Bagheri
bullets: Addresses the high pretraining and full-fine-tuning costs of building diffusion language models.
Uses an architecture-agnostic, LoRA-only conversion recipe with all base-model parameters frozen.
Demonstrated on Gemma 2, Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5, and Ministral; the latter is reported as the first Mistral AR-to-DLM conversion.
Converted models support fully masked generation, bidirectional context, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge.
Task performance is competitive, but open-generation quality at low sampling budgets remains the main limitation.

papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan, Xin Li, Linqi Song
bullets: Targets failed prerequisites and flawed decompositions, rather than relying on another plausible action.
Extends ReAct with a bounded goal stack and dual-horizon checks for goal relevance and current feasibility.
Uses typed failure attribution to trigger Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo-parent operations.
Improves over ReAct and reflection-based control across all tested backbone–benchmark pairs; AppWorld gains reach up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct.
Ablations show verification and diagnosis are complementary, with removing either sometimes reducing performance below ReAct.

papers.abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
authors: Mahmoud S. Mayaleh, Fetia Bannour, Nour-El-Houda Yellas
bullets: Multi-domain slice placement jointly decides function hosting, inter-domain routing, and admission under an NP-hard online setting.
Fixed planning strategies do not generalize across topology regimes, and many rejected requests may have feasible but undiscovered placements.
ORION combines LLM-based intent and plan generation with multi-agent RL for cross-domain selection and per-domain function placement.
Its outcome-driven episodic memory stores network conditions, plans, and verified success or failure outcomes to guide future planning.
On held-out topology families, memory improves admission by 4.6–11.5 percentage points; importance-based retention outperforms FIFO storage.

papers.abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses class imbalance and ambiguous boundaries between adjacent CEFR levels.
Combines focal loss to emphasize difficult or underrepresented examples with supervised contrastive learning for more discriminative representations.
Evaluates sentence- and document-level assessment in monolingual and multilingual settings.
Consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple CEFR benchmarks.

papers.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.
bullets: Compares closed-source LLM prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, SLM–LLM enhancement, and newly proposed hybrid strategies.
Introduces two manually annotated NLP datasets covering academic abstracts and full-text articles.
LoRA-adapted T5 achieves macro F1 scores of 0.7408 on abstracts and 0.7013 on full text.
LLM-generated entity descriptions improve SLM performance, though error mitigation varies by error type.
Combining strategies with complementary error patterns further improves KERE performance.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning from observations must recover behavior from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence. Differentiable simulators provide pathwise policy gradients, but differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories can make optimization unstable. We introduce FOCUS, which combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor-critic learning. FOCUS matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments using a soft best-of-$K$ objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches. The resulting transport-based costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, while a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. FOCUS requires neither temporally aligned trajectories nor expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing. Across contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.
authors: Jo\~ao A. C\^andido Ramos, Lionel Blond\'e, Hugues Vinzant, Jacopo Castellini, Alexandros Kalousis
bullets: Addresses imitation from observations without temporal correspondence between demonstrations and rollouts.
Matches rollout windows to multiple expert segments using a soft best-of-K objective to find locally compatible alignments.
Uses transport-based alignment costs as differentiable rewards and a learned critic to extend value estimates beyond short horizons.
Avoids expert-aligned initialization and teacher forcing.
Improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial and prior differentiable imitation-from-observation methods on contact-rich DFlex locomotion tasks, including a 152-muscle humanoid.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
authors: Alessandro Previti, Konstantinos Vandikas, Mario Alviano, Mats Carlsson, Albin Larsson Forsberg, Alexandros Nikou, Athanasios Karapantelakis, Aneta Vulgarakis
bullets: Refines the decoding grammar at each step by removing values that cannot lead to a specification-satisfying output.
A forward-only variant guarantees compliance by construction and reduces repeated LLM inference versus rejection sampling.
A backtracking variant revises earlier choices when later constraints leave only values the LLM considers unsuitable.
Model-agnostic and compatible with existing grammar-constrained decoding, with modest symbolic-reasoning overhead.
Evaluated on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks, improving specification adherence and alignment with the model’s prompt interpretation.

papers.abstract: High-resolution 3D indoor scene generation is crucial for immersive applications such as virtual reality, spatial computing, and robotics simulation. We introduce VoxLution, a coarse-to-fine transformer-based approach that generates high-fidelity indoor scenes with rich details, overcoming the overly smooth geometry typical of existing generative models. First, we generate a low-resolution spatial layout; then, based on this structural information, we progressively refine the scene geometry locally in chunks. Key to our approach is formulating 3D super-resolution as a sequence modeling problem over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids. To achieve this, we introduce a training-free, resolution-invariant tokenization scheme that compactly encodes the geometric information of eight octants into a single decimal number. We formulate the transformer sequence to include multiple resolutions, allowing the coarse layout to guide the generation of fine local details. To ensure coherence across local chunks, we incorporate adjacent chunk boundary information directly into the transformer sequencing. VoxLution achieves scene generation at a finer voxel resolution than existing baselines, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks with 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++.
authors: Daoyi Gao, Xinyi Zhang, Alexey Bokhovkin, Lei Li, Angela Dai
bullets: Targets overly smooth geometry in existing 3D scene generators for immersive applications.
Uses coarse-to-fine generation: a low-resolution layout guides local, chunk-based geometry refinement.
Models 3D super-resolution as sequence generation over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids.
Introduces training-free, resolution-invariant tokenization and includes neighboring chunk boundaries for spatial coherence.
Reports lower FPD and FID than baselines on 3D-FRONT and ScanNet++, with improvements also at finer voxel resolutions.

Middle: each cascade transformer Φ(k) (k ≥ 1) consumes a sparse multi-resolution sequence with coarser-level and neighboring context, refining chunks to finer voxel resolution. Right: a sparse VAE Φm decodes the final voxel grid into dual-contouring attributes that produce the final triangle mesh.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.
authors: Jonghyeon Choi, Yeonjun Choi, Beakcheol Jang
bullets: Evaluates nation-level bias using 722 official UN Security Council records and five complementary tests: opinion ranking, association sorting, vote simulation, opposition attribution, and framing.

Across four evaluated LLMs, outputs lean opposition-oriented for China and Russia, and supportive-oriented for the U.K., U.S., and France.
Highlights the need for grounded, multi-test audits of LLMs used in international-relations applications.

papers.abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.
authors: Jinkyeong Choi, Chaebin Jeong, Junsung Jeon, Donghyeon Park
bullets: Introduces self-consistency bias: the persistence of incorrect claims in incoming memory.
Compares four auxiliary objectives by information content and update sensitivity within a shared recursive interface.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu

Reports absolute gains of 16.5% on Toolathlon, 10.2% on MCPMark, and 12.6% on MCP-Atlas over the initial student.

papers.abstract: Achieving safe navigation in confined dynamic environments remains a challenging problem, as robots must balance navigation efficiency with safety. Existing actor--critic MPC architectures typically employ differentiable MPC layers, but this way cannot readily accommodate explicit state constraints, making it intractable to involve collision avoidance within learning-based planning. To address this issue, we propose an actor--critic model predictive control framework with state constraints. We first use vertices to represent the robot and obstacles, and half-spaces to represent the workspace. Based on these, the nonlinear robot dynamics is locally linearized and the hyperplane-based collision avoidance constraints are convexified into the differentiable MPC layer, and then the actor exploits closed-loop feedback to adjust the MPC objective parameters that shape local motion behavior, while the critic evaluates long-term task performance. We further relax the convexified constraints with bounded and penalized slack variables to form an elastic quadratic program, accommodating cases where the local constraint approximations cannot be satisfied simultaneously. Simulation tests and experiments, involving dynamic collision avoidance for multi-robot in narrow cases, illustrate the advantages of the proposed framework in adaptively adjusting the learned policy and improving navigation efficiency over existing approaches while maintaining the motion safety.
authors: Chaoran Wu, Jiayu Fan, Qichen Tan, Yuyi Liu, Jin Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of incorporating explicit collision-avoidance state constraints into differentiable actor–critic MPC.
Represents robots and obstacles with vertices and the workspace with half-spaces, then locally linearizes dynamics and convexifies collision constraints.
Uses an actor to adapt MPC objective parameters through closed-loop feedback and a critic to assess long-term task performance.
Introduces bounded, penalized slack variables in an elastic quadratic program for locally infeasible constraints.
Simulations and experiments on dynamic multi-robot collision avoidance in narrow spaces show improved navigation efficiency while maintaining safety over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Robotic exploration can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments by autonomously searching unknown areas for objects of interest while constructing a complete, risk-aware map. However, existing autonomous exploration approaches typically prioritize geometric coverage or information gain, without explicitly coupling semantic object detection and the risk associated with operating near potentially hazardous objects. Moreover, many systems have been demonstrated primarily in simulation or controlled environments, leaving limited validation of risk-aware semantic exploration in complex, unstructured field settings. To address this gap, we propose SAFARI, a framework that treats object detection as a native channel of a unified probabilistic map, thereby jointly informing exploration and planning with both geometric and semantic evidence. We evaluated SAFARI in 11 missions across three field sites on a quadruped platform. The framework achieved an average coverage of 98.7% of the accessible mission area, without operator intervention for 97.6% of mission time, and detected objects with characteristic dimensions as small as 15cm. Lastly, through ablation studies and a detailed analysis of system behavior, we show that object-size awareness and safety-aware path planning are crucial for effective hazardous-object search.
authors: Ugur Kafkasyali, Mihnea Toader, Julia Richter, Turcan Tuna, Cesar Cadena, Marco Hutter

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3 End-to-end SparseGDN execution pipeline. The block-adjacent intra-chunk kernel computes transformed values U, compact update coefficients, and selector scores. The dynamic selector converts these scores into a structured event mask. Only selected events trigger deferred W materialization and recurrent-state updates, producing compact event states. During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

Figure 1 GDN-core prefill latency across context lengths for Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B. Compared with FLA GDN, SparseGDN additionally includes the online selector overhead. Latency is aggregated over all 24 GDN layers. SparseGDN reduces latency at every context length, reaching 1.93× and 1.94× speedup at 128K for the 9B and 4B models, respectively. Lower is better.

Figure 9 Accuracy--efficiency trade-off across retention budgets. Each panel plots the aggregate RULER score difference ∆, defined in Table 3, against the geometric mean GDN-core speedup over 4K–128K. Point labels show measured recurrent-event keep rates. Solid lines connect nondominated configurations among the evaluated sparse operating points. The cross marks the approximately 49%-keep configuration, which is dominated by the approximately 39%-keep configuration for both models under these aggregate metrics. Speedups include online selection. Higher and farther right is better.

Figure 10 Tail-window ranking quality, scan cost, and illustrative task scores. Left: change in retained nonanchor dense-decode importance mass relative to Tail-16 on 130 stratified 8K requests per model, with task-stratified paired 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Pair-tier assignments, exact per-pair keep counts, and anchors are fixed to Tail-16. The gray curve reports standalone score-kernel latency per layer at 8K. Right: illustrative 128K score curves. The shaded bands highlight the default Tail-16 window in both panels.

Figure 5 Dynamic event selection and packing. Here, ZBi denotes the i-th 16-token block of the pre-activation output-gate tensor Z within a chunk. Chunk scores determine the retention order within each head pair. Recurrent lifetime and output-visibility proxies weight the estimated gains from larger budgets, which determine the low-, medium-, and high-retention tiers. The example assigns 9, 4, and 3 pairs to these tiers. Selected events are packed in temporal order into CSR chains for recurrent execution.

Figure 11 Complete-model prefill peak allocated memory across context lengths. Measurements use BF16, batch size one, use_cache=True. The shaded region shows the absolute memory saved by SparseGDN wherever both paths complete. The dashed line marks the nominal 80 GB device capacity as a reference. Crosses indicate Native OOM at 256K and are placed on this reference line for display; they do not represent measured allocation peaks. SparseGDN completes at that length for both models. Lower is better.

Figure 7 Per-stage GDN-core prefill latency. The top and bottom rows show Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, respectively. The left column compares native Intra with SparseGDN Intra plus online Selector; the middle and right columns compare H and O. For SparseGDN, H includes deferred W materialization. Each component reports the median of per-iteration CUDA-event times summed over all 24 GDN layers. The stacked Intra-plus-Selector bars sum the two component medians. Boxed values denote the corresponding native-to-sparse latency ratios. Lower latency is better.

Figure 8 GDN-core speedup across batch sizes and context lengths. Speedup is Native/Sparse, includes online selection, and uses batch latencies aggregated over all 24 GDN layers. Crosses mark configurations without a paired speedup because Native runs out of memory. Crosses are placed at a fixed height for display and do not represent measured speedups. The corresponding sparse-only outcomes are detailed in Table 2. Every completed paired configuration favors SparseGDN. Higher is better.

Figure 2 Two empirical structures observed in layer 16 of native-dense Qwen3.5-4B on an 8K RULER input (niah_multikey_3, row 0). (a) Adjacent chunk-boundary states are frequently nearly stationary, while the magnitudes of their changes vary substantially across value heads. (b) The left panel shows |M−1 − I|, averaged over 123 complete 64-token chunks and all 32 value heads. Here M is the native Delta-solve matrix defined in Section 2.3; subtracting I removes the unit diagonal, and absolute values are taken elementwise before averaging. The coefficients concentrate near the causal diagonal and weaken across more distant token blocks. This observed locality motivates the block-adjacent approximation, whose computation support is shown in the right panel.

Figure 6 Tier-aware scheduling of heterogeneous recurrent event chains. High-, medium-, and low-retention head pairs induce event chains with different workloads. Scheduling them in physical-head order can place a long high-tier chain behind shorter tasks, creating an SM straggler and extending kernel completion time (left). SparseGDN orders chains by expected workload and uses event-count-adaptive execution to distribute them across SMs (right), reducing load imbalance and tail latency. The red dashed line denotes kernel completion.

Table 6 Kernel-pipeline ablations at batch size one on a GPU. Speedup is the ratio of reference to optimized median latency over the stages listed in Scope. Each variant uses five warmup forwards and 30 interleaved CUDA-event measurements. Within each measurement, the indicated stage times are summed across all 24 GDN layers before computing the median across measurements. Separately timed Selector work is excluded; statistics fused into Intra remain included. Geomean is the geometric mean of speedups over the six lengths from 4K to 128K; the 128K column reports the longest-context result. Each row uses its own reference, so the isolated speedups should not be multiplied. Compact+mapped reports the joint effect of compact state storage and mapped output reads.

Table 4 Algorithmic component ablation on all 13 RULER tasks at 4K (1,300 examples per model). Scores and their arithmetic differences are expressed on the percentage scale. ∆ is the score difference from Native, computed from unrounded scores. Full64 + adaptive restores the full lower-triangular 64-token intra-chunk solve while retaining adaptive event selection; Block-adjacent + all retains every recurrent event. Adaptive and random variants use matched approximately 29% event budgets. All custom variants retain the same group-local output rule; Native uses the dense operator. Adaptive masks are recomputed for each Intra variant. Bold highlights the proposed method.

Table 1 RULER scores, recurrent-event sparsity, and GDN-core speedup for Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. Scores follow the official RULER scoring rules and are reported as percentages. ∆ is the arithmetic difference between the Sparse and Base columns, computed from unrounded scores. Both scores and their differences are expressed on the percentage scale. Speedup compares native Intra+H+O against SparseGDN Selector+Intra+H+O, using the 24-layer GDN-core timing protocol in Section 3.1. Event sparsity is the mean fraction of valid recurrent pair–chunk events omitted across evaluation requests; padding chunks are excluded. The All row averages across the six context lengths.

Table 2 Batched GDN-core speedup (Native/Sparse). OOM† indicates that Native runs out of memory in the benchmark harness, while SparseGDN completes in a separate process. Plain OOM indicates that Native runs out of memory and sparse completion has not been independently verified. Speedups include online selection and cover only the GDN core.

Table 3 Retention-rate trade-off over all six context lengths. Keep is the mean fraction of valid recurrent pair–chunk events retained across evaluation requests; padding chunks are excluded. ∆ = Ssparse−Sbase is the arithmetic difference in aggregate RULER scores, computed from unrounded scores over 7,800 examples per model using the official scoring rules. Scores and their differences are expressed on the percentage scale. Speedup is the geometric mean of the six GDN-core speedups at batch size one under the timing protocol in Section 3.1, including online selection. Higher speedup and ∆ are better.

Table 7 Complete-model prefill peak allocated memory. “Incr.” denotes the peak allocation above memory already live at forward entry. “Incr. reduction” is the relative decrease in this increment, computed from unrounded values. Native OOMs during its first 256K warmup, so no completed-forward peak or increment is available. Lower is better.

Table 5 Effect of adaptive tier counts on Qwen3.5-9B. Scores are official RULER percentages over 100 examples per task at each context length (13 tasks; 7,800 examples in total). All is the mean over the six lengths. Score differences reported in the text are computed from unrounded values. Keep is the mean per-request fraction of valid recurrent pair–chunk events retained, expressed as a percentage. Both variants use the same retention tiers; realized keep rates are not forced to match. Bold indicates the higher score at each length and in aggregate.

papers.abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. GraphMP uses local message passing to keep computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. Guided by its predictions, beam search progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. We develop the decoder model factory as a paradigm for training successive models on experience generated by earlier models during decoding. Model-guided search supplies verified trajectories for knowledge distillation, folding computation spent on decoding into reusable training data. Repeated collection and distillation improve the decoder across generations and adapt its strategy as the noise changes. These results motivate a coupled quantum--classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning renews the models from operating experience. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that produces high-performance, low-latency decoders and continually adapts them to evolving quantum hardware.
authors: Anil Bilgin, Wanda Hou, Pranav Srinivas, Yi-Zhuang You
bullets: Targets quantum LDPC decoding across code families, sizes, physical error rates, and noise models without fine-tuning.
Uses local message passing for scalable predictions and beam search to refine candidate error patterns, trading latency for lower logical error rates.
Introduces a decoder model factory that trains successive models on verified decoding trajectories generated by earlier models.
Repeated experience collection and distillation let decoders improve across generations and adapt to changing noise.
Envisions coupled rapid-decoding and slower learning cycles for continually adapting quantum hardware protection.

figures.caption: Figure 5: BP distillation supplies a transferable starting decoder, while leaving a gap to stronger classical methods. The three shaded code-capacity tasks supply training data; the other nine evaluate the same model without fine-tuning. Logical error rates use 2048 realizations per task. Bars above 0.15 are truncated. Training and comparison settings are in Appendix B.

Figure 11: The final search-enhanced model G+ 3 compared with established decoders on 12 tasks. The three shaded tasks supply training data; the other nine test the same model without further training. Comparisons use the same 2048 error realizations per task, except for shorter Tesseract runs on the largest tasks. Bars above 0.04 are truncated. Decoder settings and evaluation procedures are specified in Appendix E.4.

Figure 10: Successive models improve single-pass decoding and transfer that improvement to an unseen task. Dashed green curves show single-pass decoding; solid green curves show beam-search decoding. Horizontal lines show reference decoders. Curves are means over five independent model factory runs; bands are the range across those runs. Full generation results are in Appendix E.2.

Figure 1: AI model factories connect a source of training data to new models and their applications. The language-model analogy motivates a corresponding process for quantum computing, with quantum hardware providing experimentally testable outcomes. The return arrows represent model assistance to humans or quantum hardware. In the illustrated approach, data generation supplies training examples, and distillation trains later models on these examples. This paper develops the decoding instance through supervised distillation from search trajectories, with outcome verification supplied by simulation; hardware learning, control, and calibration are prospective applications.

Figure 7: Inference-time search trades computation for accuracy. With the starting GraphMP model fixed, broader and deeper search lowers logical error while increasing decoding time. The surfaces aggregate the three training tasks; measurements and budgets are given in Appendix C.3.

Figure 12: Accuracy and decoding time on a training task and an unseen task. Logical-error curves are fitted to measured data; bands are 90% bootstrap intervals conditional on that model. Times compare GPU GraphMP with single-core CPU reference decoders. They measure time per shot in a stream of syndromes. Fit diagnostics and timing procedures are in Appendices E.5 and E.6.

Figure 13: Adaptation after the noise changes at G3. The same model is evaluated immediately before and after the switch from depolarizing to XZ noise; G4–G6 learn from newly collected trajectories. (a) Mitten150 supplies training data; (b) LP3,5 20 tests adaptation without further training on that task. Dashed green curves show single-pass decoding; solid green curves show beam-search decoding. RelayBP is evaluated with its original and updated noise priors; GraphMP’s beam-search candidate selector retains the original prior. Bands are 90% Wilson intervals. The full experiment is described in Appendix E.7.

Figure 8: Outcome feedback selects search trajectories for training. The collector retains syndromeconsistent, logically correct final predictions together with the intermediate states along their search paths. This work obtains logical feedback in simulation, while dedicated quantum-memory experiments provide a route to device-based verification.

Figure 3: Detector error model. Hidden error events connect to the syndrome bits and logical observables they flip. The decoder sees the syndrome and predicts an error pattern. Highlighted nodes illustrate one realization and its syndrome and logical outcome.

Figure 15: Gradient signal of the two objectives at random initialization: SNR (8) of the gradient signal on the shared model parameters, estimated over 8 minibatches of 64 syndromes (mean over 5 initializations, bars the range), for 15 qLDPC codes at code-capacity depolarizing noise p = 0.05. The dashed line marks SNR = 1. Codes sharing a distance are offset horizontally.

Figure 30: Training data for noise adaptation. Starting from the same G3 collector, equal-budget continuations train on fresh depolarizing data or fresh XZ data. Logical error rate is shown for a single pass (top) and for beam search (bottom), on the same 8192 realizations per task under each noise model, averaged over three training seeds. Wilson intervals summarize the pooled shot-level variation; the mean weights the three target tasks equally. Each panel reports ZA→B of Eq. (36) from the depolarizing-data student to the XZ-data student. The unmodified G3 mean is marked for reference. An escape counts as a logical success.

Figure 29: Generation progress after the noise model changes from the depolarizing noise model to the XZ noise model at G3. The nominal error-rate setting and decoding graph remain fixed. Dashed: single-pass decoder GraphMP Gx; solid: search-enhanced decoder GraphMP G+ x ; bands are 90% Wilson intervals on 8192 realizations per task. The BP teacher and Relay-BP step at G3 to their logical error rate under the original prior; the faint lines give their rate under the updated prior. The model factory collects on the first three target tasks only; LP3,5 20 is unseen during adaptation.

Figure 20: The BP-distilled starting model G0 at fixed search width W = 8 on the three code-capacity training tasks. The left endpoint is single-pass decoding; the remaining points increase the search depth. Residual-syndrome density of the predicted error pattern is shown above logical error rate, which is decomposed into failures and miscorrections. Shaded bands are 90% confidence intervals; 8192 shots per task, the same shots at every search depth.

Figure 17: Logical error rate pL of GraphMP, its BP teacher, and reference decoders on the decoding tasks of Appendix A.1, with 2048 samples per task. The shaded band marks the three code-capacity training tasks. The same model is applied without fine-tuning to the unshaded unseen tasks. The BP teacher, BP+OSD/LSD, and Relay-BP configurations are those of Section A.5.

Figure 26: GraphMP G+ 3 against classical decoders on 12 decoding tasks at the nominal error-rate setting under each task; the same tasks and realizations as Figure 17, except for shorter Tesseract prefixes (256 realizations on code-capacity GB900, LP3,5 20 and LP3,7 16 , and 128 on phenomenological LP3,5 20 ). The three shaded tasks form the model factory’s target portfolio and supply its training data. The other tasks are unseen during training and evaluate transfer beyond that portfolio. Baseline configurations are defined in Section A.5. Bars above 0.04 are truncated.

Figure 24: Later datasets challenge a fixed decoder, while later models achieve higher label-relative completion on fixed datasets. Figure 24(a): the highest nominal error-rate setting used for collection. Figure 24(b) and Figure 24(c): completion relative to the recorded final label, the fraction of states on which the prediction matches that label’s syndrome and logical outcome. Each cell pools up to 8192 sampled records per target task; root and pinned states are sampled separately. Columns D1–D3 are the new datasets defined in Appendix E.1. These are diagnostics on the archived training buffers. G0 has no pin-conditioned input and is examined only at root states.

Figure 21: Accuracy–cost tradeoff of beam search with the BP-distilled starting model G0. (a) Pooled logical error rate pL over search width W and depth R on the three training tasks at nominal evaluation error-rate settings 0.08 on BB144, 0.05 on Mitten150, and 0.08 on GB180; 24 576 shots per cell, with the same sampled errors in every cell. (b) Throughput-level decoding time (s/shot), averaged over the same three tasks. Circles mark the primary evaluation setting W = 8, R = 10.

Figure 4: GraphMP predicts errors through local message passing. The syndrome enters at detector nodes; shared learned updates update node states and messages, and error nodes read out probabilities. The same learned functions operate on different decoding graphs. Hidden states and logits are illustrative.
Figure 14: Detector error model. The fault e is drawn from the error-variable prior. The syndrome s = He is observed; the logical error l = Le is not.

Figure 25: Logical error rate of the trained students, single pass (top) and beam search (bottom). Each panel pools three training seeds. Filled points pool the seeds; open points are the individual seeds. The 95% Wilson intervals summarize pooled shot-level variation; open points show variation across training runs. Scores follow Eq. (36) from the first legend entry to the second. In panel (c) both sets are D2 collected by G1, one at a fixed error rate and one at an adaptive error rate. An escape counts as a logical success.

Figure 27: Logical error rate against physical error rate on the six decoding tasks of Figure 23, for GraphMP G+ 0 to G+ 3 , BP+OSD (BP+LSD on phenomenological tasks), and Relay-BP. Curves are fitted to the measured points; bands are pointwise 90% parametric-bootstrap intervals conditional on the fit family.

Figure 28: Decoding time per shot on the six tasks of Figure 27. GraphMP runs on one GPU with the inference implementation described in the text (single-pass G3 dashed, search-enhanced G+ 0 to G+ 3 solid, beam search in decoding mode); BP+OSD, BP+LSD, and Relay-BP run on one CPU core with one thread. Points above 1 s per shot are clipped, and BP+LSD is omitted on LP3,5 20 above p = 0.03, where it is excluded from the accuracy evaluation as well.

Figure 19: Beam search on a toy decoding task. Each box is a search state on the code’s Tanner graph. Squares are checks, filled according to the residual syndrome left by the predicted error. Circles are error variables, shaded by their predicted error probability from cream at 0 to orange at 1. The soft decoder runs two rounds of belief propagation. A thick border marks a pinned variable. Each step pins the least-confident variable to 0 and to 1. A state with no residual syndrome is completed (thick frame). The search returns the completed state of lowest weight, and the green edges mark the trajectory that leads to it.

Figure 2: Proposed coupled quantum–classical deployment of a local learned decoder. Circles represent qubits and square groups represent local classical memory. Solid and dashed links indicate quantum couplings and classical message passing; vertical arrows carry measurement data and recovery feedback between the layers.

Figure 16: GraphMP forward pass. The syndrome s and the mask µ are encoded. The decoding graph H specifies the bipartite support of the T check↔variable message-passing rounds (dashed). Readout emits logits z; per-variable probabilities are σ(zi), with σ the logistic sigmoid Eq. (10).

Figure 22: The GraphMP collection-and-training loop for x ≥ 1. Accumulated data train Gx; G+ x collects verified trajectories that supply records Dx+1. Appending those records and advancing x starts the next round. The labels B, C, and D refer to the preceding appendices.

Figure 18: Decoding-outcome profiles of GraphMP in single-pass decoding, its BP teacher, and RelayBP. Each profile classifies decoding outcomes as in Table 2. Columns report the fraction of error realizations in each category. The logarithmic scale keeps rare outcomes visible. The shaded bands between columns follow groups of error realizations from their bucket under GraphMP to their bucket under each reference decoder; band width shows how many realizations take that path. Percentages are pooled over three code-capacity training tasks.

Table 4: Representative model interfaces. Input representations and output targets are separate design choices. The demonstrated range of parameter reuse depends on the training and evaluation protocol.
Table 1: Code instances studied in the experiments. A yes marks a code used to train the decoder model. Distances written ≤ d are the published upper bounds.

Table 12: Statistical support for the fixed-model benchmark in Figure 26. Entries give logical error probabilities and pointwise 95% Wilson intervals, including an upper bound when no logical error is observed. BP+OSD is used on the code-capacity tasks and BP+LSD on the phenomenological tasks. Paired p-values are adjusted across the 12 comparisons shown; this family excludes the other decoder arms.
Table 5: Supervised formats. GraphMP distills from a simulator or a decoder teacher. A simulator supplies a hard label; a decoder may supply a hard label, a soft label, or both.

Table 11: Final-generation logical error rate, syndrome-inconsistency rate, and joint failure rate. Entries are mean probabilities over five independently trained models, each evaluated on the same 8192 realizations per task at the settings of Figure 23. Joint failure means that the predicted error has a wrong logical outcome, a nonzero residual syndrome, or both.
Table 3: Three training objectives and their probability models. MLD is optimal [A10, A23]; MLE and bit-wise MAP are successive approximations.

Table 6: Logical error rate pL of GraphMP G3, with pointwise 90% Wilson confidence intervals. Each code is evaluated on 8192 sampled errors. Single-pass decoding and both search settings process the same samples; the pooled row contains 24 576 samples. Single-pass decoding consists of one GraphMP forward pass. Search repeatedly queries that model with width W and maximum depth R = 10.
Table 9: Model initialization, training data, and subsequent data collection. Every model trains for 20 000 updates on the three target tasks. The model factory run ends at G3.

Table 8: The same two models as Table 7, deployed as decoders on Mitten150 at nominal error-rate setting 0.03. Trajectory training improves both modes, with the larger relative gain inside beam search. A prediction fails when it is syndrome-inconsistent or logically incorrect. Every model is scored on the same 32 768 error realizations; mean ± standard deviation over 3 training seeds. The comparison includes differences in source sampling as well as conditional-state training.

Table 7: The misalignment measured at the states a search visits. Two GraphMP models trained on the same trajectories, one on their root records only and one on every record, are evaluated at the recorded states of 622 held-out successful searches on Mitten150 (nominal error-rate setting 0.06, search width W = 32). The root-state-trained model fails on most pinned states even though the pinned values are correct; the trajectory-trained model turns the pinned values into completions. The pinned-state column averages over the states of a trajectory and then over trajectories. Mean ± standard deviation over 3 training seeds. A prediction fails when it is syndrome-inconsistent or logically incorrect. The probe evaluates students on selected teacher states that supply correct partial information.

Table 10: Reduction in the equal-task mean logical error rate, in percentage points, on the three code-capacity target tasks, BB144, Mitten150, and GB180. Each entry is the mean reduction over five independent model factory runs, followed by the range across those runs. Every model is evaluated on the same 8192 realizations per task.
Table 2: Classification of the residual r = e⊕ ê along syndrome consistency and logical outcome.

papers.abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.
bullets: Evaluates five LLM review paradigms across three input representations and three models using ICLR 2025 submissions.
Direct absolute rating and comparative ranking have similar rank correlation, but direct ratings are heavily compressed above the acceptance threshold.
After base-rate-matched recalibration, Direct Rating agrees more with human scores than Elo while using 24% as many API calls.
Abstract-only input outperforms full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice.
Human scores better predict citations overall; Group Rating uniquely preserves citation correlation after controlling for human scores and ranks within accepted papers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the experimental pipeline. Papers pass through three input representations (top), then through (a) absolute rating methods, which score each paper independently, or (b) comparative rating methods, which infer a latent rating from head-to-head outcomes and rescale it to 1–10. Only the comparative family is rescaled, so inflation and other absolute-error metrics are not comparable across families. Inline metrics give the best configuration in each family on the stratified 232-paper sample at the fixed ≥ 6 threshold.

Figure 7: Score distributions for the five paradigms vs. ground truth (abstract-only, GPT-4o-mini). Absolute methods (Direct, Anchor) compress scores into a narrow 6–8 range, while comparative methods (Elo, Swiss) preserve broader distributions closer to ground truth. Annotated below each: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ (Spearman correlation).

Figure 2: External validity on the 126 test papers carrying a retrievable citation count, a complete set of paradigm scores and a recorded decision. a, Paradigm rank under three evaluation targets; the lines cross, so none is best on all three. The decision target counts the 18 withdrawn submissions as non-accepted, which leaves the ordering unchanged. b, Spearman ρ with citation count, as an open circle (raw) joined to a filled circle (controlling for the mean reviewer score). Only Group Rating retains its correlation after the control (ρ = 0.304, p = 0.0006, surviving Bonferroni correction across the eighteen tests in Table 11). Anchor’s partial value is negative and Swiss’s exceeds its raw value, so the two are given as positions on a common axis rather than as a decomposition.

Figure 3: Population-scale false-positive (strong paper wrongly filtered) and false-negative (low-quality paper wrongly accepted) rates as a function of the accept threshold, swept from 5 to 7. The dashed gray line marks the fixed ≥ 6 threshold used in Table 9; the dotted green line marks the base-rate-matched threshold of Elo and Swiss; Direct Rating’s, at 7.67, lies beyond the plotted range. Direct Rating’s curves are flat across the plotted range because only 1.8% of its predictions fall below 7, which is why a fixed threshold at 6 makes it appear degenerate.

Figure 4: Error localization by ground-truth score bin (population scale, threshold ≥ 6). For each paradigm, blue bars show false-positive counts (strong papers wrongly filtered) and orange bars show false-negative counts (low-quality papers wrongly accepted). Direct’s errors are almost entirely false negatives, since its inflation accepts nearly all low-quality papers, whereas Elo and Swiss distribute the error budget across both classes, with false positives concentrated at borderline ground-truth scores.

Figure 6: Score distributions by input representation (all paradigms pooled, GPT-4o-mini). Violin shapes show density and box plots show quartiles; ground truth (gray) is shown for reference. The three representations differ little in spread (pooled σ 1.56, 1.62 and 1.59 for abstract-only, vanilla and objective), and all are far narrower than ground truth (σ = 2.16). Annotated below each group: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ̄ (mean Spearman correlation with ground truth across paradigms).

Figure 9: Cross-model performance heatmaps. Left: Cohen’s κ (practical decision utility). Center: Spearman ρ (ranking potential). Right: grade inflation (calibration). GPT-4o-mini Elo achieves the highest κ despite slightly lower ρ than Direct.

Figure 12: Ranking potential versus grade inflation (left) and versus decision utility (right) for all 15 configurations. GPT-4o-mini Direct sits at high ρ but near-zero κ, while Elo converts similar ρ into higher κ through calibration.

Figure 11: Model capability profiles averaged across paradigms, on five axes: the decision utility metrics (κ and macro F1), the threshold-free AUC-ROC, ranking potential (ρ), and a calibration axis plotting 1− inflation/4 so that a larger radius is better on every axis.

Figure 5: Interaction between paradigm and input representation. Left: Spearman ρ (higher is better). Right: Mean Absolute Error (lower is better). Abstract-only consistently outperforms across paradigms, and Elo achieves the lowest MAE regardless of input representation.

Figure 8: Robustness check: Spearman ρ (left) and Cohen’s κ (right) under four ground-truth aggregations, of which the trimmed mean coincides with the mean (Appendix M). Paradigm rankings are identical across variants.

Table 2: Best paradigm per model by ranking potential (ρ) and by decision utility, measured here by κ, abstractonly, 232-paper sample. The best paradigm differs by model and by criterion. Appendix N reports all fifteen configurations.

Table 8: Cross-model comparison, all fifteen configurations: five paradigms × three models (abstract-only, 232- paper sample). The Group rows, including GPT-4o-mini’s, use the original score-ordered grouping (Appendix D); the corrected GPT-4o-mini abstract-only Group run is reported in Table 1. Three cells rest on fewer papers, where a response or a group assignment failed: GPT-4o-mini Group n = 230, GPT-oss-120B Direct n = 230 and GPT-oss-120B Anchor n = 228. Table 2 summarizes the per-model best.

Table 5: All review methods, ranked by Pearson correlation (GPT-4o-mini, 232-paper sample). Input: input representation; Corr.: Pearson r against ground truth; Acc.: exact-match rate on the rounded 1–10 score scale, which is not the binary accept/reject accuracy of Table 6; Infl.: grade inflation. The Group vanilla and objective rows are computed on 230 papers, two having failed group assignment; the Group abstract row is the perpaper mean of the three randomized-grouping runs and covers all 232.

Table 7: Ordering-quality metrics for six representative methods, chosen to span the paradigms and input representations discussed in the text rather than to rank the top six on any single column. The first three numeric columns are NDCG@10, NDCG@20, and NDCG over all papers. Top-k precision is computed with a stable sort, so for paradigms that assign the same score to large blocks of papers it reports one arbitrary tie-break rather than a property of the ordering; see the discussion of Direct + Abstract below.
Table 1: Review paradigm comparison under abstractonly input (GPT-4o-mini). Column headings as in Table 4. The Group row is a three-run mean (Appendix D); all other rows are single runs.

papers.abstract: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR remain among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but they compare every query with the stored training set, so their inference cost and memory grow with the data and the data must be kept at deployment. We ask whether the neighbourhood geometry these detectors exploit can be compiled into a small network that scores a query with a single forward pass. We propose the Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN), which regresses each normal point onto the mean of its $k$ nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. This displacement is an empirical mean-shift vector, whose fixed-radius population counterpart locally approximates a scaled gradient of the log density. We show that Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-$t$ expert densities, and establish a constructive approximation bound for the corresponding population neighbourhood-mean map using a single-hidden-layer Cauchy network. We further show that the bounded network output guarantees asymptotically linear residual-score growth along every fixed direction. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, while scoring $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.
bullets: Addresses the inference-time and memory costs of retaining the full training set for KNN-, LOF-, and LUNAR-style detectors.
Uses a single-hidden-layer network with Cauchy activations to predict each point’s mean $k$-nearest-neighbour displacement; anomaly score is the residual length.
Connects the displacement to empirical mean shift and, locally, to the gradient of log density.
Provides theoretical results on Student-$t$ score-field representation, approximation of the population neighbourhood-mean map, and asymptotic residual growth.
On 46 datasets and 28 baselines, achieves the best mean rank for both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR; scores $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on one CPU thread.

papers.abstract: Executing an unfamiliar laboratory protocol requires a robot to identify missing capabilities and determine whether each operation remains valid as the experiment progresses. This letter presents BioAgent, an embodied agent that addresses these coupled challenges of capability sufficiency and experimental validity. It matches human-reviewed requirements to validated skills and task packages, selects tool-based implementations for missing behaviors, and requests human teaching when needed during learning. Learned skills undergo sequential task-package validation to check outcomes and compatibility between successive operations. During execution, precondition, outcome, and experimental-state checks govern progression, autonomous recovery, or termination. Execution evidence guides tool selection, while accepted experience supports offline policy updates and task packaging. On the second task, BioAgent reuses 17 skill types unchanged, revises two existing implementations, and acquires five new types. On two dual-arm laboratory tasks with 20 and 31 ordered skill invocations, BioAgent achieves complete-task success rates of 66\% and 58\% with autonomous recovery over 50 runs per task. Across 25 atomic skills evaluated over 50 autonomous trials each with recovery disabled, success rates range from 84\% to 100\%, with 17 skills achieving 50/50.

bullets: Identifies missing capabilities and checks whether each operation remains valid as the experiment progresses.
Matches requirements to validated skills, selects tool-based implementations, and requests human teaching when needed.
Sequentially validates learned skills and task packages for outcome quality and compatibility between operations.
Uses precondition, outcome, and experimental-state checks to continue, recover autonomously, or terminate.
Achieves complete-task success rates of 66% and 58% on two dual-arm laboratory tasks; 17 of 25 atomic skills succeed in all 50 trials.

papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a core design principle for sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems, yet fixed antenna geometry limits its performance. Pinching antenna systems (PASS) guide electromagnetic waves along dielectric waveguides and radiate them through position-adaptive antennas, allowing communication links and sensing observations to benefit from spatial reconfiguration. This article reviews PASS-enabled ISAC through single-waveguide, multi-waveguide, and segmented-waveguide architectures, comparing their feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support. We organize solution pathways around physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control. A segmented waveguide-enabled pinching-antenna array (SWAN) case study demonstrates joint segment selection, antenna po?sitioning, and transmit beamforming using segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning. The results illustrate how waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication-sensing tradeoffs. We conclude with research directions in joint transmit?receive operation, measurement-calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.
bullets: PASS uses dielectric waveguides and position-adaptive radiators to provide spatial reconfiguration for communication and sensing.
It reviews single-, multi-, and segmented-waveguide designs, including feed structures, spatial degrees of freedom, operating protocols, and uplink/downlink support.
Key solution areas are physics-consistent modeling, joint spatial-signal optimization, dynamic channel acquisition, and stable real-time control.
A segmented-waveguide case study combines segment selection, antenna positioning, and beamforming with segment-hysteresis reinforcement learning.
Waveguide loss and per-segment aperture gain create communication–sensing tradeoffs; future work includes joint transmit–receive operation, calibrated digital twins, and trustworthy control.

papers.abstract: Real-world robotic manipulation requires reasoning about cluttered scenes, partially observable or hidden objects, and semantically appropriate actions, in addition to low-level execution within those scenes. However, existing simulation benchmarks primarily test the latter and remain dominated by comparatively clean environments with limited clutter and narrowly scoped task structure, leaving many forms of commonsense reasoning untested. We address this by introducing a taxonomy of reasoning processes for robotic manipulation grounded in developmental cognitive science. We operationalize this taxonomy through a new benchmark of robot tasks, MolmoSpaces-CommonSense, that requires reasoning about occlusion, containment, support relations, semantically correct grasp points, spatial affordances, and hidden objects. These evaluations require policies not only to recognize relevant scene structure but also to execute correct actions in them. We evaluate several zero-shot generalist manipulation policies. Across model types and architectures, we observe consistent failures in commonsense reasoning: success rates in cluttered scenes drop by over 50% as distractors increase, policies act on incorrect objects in cluttered settings 30% of the time, and affordance-sensitive grasping remains unreliable even with highly specific language prompts, with correct object part selection happening only about 50% of the time. Further, VLM-based success estimation struggles to reliably evaluate rollouts in these settings, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond control to the broader perception-reasoning-action stack. Our results suggest that existing benchmarks may substantially overestimate zero-shot real-world readiness. Code and policy leaderboard link at https://github.com/allenai/molmospaces.
authors: Arjun Guru, Max Argus, Jae Sung Park, Jiafei Duan, Ali Farhadi, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Introduces a developmental-cognitive-science taxonomy for commonsense reasoning in robotic manipulation.
Benchmarks occlusion, containment, support relations, grasp-point semantics, spatial affordances, and hidden objects.
Evaluates several zero-shot generalist policies on tasks requiring both scene reasoning and physical execution.
Policies show substantial failures: cluttered-scene success drops by over 50%, incorrect-object actions occur 30% of the time, and correct grasp-part selection is about 50%.
VLM-based rollout evaluation also struggles, indicating challenges across the perception–reasoning–action stack.

papers.abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.
authors: Ezza Ali, Sehrish Bibi, Momina Moetesum, Faisal Shafait
bullets: The study isolates replacement operators while keeping the pruning mask fixed across several MoE models and routers.
Survivor gate renormalization can reduce accuracy by 0.8–8.5 points on routers not trained with top-k renormalization and can reverse method rankings.
The proposed tilted novice improves over MoNE’s constant replacement by 3.45 points on OLMoE and 1.37 points on Moonlight at 50% pruning, with small parameter overhead.
Operator performance is model-dependent: trained-scale rerouting leads on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, while partial expert copies match the tilted novice on two models.

Evaluation task and calibration domain matter substantially; multiple-choice retention can overstate performance on math and code tasks, while calibration shifts the pruning mask more than resampling.
