papers.abstract: Historically rare ''one-in-a-generation'' storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, causing catastrophic damage and mounting casualties, and exposing the vulnerability of infrastructure designed around short observational records. To overcome the limitations of sparse data, we present StormGen, a generative machine-learning model that transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete, physically plausible hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes. Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, StormGen produced close counterparts for 4\5% of the most severe 2\% of storms--compared to just 3\% for stochastic storm transposition--and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. Crucially, from a single hour of initial rainfall, the model successfully reconstructed the specific lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey itself, despite the event being entirely absent in training. Because storm timing alone can more than double peak flows, these complete generated scenarios provide a vital mechanism to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes.
authors: Valerie Tsao, Nathaniel W. Chaney, Manolis Veveakis, Marta Zaniolo
bullets: Addresses infrastructure vulnerability caused by short rainfall records and increasingly frequent rare storms.
Uses generative machine learning to complete observed storm beginnings into full hourly rainfall sequences.
On a decade of southeast Texas data, closely matched 45% of the most severe 2% of storms, versus 3% for stochastic storm transposition.
Reconstructed Hurricane Harvey’s lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals from only its first hour, despite its absence from training.
Generated scenarios can stress-test flood protections because storm timing strongly affects peak flows.

papers.abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
authors: Kwan Yan, Jialun Zhong, Yanzeng Li
bullets: Addresses degraded length-prediction ranking under domain/task shifts and the cost of predictor inference or retraining.
Uses a linear readout over serving-model prefill hidden states, adapted online via recursive least squares from completed requests.
Runs prediction and updates asynchronously on the CPU while overlapping prediction and initial scheduling with GPU prefill.
Improves Spearman correlation by 64.7% under a larger domain shift and reduces average per-token latency by 15.9–40.8% in serving experiments.
Achieves 1.9% higher throughput than the strongest evaluated baseline with 30,569× fewer predictor parameters.

papers.abstract: General humanoid motion trackers typically rely on deterministic policies that cannot adapt online without brittle reference editing or costly retraining. We present DiffWBC, shifting whole-body control to a generative paradigm via a one-step diffusion model. By modeling distributions over future trajectories, DiffWBC unifies general tracking, test-time steering, and simulation-free failure discovery within a single controller: (1) Generative general tracking: DiffWBC requires a single forward pass per 50 Hz control step and can be distilled from an RL teacher or trained from scratch via model-based RL, achieving the lowest local tracking error among six general trackers on held-out benchmarks (20.1 mm on BONES) and deploying on a physical Unitree G1. (2) Zero-shot test-time steering: differentiable cost gradients and body-group masks modulate the frozen controller online, substantially outperforming kinematic reference editing (0.84 clean pass at 1.25 m ceiling vs. 0.10) and zero-shot generalizing across hurdles, spatial reaching, actuator faults, and tray balancing. (3) Simulation-free failure discovery: plan dispersion across generation noise effectively identifies physical tracking failures (91% precision in top 2%) without physics simulations; targeted fine-tuning on flagged clips resolves 50% of failure cases. Videos and interactive demonstrations are available at https://diffwbc.github.io/#selfassess.
authors: Yifei Huang, Yazhao Yang, Weijia Li, Zhiheng Ma, Dian Shen
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of deterministic trackers, which typically require reference editing or costly retraining.
Models future whole-body trajectories with one forward pass per 50 Hz control step, trained via RL distillation or model-based RL.
Enables zero-shot test-time steering through differentiable cost gradients and body-group masks while keeping the controller frozen.
Detects physical tracking failures from generation-noise dispersion without physics simulation, supporting targeted fine-tuning.
Demonstrates low tracking error on held-out benchmarks, physical deployment on a Unitree G1, steering across multiple tasks, and 91% precision among the top 2% flagged failures.

Test-time costs steer the plan via analytic gradient descent on the generator input noise while weights remain strictly frozen; the renders depict nominal vs. steered plans under a 1.25 m ceiling (simulation). papers.abstract: Camera--LiDAR perception on mobile robots and intelligent vehicles depends on reliable sensor geometry throughout deployment. Installation variations create uncertainty in the initial extrinsics, while changing observation quality makes frame-wise estimates fluctuate during operation. This paper presents CalibSwitch, an observation-driven framework that separates absolute extrinsic recovery from selective state maintenance. A cross-modal absolute extrinsic generator (CAEG) combines projection-free bidirectional feature interaction with geometry-regularized learning to recover complete SE(3) candidates from image--point observations and coarse view context, without a supplied numerical initial transform. A selective recurrent calibration policy (SRCP) combines observation quality and temporal history to determine when a candidate should replace the working geometry consumed by a frozen multimodal detector. On nuScenes, CAEG achieves mean translation and rotation errors of 0.248 m and 5.884$^\circ$. Under sustained geometric transitions, SRCP reaches a mean composite error of 1.46 with 9.70\% candidate commitments, outperforming quality-based and temporal-consistency gating at comparable commitment rates. Relative to unconditional per-frame updating, it improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points. Paired geometry--observation uncertainty tests, two real-vehicle platforms, and 13.5-FPS single-camera Jetson execution demonstrate the system value of selective geometric-state maintenance for continuous perception.
authors: Haifa Zhang, Yijing Wang, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses uncertain installation geometry and unstable frame-wise calibration estimates in mobile perception.
Uses CAEG to generate complete SE(3) extrinsic candidates from image–LiDAR observations and coarse view context via feature interaction and geometry-regularized learning.
Uses SRCP to combine observation quality with temporal history and decide when candidates should replace the working geometry of a frozen detector.
On nuScenes, CAEG reports 0.248 m mean translation error and 5.884° mean rotation error; SRCP achieves 1.46 mean composite error with 9.70% candidate commitments.
Selective maintenance improves frozen-detector mAP and NDS by 1.43 and 0.92 points over unconditional per-frame updating; evaluation includes real vehicles and 13.5-FPS Jetson execution.

papers.selection_reason: Selective maintenance of working sensor geometry during deployment is a test-time adaptation mechanism for embodied perception, with cross-modal geometry recovery relevant to embodied AI.
papers.title: CalibSwitch: Observation-Driven Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Recovery and Selective Maintenance for Multimodal Perception
papers.tldr: CalibSwitch recovers camera–LiDAR extrinsics without a known initial transform and selectively updates them during deployment to maintain multimodal perception under changing observation quality.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we focus on interaction-preserving motion retargeting, which transfers human demonstrations to humanoids while maintaining spatial relationships with objects and terrain. Previous work, such as OmniRetarget, addresses this task through temporally coupled constrained optimization, requiring repeated sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations at each frame. We study this problem from an ordinary differential equation (ODE) perspective by modeling the continuous-time limit of its framewise Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions as an ODE on the robot configuration manifold. This viewpoint offers two benefits: (i) it connects OmniRetarget's SQP iterations to a backward discretization of the ODE, enabling us to establish their local convergence under suitable regularity assumptions; and (ii) it leads to TaSP-KKT (tangent-space parametrization for KKT flow), a new retargeting method based on a forward discretization of the KKT flow. The proposed method achieves the same first-order convergence to the ODE solution as the corresponding backward scheme while requiring only one weighted tangent-cone projection and a closed-form manifold update per step, thereby avoiding repeated inner SQP iterations. Numerical experiments show that TaSP-KKT achieves retargeting quality comparable to, though slightly lower than, that of OmniRetarget while running approximately twice as fast.
authors: Pengyu Zhu, Heye Wang, Xi Wang, Xuyang Wu, He Kong, Guodong Shi
bullets: Targets interaction-preserving transfer of human motion to humanoids while maintaining relationships with objects and terrain.
Models the continuous-time limit of framewise KKT conditions as an ODE on the robot configuration manifold.
Introduces TaSP-KKT, a forward KKT-flow discretization using one weighted tangent-cone projection and a closed-form manifold update per step.
Establishes local convergence of OmniRetarget’s SQP iterations under suitable regularity assumptions and matches its first-order convergence to the ODE solution.
Experiments show comparable, though slightly lower, retargeting quality than OmniRetarget with approximately 2× faster runtime.
papers.selection_reason: Humanoid motion retargeting via manifold ODE formulation of constrained optimization.
papers.title: Geometry-Aware Humanoid Retargeting via Manifold ODEs
papers.tldr: TaSP-KKT reformulates humanoid motion retargeting as a manifold ODE, avoiding repeated SQP iterations while achieving comparable quality at roughly twice the speed.

papers.abstract: Robots deployed in unstructured environments are susceptible to actuator-authority degradation, which reduces the effective control authority of individual actuators and can cause reinforcement learning policies trained under nominal dynamics to fail. Existing robustness approaches rely on discrete fault labels, broad domain randomization, or global latent variables, often without explicitly modeling continuous per-joint residual actuation capability. We propose a joint-health-aware reinforcement learning framework for robust robot control under simulated actuator degradation. Our framework encodes actuator condition in a continuous joint-health vector and models degradation as multiplicative attenuation of executed actions. A dedicated HealthNet estimator infers per-joint health from recent observations and actions, allowing the policy to redistribute control effort across healthy and degraded joints. We evaluate the method on Walker, Go2, Cassie, and Panda-based ManiSkill manipulation tasks under diverse degradation masks and severity levels. The method outperforms nominal and degradation-trained no-health baselines on the main evaluated metrics. Relative to the nominal baseline, task-level locomotion returns improve by up to 250.1\% and manipulation success rates by up to 15.2 percentage points; in the high-degradation Cassie group, return increases from 3.94 to 40.50 (+928.0\%). Ablations support the contribution of per-joint health estimation, action-degradation modeling, and health-conditioned control.

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from human videos remains an open challenge, particularly in the context of transferring a single demonstration into a spatially generalizable robotic skill and maintaining physically plausible human-like interactions. Unlike prior works that emphasize hand-motion imitation, we introduce an object-centric framework for acquiring dexterous skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos. Within our framework, we formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) objective in terms of object motion to decouple the underlying skill from the specific hand trajectory and impose constraints on hand-object interaction states to promote more anatomically natural hand configurations. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate that our method enables efficient learning from human videos and generalizable skill transfer across novel spatial configurations.

papers.abstract: Recent generative models are widely used to provide whole-body motion for humanoid tracking. Current methods combine motion generators with controllers in an open-loop paradigm, which leads to critical issues: tracking errors can accumulate into spatial drift, and the planner cannot adapt to unexpected physical disturbances without feedback from physical execution. However, directly feeding realized states back to the planner in a closed loop can cause discontinuities, resulting in physical jitter and even falls, since such states are out of distribution during training. To bridge this gap, we propose HIPC, a real-time Humanoid Iterative Planning and Control framework that couples a generative model with motion tracking into a unified planning-and-control paradigm. HIPC introduces a goal-conditioned motion planning trained with a canonical motion representation that avoids gimbal-lock singularities under extreme orientations and supports motion generation on diverse geometric and semantic conditions. Then, HIPC adopts two strategies, deviation-decayed recovery and history re-anchoring, to mitigate the out-of-distribution shift caused by realized-state feedback. Finally, HIPC operates a real-time asynchronous planning-and-control system, with latency compensation to reduce temporal mismatch for inference delay. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of HIPC under switching and composition of diverse conditions. Results show that HIPC achieves state-of-the-art goal-reaching accuracy among existing methods while simultaneously demonstrating robustness to physical perturbations and the ability to recover from falls.

papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.

papers.abstract: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a body-agnostic world model and each robot's differentiable ego-dynamics, which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it. The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and camera mounts; each robot's ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template with identified physical parameters. A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction: each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model, and imagination training through each robot's template makes the policy body-aware. On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the same world model by 3.8--10.6 percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher within 1.4--2.8 points without an online map. After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor scenes.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial reasoning is essential for connecting visual intelligence to thephysical world, yet remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), which must preserve scene state while tracking how spatial relations evolve over time. Meanwhile, video generation models (VGMs), trained to synthesize temporally coherent world dynamics, offer a rich source of spatiotemporal representations. We present GenDSR, a framework that transfers intermediate representations from VGM into VLM for dynamic spatial reasoning. Rather than treating a VGM feature as a monolithic prior, GenDSR constructs two complementary branches: a raw branch preserving holistic generative context and a delta branch emphasizing temporal variation. Task-conditioned tokenwise gates then fuse both signals and inject the result into the native visual representation. On DSR-Bench, GenDSR achieves 67.2%, surpassing the previous best result and establishing a new state of the art.

papers.abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method for multimodal prompt-injection defense that preserves task utility by erasing injected regions while maintaining surrounding media.
papers.title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: ERASE defends multimodal models against indirect prompt injections by replacing the injected region with blank modality-specific content while preserving the surrounding task-relevant media.

papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.
authors: Antonio Terpin, Francesco Banelli, Alan Bonomi, Raffaello D'Andrea
bullets: PIV performance depends on expert choices in preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing, which may fail as conditions change.
A learned agent selects configurations from a speed-budgeted library for a chosen measurement objective.
Across correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, it lowers average end-point error by 12.2–22.4% at matched speeds, including 1000–4000 image pairs/s.
In simulated velocity regulation, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24–13.59 percentage points versus a tuned fixed estimator.
Experiments in a water-channel fluidic pinball demonstrate adaptive estimator and region-of-interest selection, including physical-world reinforcement-learning control.

papers.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
papers.tldr: ART of PIV uses a learned agent to adaptively select fast PIV processing configurations, improving measurement accuracy and supporting real-time flow control under changing conditions.

papers.abstract: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.
bullets: Answer-level rewards treat equally correct traces as identical, missing differences in their learning value.
The study compares confidence-based SC with entropy-based UID-Conj., which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness.

papers.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR) and a benchmark, reformulating ASR as text generation rather than transcription, which is a significant application of Speech-LLMs.
papers.title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
papers.tldr: This work reframes speech recognition as generating any semantically grounded text supported by speech and introduces a benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring such reformulations beyond exact transcript matching.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.
authors: Xuning He, Kai Fan, Runyu Zhang, Binghuan Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong
bullets: Long-horizon agents accumulate costly contexts that can obscure decision-relevant information.

Compact sequences enable reusable KV caches and reduce later-layer computation across the agent trajectory.

papers.abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Huachuan Qiu, Ruocheng Guo, Zijun Shi

Ablations indicate that the two channels support clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to follow a language-specified person under occlusion, look-alike distractors, and ambiguous instructions. We show that improving tracking persistence can simultaneously increase safety violations. Using a compact 0.6B vision-language-action (VLA) tracker with a frozen backbone, we update only the planner head with proximal policy optimization (PPO). PPO improves success and following rates across all three EVT-Bench settings, but increases the collision rate on distracted tracking because episodes that previously ended in target loss can instead end in contact. We introduce TRACE, an execution-time target-state risk gate that preserves the learned policy and intervenes selectively. A lightweight risk head processes 84 cues, including candidate boxes, identity margins, a learned range-and-bearing probe, and the policy's commands. When the calibrated risk exceeds a threshold, TRACE rescales the translational component of the next waypoint while leaving yaw unchanged. The executed action is identical to PPO's on more than 98% of steps. In paired evaluations on identical episodes, TRACE reduces the distracted-tracking collision rate by 3.96 percentage points, while further improving success and following rates. Matched slowdown controls without target-state timing do not reproduce this improvement. Concurrent evaluation reproduces a collision reduction of 3.77 points, compared with 0.29 points for identical-arm null pairs, indicating that the effect exceeds evaluation variability. These results show that target-state-aware execution can recover the safety cost of policy post-training with minimal intervention.
authors: Mingyang Lyu, Gongce Cao, Yiyang Jia, Lu Jia, Erliang Lin, Yuhao Zhang, Yinqian Sun, Pin Lyu, Feifei Zhao, Bo Wang
bullets: PPO improves tracking success and following rates but increases collisions in distracted tracking because some target-loss episodes become contact events.
TRACE uses a calibrated risk head over 84 visual, geometric, identity, and action cues to detect risky executions.
When risk is high, it rescales only the next waypoint’s translational motion and leaves yaw unchanged; actions remain unchanged on over 98% of steps.
On paired evaluations, TRACE reduces distracted-tracking collisions by 3.96 percentage points while further improving success and following; concurrent evaluation shows a 3.77-point reduction.
The approach targets safety-cost recovery after policy post-training, with matched slowdown controls failing to reproduce the improvement.

Outside the triggered window the gated run’s dt medians differ from PPO’s by 0.017m, consistent with an intervention that is sparse and targeted rather than a blanket slowdown.

papers.abstract: Continuous-time world models generate a latent trajectory through a single ODE integration, but adding stochastic conditioning does not ensure that the model uses it. In our teacher-forced baseline, posterior means vary by only about 1% of the prior scale, and matched and swapped latents yield indistinguishable reconstruction PSNR at the reported precision. We study a supervision-shortcut hypothesis: ground-truth intermediate states can reduce the need for trajectory-associated latent information. We introduce SPT-Flow, which samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times. Re-anchoring experiments support the proposed mechanism. On LIBERO, with both models trained for 30k optimizer steps, SPT-Flow improves best-of-10 PSNR over our retrained ODEWorld baseline by 2.0 and 2.4 dB at the mid-trajectory and final frames and reduces mean LPIPS by 23%, with comparable per-sample inference cost. The rollout control recovers most of the accuracy gain; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains while reducing mean sample accuracy relative to this control. The diagnostics support trajectory-associated latent utilization; semantic mode coverage under matched conditions in the robotic setting remains unverified.
authors: Mingyang Lyu, Yinqian Sun, Gongce Cao, Yuhao Zhang, Lu Jia, Qian Zhang, Bo Wang, Pin Lyu
bullets: Teacher-forced training can make stochastic latents nearly unused because ground-truth intermediate states provide a shortcut.
SPT-Flow samples one latent per trajectory and matches a free-running ODE rollout to demonstration states at multiple readout times.
On LIBERO, it improves best-of-10 PSNR by 2.0 dB mid-trajectory and 2.4 dB at the final frame, while reducing mean LPIPS by 23% versus the retrained ODEWorld baseline.
A rollout-control variant recovers most accuracy gains; learned latent conditioning adds diversity and best-of-K gains but lowers mean per-sample accuracy.
Semantic mode coverage under matched robotic conditions remains unverified.

papers.selection_reason: Continuous-time world models with latent conditioning and ODE rollout; directly fits world models.
papers.title: SPT-Flow: One Integration, Many Futures in Continuous-Time World Models
papers.tldr: SPT-Flow improves continuous-time world models by training trajectory-level latents against free-running rollouts, encouraging latent use and producing more accurate, diverse futures.

papers.abstract: Flow matching depends critically on the coupling used to pair source and target samples. Optimal transport (OT) couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories; but, in practice, challenges remain: the source comes from a continuous distribution, only a finite number of target samples data are accessible, and the neural network has finite capacity. For these reasons, making the coupling more OT-like may not consistently improve sampling quality, in particular in the low number-of-function-evaluation (NFE) regime. Motivated by this, we introduce ReCouple, a controllable framework that constructs coarse-grained OT couplings, to better understand rollout-free OT-based post-training. We also consider extensions of this basic framework: ReCouple+ extends this toward the continuous-source setting by increasing source resolution, converging to semi-discrete OT in the appropriate limit; and ReCouple++ further adds spatial regularization, motivated by the observation that straight trajectories need not correspond to spatially simple velocity fields. Empirical validation demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods, and it reveals an NFE-dependent interplay between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and generation quality.
authors: Soon Hoe Lim, Aditi Gupta, Michael W. Mahoney, N. Benjamin Erichson
bullets: Flow matching quality depends strongly on how source and target samples are coupled.
More OT-like couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories, but may not help with finite data, continuous sources, limited network capacity, or low NFE.
ReCouple constructs coarse-grained OT couplings; ReCouple+ increases source resolution toward semi-discrete OT.
ReCouple++ adds spatial regularization because straight trajectories do not necessarily yield spatially simple velocity fields.
Experiments show an NFE-dependent trade-off between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and sampling quality.

Table 8 Additional distributional metrics on the 2D task at NFE 8. Higher is better for precision, recall, density, and coverage; lower is better for sliced Wasserstein distance (sW2).

papers.selection_reason: Coarse-grained OT coupling and rollout-free post-training for flow matching are transferable to generative video and world-model pipelines.
papers.title: Coarse-Graining Optimal Transport for Rollout-Free Post-Training of Flow Matching
papers.tldr: ReCouple provides controllable, rollout-free coarse-grained OT couplings for flow matching, exposing how coupling optimality, model realizability, and NFE affect generation quality.

papers.abstract: While modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been remarkably successful in general scene text recognition, they consistently struggle with the long-tail distribution of text that is degraded by motion blur or low resolution. These limitations are particularly apparent in egocentric applications like smart glasses, where text is often captured in noisy environments. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{BSTRB} (Blurry Scene Text Recognition Benchmark), a novel benchmark of 8,398 noisy image samples with high-fidelity annotations derived from 1,699 real-world video sequences. To support this, we present \textbf{Hawkeye}, a VLM fine-tuned on BSTRB to read and reason about illegible text by leveraging contextual priors and pixel-level alignment. Our results show that \name matches much larger VLMs on BSTRB overall and exceeds them on text at or below 20 pixels, in a single pass suited to real-time deployment. We characterize the resolution at which current VLMs begin to fail.
bullets: Introduces BSTRB, a benchmark of 8,398 noisy text images from 1,699 real-world video sequences with high-fidelity annotations.
Fine-tunes Hawkeye on BSTRB to read illegible text under motion blur and low resolution.
Hawkeye matches much larger VLMs overall and outperforms them on text at or below 20 pixels.
Characterizes the resolution threshold where current VLMs begin to fail.
Scope: focuses on degraded scene text, especially conditions relevant to smart glasses and other egocentric settings.

papers.abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
authors: Yunhui Jang, Zach Wang, Jai Doshi, Kangway Chuang, Sidney Lisanza, Taylor Joren
bullets: Targets the limitations of free-form, rewritten language memories for scientific optimization, where experience is measured quantitatively under specific contexts.
Uses domain-grounded identifiers to index insights and accumulates property-oracle measurements through local updates.
Links jointly applied interventions and decomposes evaluated sets to estimate their epistatic interactions.
Improves performance in most tested settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
Scope: results are reported for in silico antibody optimization; the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMIG. MEMIG constructs an epistasis graph with antibody-grounded identifiers. Directed edges organize property → germline → region → mutation hierarchies, while undirected edges connect co-occurring mutations and store their epistatic effects.

Figure 3: Memory retrieval of MEMIG. Given a starting antibody, MEMIG identifies the matching identifiers, retrieves the corresponding insights with their neighbors, and curates them into natural language. Blue denotes the antibody-grounded identifier and the corresponding node, green its quantitative record, and yellow the epistasis graph neighbors and the curation based on them.

Figure 5: In silico antibody binding optimization. Each numeric label corresponds to an antibodyantigen cluster, clustered by CDR sequence identity. ∗ denotes the structural baselines (dashed), which have access to the complex structure.

Figure 6: Cumulative performance progression. Vertical lines mark memory updates, where the rollouts between two lines are generated concurrently under the same memory. The curves report the centered rolling mean with a half-width of 30 rollouts, computed within each memory step. Notably, the ordering of rollouts within the same memory is random, so a downward slope does not imply performance decrease. Each dot marks the mean over all rollouts of that memory step.
Figure 2: Antibody optimization task.

Figure 7: Cumulative performance progression without a rolling average. Vertical lines mark memory updates, where the rollouts between two lines are generated concurrently under the same memory. Each point is the mean improvement over all rollouts sharing a memory step, and error bars indicate the standard error across those rollouts. To remove this smoothing, we report the mean improvement of every rollout sharing a memory step as a single point in Figure 7, with error bars indicating the standard error across those rollouts. We observe the same trend as in Figure 6, where MEMIG improves over successive memory steps while the vanilla LLM does not, which confirms that the progression is not an artifact of the smoothing.

papers.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.
authors: Tian Wang, Yongding Tao, Yihong Dong, Xiaoming Wu, Ying Guo, Ge Li
bullets: MoE expert outputs contain substantial, structured redundancy, with fewer effective modes than the nominal expert count.
Expert pruning is formulated as structure-preserving subset selection rather than independent expert ranking or exhaustive combination search.
PEEP preserves the experts’ functional subspace, while DCEP preserves their distributional geometry; both use router-derived importance weights.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, both methods perform best on average across general and mathematical reasoning benchmarks at 75% and 50% expert retention.

papers.abstract: Centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization in GPS-denied environments is generally computationally intractable when formulated in full belief space due to tightly coupled uncertainty dynamics. Prior work typically approximates belief dynamics or restricts inter-agent coupling. This work examines a multi-agent planning problem in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We obtain a tractable surrogate of the underlying belief-space problem by optimizing over the mean-state trajectories of all agents and propagating covariance for terminal constraint evaluation only. We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a discrete-to-continuous pipeline combining hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based trajectory refinement. Across 50 randomized scenarios, the planners separate as the terminal uncertainty bound tightens, with CONSORT solving 80% of scenarios where the strongest baseline solves 54%, at comparable path length. In marine simulations, with the plans executed under feedback control on an independently developed factor-graph estimate, the trajectories remain collision-free and their terminal uncertainty falls within 6% of the planner's prediction.
authors: Tony Zhang, Ryan Bartholomew, Kalliyan Velasco, Joshua Mangelson, Brady Moon
bullets: Targets minimum-time navigation with chance-constrained collision avoidance and bounded terminal localization uncertainty.
Uses mean-state trajectory optimization, with covariance propagated only for evaluating the terminal uncertainty constraint.
Combines hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based continuous trajectory refinement.
Solved 80% of randomized scenarios versus 54% for the strongest baseline at comparable path length.
Marine feedback-control simulations remained collision-free, with terminal uncertainty within 6% of predictions.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Gaige Wang, Bowen Pan, Hao Ren, Jiangjing Lyu, Chengfei Lyu
bullets: Addresses poor orientation control and weak image-to-3D structural alignment in coarse 3D generation.
Uses a first-frame-anchored canonical space to align orientation with the input view while retaining object-centric normalization.
Combines a dual-tower DiT with auxiliary reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features.
Applies spatial-prior-guided attention using pixel-to-voxel correspondences.
Can replace existing coarse stages and consistently improves final 3D generation, with state-of-the-art performance reported.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Coarse3D. (A) First-frame Anchoring rotates the canonical geometry to zero the first view’s azimuth, turning orientation prediction into a well-defined, first-frameconditioned task. (B) Dual-tower DiT couples an Image-Tower, supervised by auxiliary tasks (Lrecon) to encode cross-view geometry, with a Geometry-Tower predicting the velocity field (Lgeo) via layer-wise cross-attention, trained end-to-end. (C) Spatial-prior-guided Attention regularizes cross-attention with a rasterized voxel-to-pixel prior (Lattn), strengthening 2D-3D correspondence.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison across three baselines (TRELLIS, TRELLIS2, and ReconViaGen). For each baseline, we show the original result (Baseline) and the result after replacing its first stage with our Coarse3D (+ Ours). Anchored by the first frame of the multi-view input (leftmost), our method yields (i) more controllable orientations, (ii) higher structural fidelity, and (iii) seamless plug-and-play integration without modifying subsequent stages.

Figure 5: Effect of spatial-prior guided attention. For a representative voxel query, we visualize the attention map over pixel tokens of four input views. Top: spatial prior Asp derived from geometric projection. Middle: base model attention Adense, which spreads diffusely across the object. Bottom: our guided model concentrates on the pixels the query voxel actually projects to.

Figure 2: Comparison of three coordinate definitions: canonical space uses a fixed semantic orientation that is ambiguous; pixel-aligned camera space is aligned with the input view but not objectcentric; ours is aligned with the first input view and object-centric.

papers.abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $\alpha_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(\Phi, t_n)$ alone. Here $\alpha_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $\alpha_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
authors: Jiasong Han, Yunkai Chai, Jintao Wang
bullets: Defines a transfer operator that reevaluates a length-$L_0$ positional kernel on longer grids and computes a pre-training witness $\alpha_L$.
Characterizes relative-head generalization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer and establishes an absolute/relative duality.
Shows that learned-absolute schemes are underdetermined and derives a static expressivity bound.
Experiments on 2,625 controlled trained-model measurements show $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the studied generalizing and non-generalizing positional-encoding/task cells.
The theory does not cover content-dependent tasks such as addition or sorting; the general deterministic case remains an open conjecture.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. Select (fit) a single positional head’s kernel at length L0 realizing the task’s target pattern RL0 ; transfer the same kernel to a longer grid via TL (re-evaluate ΦLWΦ⊤ L , no retraining); old rows keep their argmax by the causal-mask identity (Thm 1); score the new rows [L0, L) to read off αL ∈ [0, 1]. The whole pipeline uses only (Φ, tn), with no Transformer training, no data samples, and no learned Transformer parameters (only a deterministic kernel-selection on the PE basis).

Figure 2: The offset taxonomy, derived (Theorem 2, Prop. 4). A relative kernel length-generalizes a fixed relative offset; a clamped learned-absolute encoding does the reverse; and neither handles a growing offset (the shared blind spot, right column). Throughout, the relative statements are for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer, the hypothesis of Theorem 2; the accompanying text explains why it is needed and what the L0-fit contributes. This 2 × 3 verdict is exactly the empirical PE taxonomy, here a consequence of what a single positional head can realize.
Figure 4: Empirical LG (solid) and training-free αL (dashed) vs. test length L (train L0=20), 1L1H. αL tracks both who generalizes and how LG decays with L.

Figure 5: Training-free α60 (left) and empirical LG@60 (right) over (PE, task), 1L1H. Agreement is strong in this single-head regime; the content-driven disagreements (which emerge at depth, not shown here) are characterized in §7.

Figure 3: Training-free αL vs. empirical LG across the three tiers (5 seeds). Left (1L1H, the setting the theory describes): learnable cells (blue) give Spearman ρ=0.90. Center, right (scale, 2L4H, 4L4H): the graded rank correlation weakens (its bootstrap CI includes 0) as the content channel rescues low-αL cells, yet high αL remains a sufficient screen at every depth (precision ≥ 0.92).

Figure 6: H3: learnable-cell Spearman ρ(αL, LG) (circles) drops with depth (its bootstrap CI includes 0 at depths 2, 4), while sufficiency precision (squares) stays ≥ 0.92 with tight CIs. αL remains a sufficient screen at all depths.

Table 1: Positioning against the closest LG frameworks. αL’s niche: pre-training, keyed to the PE’s feature map, continuous, single-head, with matched sufficiency and relative-head necessity (the general necessary condition is conjectural).

Table 3: Training-free αL (at L=60) vs. empirical LG accuracy (mean over 5 seeds), 1-layer 1-head and scale (2L4H) tiers. Top: αL tracks 1L1H LG. Bottom: at scale, the content/recency channel (outside the positional-only abstraction, S3) lets ALiBi/NoPE generalize where αL=0, making the predictor’s onesidedness visible.

Table 10: RoPE frequency sweep on content-neutral skip-3 (1L1H). No discriminating cell: where the model generalizes the taxonomy is right; at scale 0.03 αL under-predicts (false negative); at 0.01 the model cannot learn at all.
Table 2: The evaluation grid. Each axis follows the theory’s categories or standard practice; the reason given for each level is the reason it was included.

Table 6: Interior fixed-absolute positions (1L1H, mean over 5 seeds). Absolute encodings realize and transfer them; relative encodings do not learn them at all. Compare first, where RoPE scores α60 = 0.20 purely because position 0 is the causal boundary.

Table 8: L0-sensitivity (1L1H, predictor αL / empirical LG at L=3L0). The screen AUC is 1.0 at every training length and the per-cell verdicts are stable; the separation is not an artifact of L0=20. Generated by experiments/l0_sensitivity.py.

Table 7: Scale robustness: cell-level Spearman ρ(αL, LG) on learnable cells, at the paper’s default size vs. a larger model. The predictor is identical; only the trained models change. The scale study uses 2 seeds (700 rows), and both columns are computed on the cells the two studies have in common, so the 2L4H entry (0.36) is over 19 cells rather than the 20 of Table 4, where the same quantity over all 20 cells is 0.31.

Table 9: Content-driven induction (target = token after the previous occurrence of xi): positional αL = 0 for all PEs, yet 2-layer models generalize (LG up to 0.84). α+ L flags the realizable through the content channel regime αL misses; residual PE-modulation of content LG is future work.

Table 12: αL for sinusoidal under the same sweep. The absolute verdict is invariant (first≈1 everywhere; growing offsets ≈0). The bounded-offset cells (prev/skip3) are the only entries whose verdict moves with frequency – they degrade as frequencies are added (num:8→32 drives prev 0.47→0.00); the other cells’ raw αL shifts stay sub-threshold (e.g. first 0.93→1.00) and never flip the verdict. This is what the theory predicts: enlarging the realizable space does not help the L0-fit select a transferring kernel (existence ̸= selection, Prop. 3). Verdict movement appears precisely at the selection gap and nowhere else.

Table 11: αL for RoPE under varying frequency count num (feature dimension m=2 num) and θ-base. The verdict is invariant: fixed relative offsets transfer (prev, skip3=1.00 everywhere), growing offsets never transfer (copy/reverse≈0), and the kernel the L0-fit selects does not hit a fixed absolute position (first stays at chance; a monotone kernel in the family could, but the fit does not select it, see the discussion after Prop. 4). For low-frequency scaling see Table 10.

Table 4: Depth trend (H3), learnable cells (train acc > 0.8), 5 seeds. The Spearman column is cell-level with a bootstrap 95% CI over the (PE, task) cells; the precision column is the rate Pr[LG ≥ 0.7 | αL ≥ 0.5] with a bootstrap 95% CI over the high-αL rows. αL stays a high-precision sufficient indicator at every depth (precision CIs well above chance); the graded rank correlation, by contrast, is significant only at depth 1 – at depths 2, 4 its CI includes 0, consistent with αL acting as a binary screen rather than a graded predictor once content rescues low-αL cells.
Table 5: Inductive-bias ablation (75 rows in the 1L1H setting). The cross-entropy fit, not the min-norm interpolant, drives the αL–LG correlation.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.
authors: Shengran Guo, Min Chi, Feifei Qiao, Varad Patwardhan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating symbolic, formula-based answers and distinguishing different skill states behind identical scores.
Uses a shared RoBERTa encoder with regression, ordinal, and classification grading heads, plus Q-matrix-guided prediction of skill mastery and learning gain.
Detects likely Gen-AI assistance and converts assistance probabilities into weights that reduce the influence of potentially unreliable cognitive evidence.
On 49,402 responses across 19 semesters, AICG reduces MAE by 50.3% versus RoBERTa regression and raises QWK from 0.798 to 0.927.
Cognitive supervision drives most of the gains; AI-aware weighting provides additional improvements, especially in recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models. To address this challenge, we propose the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints. To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field (RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot's state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control limits without relying on predefined robot identities. We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without retraining.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Janghyun Cho, Jeehyun Lee, Changjoo Nam, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing GCBFs, which generally assume homogeneous dynamics or predefined robot classes.
Uses a shared second-order reference-point space to represent safety while preserving each robot’s dynamics and control constraints.

papers.abstract: Real-world image editing requires coordinating multiple visual transformations with content preservation and reference constraints, yet aggregate scores can readily obscure unmet local requirements. Effective evaluation must therefore identify local failures and translate them into priorities for subsequent model improvement. We introduce WeGenEditBench, comprising 2,740 evaluation instances and 148 task types across single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing. Pre-generated checklists shared across models decompose each request into atomic requirements; item-level deductions and visual evidence are established first and then summarized into scores for edit execution, preservation, visual quality, and task-specific correctness. To support the experience-acquisition component of recursive self-improvement (RSI), we develop WeGenEvoStudio, a unified multi-agent harness for RSI-oriented learning that integrates model-conditioned failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation. Among 15 evaluated configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing with an Overall score of 4.076, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing at 4.291. Evolution experiments across four generation and editing benchmarks demonstrate substantial targeted gains: on their report-selected Top-5 single-image targets, FLUX.2 [dev] improves Overall from 1.083 to 3.517, while Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 gains 13.2%. Together, our benchmark and harness provide a foundation for developing more reliable image models through interpretable evaluation and feedback-driven learning.
authors: Jun He, Canmiao Fu, Ying Zhang, Zhipeng Huang, Chenyu Mu, Yazhen Xie, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Weijia Li, Xiang Zhang
bullets: Benchmarks 2,740 instances across 148 single-image, text-intensive, and multi-reference editing tasks.

WeGenEvoStudio combines failure diagnosis, retrieval-grounded data construction, supervised adaptation, and re-evaluation for recursive self-improvement.
Among 15 configurations, GPT-Image-2 leads single-image editing, while Seedream-5.0-Pro leads text-intensive editing.
Evolution experiments show targeted gains, including FLUX.2 [dev] improving from 1.083 to 3.517 on selected single-image targets.

papers.abstract: RGB-thermal (RGB-T) object detectors combine visible and thermal imagery for robust detection, but signal corruption in either stream can substantially degrade accuracy. Restoration-based methods incur significant latency and do not consistently improve downstream accuracy, raising a more direct question: rather than restoring corrupted inputs, can we efficiently adapt the detector to their varying signal quality? Conventional PEFT offers an efficient route, but its input-independent corrections cannot track diverse test-time corruptions. Our controlled corruption sweeps show that corruption types have similar effects near clean conditions but diverge increasingly with severity, motivating corruption-aware, per-input adaptation. We therefore propose PG-FM (Prompt-Guided Feature Modulation), which adapts RGB-T object detectors to the estimated corruption type and severity of each modality. Under controlled RGB-T corruption simulations, PG-FM preserves clean-set performance, improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST, and transfers without retraining to unmodified, naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.
authors: Liuyin Shi, Chengqi Li, Wenbo He
bullets: RGB-T detection can degrade sharply when either the visible or thermal stream is corrupted.
Fixed, input-independent parameter-efficient adaptation cannot handle diverse, severity-dependent corruptions.
PG-FM uses prompts to guide geometric feature modulation based on estimated corruption type and severity for each modality.
Under simulated corruptions, it preserves clean performance and improves mAP50 by up to 20.8 points on FLIR and 19.9 points on KAIST.
The method transfers without retraining to naturally acquired external RGB-T datasets.

papers.abstract: Cameras and vision sensors are widely used for product and process inspection in manufacturing environments. Traditionally, this process required thousands of images of both nominal and defective products to train such models. Recent research shows that vision transformer (ViT) models, such as CLIP, can reduce this requirement to 50-100 images per nominal and defective class. However, collecting even 50 defective images can be difficult in high-yield or low-volume manufacturing processes. In this paper, we examine the utility of two recently proposed structured decision models (Jev and Clef-Flash) in applications using as few as k=2 reference images per class at inference. In the process, we provide three main contributions: (a) a framework for k-shot learning of these models for image classification/inspection applications; (b) an agentic approach for automatically refining the text descriptions that guide image classification in these decision models; and (c) an approach to calibrate the resulting defect probabilities to improve their reliability for inspection decisions. We test these contributions in five manufacturing case studies. Using two reference images per class, both Jev and Clef-Flash outperform CLIP's test accuracies with the same references (0.75-1.00 [Jev] and 0.71-0.99 [Clef-Flash] vs 0.67-0.84 [CLIP]). Furthermore, we show that our agentic refinement of text descriptions significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and our calibration approach reduces the Brier score in 13 of the 15 model-application configurations. To support the reproducibility of our work, we provide our replication code and have created the R "decisions" package for evaluating additional models. We also provide a publicly available web app that allows practitioners to inspect their own images with no code.
bullets: Addresses inspection settings where defective examples are scarce, requiring far fewer references than conventional models.
Introduces a k-shot learning framework for structured decision models in image classification and inspection.
Uses agentic refinement of text descriptions, improving accuracy in 6 of 8 model-application combinations.
Calibrates defect probabilities, reducing Brier score in 13 of 15 configurations.
Provides replication code, an R package, and a no-code web app for practitioner use.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental capability for 3D spatial perception in robotic and intelligent systems. While data-driven discriminative methods have achieved compelling performance for monocular depth estimation, generative approaches can reconstruct fine structural details with stronger generalization. However, most existing generative diffusion models suffer from low inference efficiency caused by multi-step sampling, whereas single-step diffusion models struggle to recover high-fidelity depth maps. To mitigate these drawbacks, this paper presents FlowMoDE, a coarse-to-fine flow-matching-based framework for efficient, structure-aware monocular depth estimation supporting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization. The core architecture first conducts coarse-level decoding conditioned on diffused features extracted from a pre-trained semantic encoder, and subsequently restores fine-grained structural patterns via expanded decoding layers. Trained exclusively on a single synthetic indoor dataset, our proposed method outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, yielding an average 14.1% reduction in relative error against state-of-the-art works as well as 9.9\% reduction in chamfer distance for point cloud reconstruction. We further validate the generalization capability of FlowMoDE on realistic robotic scenes, with qualitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. The project page is https://flowmode-shao.netlify.app/
authors: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Jinsong Lin, Zhiwei Fang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of multi-step generative depth models and the fidelity limitations of single-step alternatives.
Decodes depth coarsely from diffused features produced by a pre-trained semantic encoder, then restores fine structural details with expanded decoding layers.
Trained only on one synthetic indoor dataset while targeting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization.
Outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, reducing relative error by 14.1% on average and point-cloud Chamfer distance by 9.9%.
Generalization is additionally assessed qualitatively on realistic robotic scenes.
