papers.abstract: Safe navigation in heterogeneous multi-robot teams faces two coupled challenges: differences in robots' braking and turning capabilities limit how each robot can respond to an approaching neighbor, while simultaneous interactions require a single control action to satisfy multiple collision-avoidance constraints. Together, these challenges can make local safety constraints incompatible with a robot's admissible controls, leaving a decentralized safety controller without a feasible action. We propose a Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF), based on the insight that navigation actions should preserve access to a certified recovery maneuver. First, we construct a backup-recoverable set in a shared Cartesian operational space by evaluating whether prescribed backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until the robots come to rest. Each maneuver respects the corresponding robot's kinematic and actuation constraints, making the recovery certificate capability-dependent. Second, CA-BRF filters candidate controls by selecting admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions while coordinating the selection across simultaneous interactions. This preserves backup recoverability while retaining as much of the candidate action as possible and ensures that all pairwise recovery conditions are satisfied by a single executable control for each robot. Together, we establish recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed-loop system even when the nominal safety-constrained optimization becomes infeasible. The validity and effectiveness of the proposed CA-BRF are validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments of robots with five different kinematic classes.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Yanze Zhang, Wenhao Luo, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses infeasibility caused by differing braking/turning capabilities and multiple concurrent collision-avoidance constraints.
Builds a shared-space backup-recoverable set by checking whether constrained backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until stopping.
Coordinates admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions across simultaneous interactions.
Establishes recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed loop, including cases where nominal safety optimization is infeasible.
Validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments spanning five kinematic classes.

papers.selection_reason: Capability-aware backup-recoverability safety filter for heterogeneous multi-robot navigation; relevant to embodied safe navigation.
papers.title: A Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: CA-BRF keeps heterogeneous robot teams safe by filtering controls to preserve a feasible, capability-specific recovery maneuver, even during simultaneous interactions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.
authors: Jihao Zhao, Shuaishuai Zu, Pengfei Li, Biao Qin, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Baochuan Yang
bullets: Aggregate acceptance metrics can obscure differences across reasoning, browsing, and tool-use states, especially in later browsing actions.
TraceSpec combines dynamic execution, fixed-prefix replay, and state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps.
TraceSpec-Traj provides 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states from browsing and software-engineering trajectories.
Adaptive intermediate-turn supervision improves replay throughput by 12.5%–22.6% over DSpark across tested target sizes and temperatures.
Scope: results focus on trajectory replay and evaluated agent workloads; findings also indicate workload and phase affect speculative-decoding behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TraceSpec, a framework for improving speculative decoding in LLM agents by connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. This addresses agent execution and LLM architecture.
papers.title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: TraceSpec improves speculative decoding for LLM agents by using trajectory-aware analysis and adaptive draft training, increasing replay throughput over its baseline.

papers.abstract: Stickers are widely used in social media dialogues to express affect, stance, and intent beyond literal text. Their meanings are often non-literal and context-dependent, making them difficult to handle with generic visual fusion or standalone captioning. We propose Sticker-to-Text Dialogue Reconstruction (S2TDR), a structured multimodal reconstruction framework that converts sticker turns into contextually appropriate textual utterances. S2TDR decomposes sticker interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction, using OCR text only as an auxiliary cue when available. The reconstructed dialogue can then be consumed by existing text-based dialogue models. Experiments on sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization show that S2TDR generally improves multiple downstream models over direct sticker integration methods. Further analyses on component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality indicate that structured reconstruction provides an interpretable and effective way to integrate sticker semantics into dialogue understanding.
bullets: Addresses the non-literal, context-dependent meanings of stickers in social media dialogues.
Decomposes interpretation into visual cue extraction, affective-intent inference, and context-aware dialogue reconstruction.
Uses OCR text only as an auxiliary signal when available.
Improves downstream sentiment analysis, intent recognition, and dialogue summarization across multiple models compared with direct sticker integration.
Analyses cover component ablations, OCR-empty stickers, and reconstruction quality, supporting interpretability and effectiveness.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a structured multimodal reconstruction framework for interpreting stickers in dialogue, combining visual and textual cues. This falls under general multimodal foundation models and fusion techniques.
papers.title: S2TDR: Structured Multimodal Reconstruction for Sticker-Aware Dialogue Understanding
papers.tldr: S2TDR improves sticker-aware dialogue understanding by reconstructing contextually appropriate text from stickers before applying text-based dialogue models.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
authors: Zhichang Yu, Baining Cao, Sbaaoui Idriss, Qi Wang, Gangqiang Xu, Ling Qin, Xiaoling Jin, An Liu, Shaohao Cai, Xiaoyang Bao, Shengle Chen, Changchang Ding, Pengfei Zhu, Jingxiang Xu, Yifeng Mao, Lu Liu, Hai Jin, Yingfeng Zhang
bullets: Agentic search harnesses can achieve strong retrieval-augmented answering with simple BM25/grep retrieval, but uncontrolled loops waste queries, reread documents, and fill context windows.
The proposed supply layer compiles documents into structures such as claim-evidence navigation trees, entity graphs, timelines, ontologies, wikis, and memories.
Claim-evidence navigation trees reduced query tokens by 38% on average, with 91% savings when the compiled evidence sufficed and a 1.9% increase otherwise.
A decision gate reduced reported latency from 140 seconds to 30 seconds, while retrieval-round substitution introduces its own latency cost.

Structural artifacts showed no detectable FRAMES accuracy gain under a competent harness, so their value is primarily efficiency, governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, and continuity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Context as infrastructure. Knowledge compilation is the supply side: an ingestion pipeline that enriches raw documents into typed context artifacts. The harness is the control side: it decides which artifact, if any, enters the window and when the loop stops. Tools are the contract between them. Arrows show the flow of context, not control. The navigation tree (highlighted), whose leaves are claim–evidence pairs, is the mechanism measured in this paper; the ontology artifact (highlighted) is the one whose value is primarily commercial rather than benchmark-visible.

The last two rows are arm means, not conditional splits: each is the mean change of that arm against the uncompiled baseline over the queries in that arm (evidence present, evidence absent), so −52% is not comparable with the −91% hit figure or with the −38% average. papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'knowledge compilation' as a memory mechanism for LLMs in agentic systems, transforming raw retrieval results into structured, navigable context to reduce token usage and improve efficiency.
papers.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
papers.tldr: Knowledge compilation can make agentic retrieval more efficient by supplying governed, navigable context, even when it does not improve benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
authors: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov, Matt Thomson
bullets: Introduces two benchmarks for evaluating deductive reasoning across increasing inference depths.
Uses a controllable formal graph benchmark and a real-world knowledge-composition benchmark.
Compares knowledge supplied in context with knowledge encoded in model weights, without chain-of-thought prompting.
In-context knowledge substantially outperforms deduction over pretrained knowledge, though both degrade with longer compositions.
Findings highlight limitations relevant to prompt-based agent control and continual learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models receive graph adjacency in-context but integrate the information poorly, failing at long-range inferences. DeepSeek, Kimi, Nemotron, and 12 other models answer questions about a random graph of 50–60 nodes given in the prompt as a list of edges, with reasoning off. Each question concerns the nodes exactly k hops from a start node, so k = 1 questions require only direct-neighbor information. a) Verify: is a given node exactly k hops away? Accuracy falls from 93–100% at k = 1 to 49–56% at k = 3, close to chance. b) Count: how many nodes are exactly k hops away? Models count correctly 43–69% of the time at k = 1 and ≤ 16% from k = 2. c) Name one: name a node exactly k hops away. Models name a neighbor at 99–100%, but a node two hops away at only 9–40%. d) Enumerate: list every node exactly k hops away. Models list all neighbors at 71–100%, but no model lists more than 12% of sets correctly from k = 2.

Figure 2: Models compose facts from the prompt far better than from memory. DeepSeek, Kimi, and Nemotron answer k-hop Wikidata questions with reasoning off and information given in context, in memory, or both. a) The chain’s facts are given in the prompt under invented names, among 16 decoy chains with the same relations. All models compose at ≥ 94% up to k = 3, but at k = 6, Kimi composes at 29%, while DeepSeek and Nemotron Ultra fall to chance. b) The facts are recalled from memory without supporting facts in the prompt. Composition reaches only 37–64% at k = 2 and ≤ 12% from k = 4, although every fact is known. c) The facts are given in the prompt under their real names, among 16 real decoy chains, so the model can use both the prompt and memory. Accuracy reaches 36–71% at k = 6.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks LLM knowledge integration across in-context and parametric memory, with direct implications for memory reasoning and continual learning.
papers.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
papers.tldr: ImplicitHop shows that LLMs struggle to integrate multi-step knowledge, with performance declining sharply as inference depth increases, especially for pretrained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. In this regime, stateless ECMP can perform poorly: hash collisions may overload one spine link while leaving others idle, stretching transfer times by seconds. Yet this same persistence makes coordination practical. Since these flows are long-lived, even lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime. We present ARK, a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism. ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without requiring switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering. Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 FCT by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.
authors: Hung-Chun Lin, Ting-Wei Hsu, Chung-En Ho, Ahmed Saeed
bullets: Disaggregated prefill/decode inference creates long-lived, bandwidth-heavy KV-cache transfers.
Stateless ECMP can hash concurrent transfers onto the same spine link, causing congestion and delays.
ARK reserves paths by coordinating senders to select source ports that map flows across distinct spines.
The mechanism requires no switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering.
RDMA simulations report up to 27.3% lower mean FCT, 34.0% lower P95 FCT, and 12.9% lower mean TTFT under moderate load.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Network topology (b) ARK path reservation controller (c) ARK deployment with separated control and data planes

Figure 2: Mean and P95 flow completion time (FCT) as a function of request rate (QPS) under Poisson arrival. ARK consistently reduces bothmean and tail FCT, with the largest improvement at QPS = 25 (mean FCT − 27.3%, P95 − 34.0%).

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the efficiency of KV cache transfers in disaggregated LLM inference by introducing ARK, a distributed path reservation mechanism to avoid routing collisions and reduce latency.
papers.title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
papers.tldr: ARK coordinates KV-cache transfer paths to avoid ECMP collisions, reducing flow completion time and time to first token in disaggregated LLM inference.

papers.abstract: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.
authors: Luyao Zhu, Fangfang Zhang, Yi Mei, Ke Chen, Mengjie Zhang
bullets: Addresses poor cross-task generalisation and knowledge loss when scheduling conditions change.
Uses an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance adaptation to new tasks with retention of prior knowledge.
Weights knowledge reuse according to task similarity.
Improves surrogate-model estimation with distance constraints.
Experiments show reduced catastrophic forgetting, strong adaptability, and better performance than compared methods.

papers.title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
papers.tldr: A surrogate-assisted genetic programming framework enables scheduling rules to adapt across sequentially changing flexible job-shop tasks while reducing catastrophic forgetting.

papers.abstract: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
bullets: The study disentangles parent inheritance from per-round feedback breadth under matched evaluation budgets.
Across 1,750 preregistered runs on nine prompt and program-synthesis benchmarks, greedy parent inheritance drives most optimization progress.
Seed-reset search remains weaker even with summaries of all failures or larger proposer models.
Full-set clustering and diverse failure selection help early seed rewrites, but inheritance quickly closes the gap by retaining solved error modes.
In GEPA, validation and minibatch gating consume most compute; proposer reflection is a small cost, suggesting simpler inheritance-based loops can capture most gains.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'Lineage' as a form of memory in LLM-guided optimization, demonstrating that parent inheritance drives optimization progress and effectively captures the benefits of complex reflective loops.
papers.title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization
papers.tldr: In short-budget LLM-guided optimization, preserving and iteratively improving a successful parent matters far more than exposing broader failure feedback.

papers.abstract: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
authors: Huancheng Chen, Xiaodi Sun, Zhaoqiong Huang, Michelle Chang, Jingwen Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of flat SkillBanks, which retrieve skills without modeling the overarching strategy for using them.
Introduces hierarchical routing: coarse-grained talents guide execution and softly prioritize associated fine-grained skills.
Uses matched rollout reward contrasts to train talent selection and group-relative advantages for downstream execution.
Across seven QA benchmarks and two agentic benchmarks, TalentRL consistently improves performance and achieves the best reported results among compared methods.
Reported peaks include 99.3% success on ALFWorld and a 90.7 score on WebShop.

papers.selection_reason: LLM agent skill routing over procedural memory fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing
papers.tldr: TalentRL improves LLM agents’ procedural-memory use by learning high-level strategy selection alongside skill retrieval through contrastive, strategy-guided reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.
authors: Junyu Huo, Zihao Wan, Ziqi Mao, Gouri Ginde
bullets: World-model releases can change model configurations, preprocessing, and test harnesses, causing inconsistent verdicts or faulty scores without crashes.
TetraState evaluates each paired possible/impossible video test under four fixed model-native configurations.
Tests are assigned one of four outcome classes based on correct verdict counts; inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately.
Per-test outcome transitions expose regressions that modal accuracy can hide: harness revisions changed 11 and 214 labels despite only 0.2- and 2.6-point modal-accuracy shifts.
The study motivates configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TetraState, a regression-testing protocol specifically designed for learned video world models (Cosmos, V-JEPA), addressing the challenge of verifying model updates and harness configurations.
papers.title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses
papers.tldr: TetraState reveals configuration- and harness-level regressions in learned world models that aggregate accuracy and verdict-flip checks can miss.

papers.abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
authors: Eadom Dessalene, Michael Maynord, Amir-Hossein Shahidzadeh, Botao He, Yasamin Tabatabaee, Ruoshi Liu, Ruohan Gao, Paul Pu Liang, Yiannis Aloimonos
bullets: Pairs egocentric video with bimanual EMG, IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation.
Uses EMG as a dense, occlusion-free alternative to costly and subjective manual action annotation.
Learns shared sensorimotor representations through video–EMG cross-modal pretraining.
Transfers the learned representations to action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction.
Also conditions video diffusion on EMG to generate fine-grained hand-manipulation videos; the approach outperforms evaluated video self-supervised baselines across four tasks and eight datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MOTORSENSE. (A) Sensorimotor Alignment. (B) Downstream Tasks. The learned representations are used for downstream tasks: 1) video diffusion consisting of a single reference frame as input along with EMG control signals, 2) action recognition, 3) 3D hand-object Reconstruction, 4) 3D hand contact prediction.

The video conditioning model misinterprets the action performed, generating a rotation of the bread as opposed to a spreading action of the spoon, whereas our method correctly generates a video of the spreading of mayonnaise with a spoon.

Figure 1: EMG captures both categorical and continuous structure of hand actions. (Top) For three discrete hand configurations repeated twice—fist, point, and flat—each pose produces a distinct and reproducible EMG signature: fist is marked by a suppressed purple channel (#7) with respect to flat and a pronounced red channel (#1) with respect to point; point exhibits lower overall amplitude, with less purple than flat and less red than fist; flat is distinguished by pronounced purple and red activation. (Bottom) A pick-and-lift sequence combines gradual and abrupt transitions: the hand moves smoothly from rest through pregrasp into grasp, changes sharply as force is applied at lift, then settles—non-instantaneously—into a steady hold. papers.selection_reason: Egocentric video and EMG sensorimotor alignment for action understanding; learns transferable embodied knowledge from human interaction videos.
papers.title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
papers.tldr: MotorSense introduces a large-scale synchronized video–EMG dataset and cross-modal pretraining approach that aligns visual and motor representations for improved action understanding and hand manipulation generation.

papers.abstract: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
bullets: Introduces 400 multiple-choice questions covering answerable inside knowledge and post-cutoff outside knowledge, with abstention available.
Defines NAS and KIS scores to reward searching for outside knowledge and avoiding unnecessary searches for inside knowledge.
Evaluates five commercial LLMs with and without vendor web search, focusing on deployed search behavior rather than verbalized confidence.
GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of outside-knowledge items but only 1% of inside-knowledge items; Mistral Small searches about 20% of outside-knowledge items.
Explicit temporal cues strongly influence search: two selective models’ NAS drops from about 0.72 to 0.57–0.58 without cues.

papers.selection_reason: Studies when LLM agents retrieve external information versus relying on static internal memory, directly informing LLM memory and retrieval decisions.
papers.title: Confident Fools or Careful Searchers? A Behavioural Study of When LLMs Search Beyond Their Static Internal Memory
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that commercial LLMs vary widely in deciding when to search, with some searching appropriately for recent facts but missing uncued knowledge gaps.

papers.abstract: Vision-language compositionality is the ability to identify which properties, relations, quantities, and states bind to which entities in both an image and a caption, and to match those bindings across modalities. Existing benchmarks evaluate this ability through image-text matching: a model ranks candidate image-caption match similarities and succeeds when the correct match comes on top. In such datasets, paired images differ by more than a single binding: scene, layout, and content all differ, with 97% of pixels changing on average. Such pairs do not isolate compositionality: results are confounded by global image differences. We introduce Compositional Single-EdiT (CompoSET), a benchmark dataset in which each base image-caption pair has an edited counterpart, or foil, that preserves the scene but differs by a single controlled edit, such as color, count, spatial relation, or object state. Base and foil images preserve naturalistic scene complexity yet are visually near-identical: only 8% of pixels change on average. Our dataset has many foils per base scene (~22) in order to separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty, a distinction one-foil-per-base benchmarks cannot make. CompoSET contains 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, spanning 16 edit types in 4 semantic categories, with captions at 3 verbosity levels. We test 22 dual-encoder VLMs and find that all models perform at or below chance level on CompoSET, despite scoring well on prior benchmarks. This suggests that apparent progress under prior image-text matching protocols may be an artifact arising from confounds in benchmark design, and that compositional understanding in dual-encoder VLMs is far from solved. CompoSET addresses the confounds and offers a better controlled benchmark to measure future progress.
bullets: Existing image-text matching benchmarks confound compositionality with large global image differences.
Each CompoSET foil preserves the scene while changing one property, relation, quantity, or state; only 8% of pixels change on average.
Multiple foils per base scene (~22) separate scene difficulty from edit difficulty.
The benchmark includes 1,776 instances across 80 naturalistic scenes, 16 edit types, 4 semantic categories, and 3 caption verbosity levels.
All 22 evaluated dual-encoder VLMs performed at or below chance, questioning progress measured by prior protocols.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled single-edit benchmark isolating vision-language compositionality and exposing limitations of multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: CompoSET: A Controlled Single-Edit Benchmark for Vision-Language Compositionality
papers.tldr: CompoSET isolates vision-language compositionality with near-identical image-caption pairs differing by one controlled semantic edit, revealing that tested dual-encoder VLMs perform at or below chance despite strong prior benchmark results.

papers.abstract: Quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has be- coming increasingly important for reducing the computa- tional costs and resource requirements for practical deploy- ment.Growinginterestinthisareahasmotivatedthecommu- nity to move beyond 8-bit quantization towards 4-bit preci- sion, leading to the development of customized 4-bit formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4. Recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) has emerged as a competitive alternative which adopts a Block Floating-Point(BFP)formatwithathree-levelscalinghierar- chy, thereby achieving a significantly larger dynamic range. While quantization can substantially reduce memory usage and accelerate inference, it frequently introduces accuracy degradation. Calibration is therefore essential for narrowing theperformancegapbetweenlow-precisionquantizedmodels and their full-precision counterparts. Nevertheless, existing calibration methods are mainly designed and validated us- ing integer-precision formats, such as INT4, lacking support for HiF4 due to its hierarchical BFP structure. In this paper, weinvestigatethreecalibrationapproaches,namelyHiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant, to further enhance model quantizationbasedontheHiF4format.Extensiveexperiments demonstratethatallthreeproposedapproachesimproveinfer- ence accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reduc- ing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and out- performing the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.
authors: Jing Huang, Yu Cheng, Ziwei Yu, Lan Zhao, Sitan Li, Guangxiu Yao, Xin Wang, Yuanyong Luo, Hengyi Liang, Ting Li, Bo Liu, Hu Liu, Michael Bi Mi, Heng Liao
bullets: HiFloat4 uses a three-level hierarchical block floating-point structure to provide greater dynamic range than other 4-bit formats.
Existing calibration methods largely target integer formats and do not directly support HiF4’s hierarchical structure.
The paper introduces HiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant for calibrating HiF4-quantized models.
Experiments show all three methods improve over direct HiF4 conversion.
The methods reduce the HiF4–BF16 accuracy gap to below 1% and outperform NVFP4 in the reported evaluations.

(a) HiGPTQ: columns in white represent the group currently being quantized; (b) HiAutoRound: learnable parameters are introduced to automatically adjust the micro-exponent and mantissa components, which are optimized via gradient descent; (c) HiFlatQuant: learnable transformation matrices P1, P2 and perchannel scaling c are introduced to flatten outliers in weights and activations, which are optimized via gradient descent.

papers.selection_reason: Calibration methods for HiFloat4 LLM quantization directly target memory-efficient model deployment and inference.
papers.title: Calibration of Large Model Quantization based on HiFloat4 Format
papers.tldr: Three HiF4-specific calibration methods substantially improve 4-bit LLM quantization, narrowing the accuracy gap to BF16 to under 1% and outperforming NVFP4 across evaluated models and tasks.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.
authors: Aryan Das, Vinay Kumar Verma, Aakansha Mishra
bullets: Targets the extra persistent memory required by Muon’s momentum buffer in EMA-teacher self-distillation.
Reuses, radial-adjusts, and spectrally normalizes the teacher–student displacement, then combines it with the NS-orthogonalized gradient.
Theoretical analysis gives linear contraction toward a residual error level under regularity and alignment assumptions.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with SDFT, it improves average accuracy by 2.6 points over AdamW and 5.4 points over momentum Muon, using 42% and 27% less persistent memory, respectively.
On Olmo-3-7B-Instruct with SDPO, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Muon-RT, a method to reduce persistent training memory in LLMs by reusing the teacher-student displacement, directly addressing memory efficiency in large-scale model training.
papers.title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Muon-RT eliminates Muon’s separate momentum buffer by reusing the EMA teacher–student displacement, reducing persistent memory while improving reported LLM accuracy.

papers.abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
authors: Chenhao Hong, Jiakai Xu, Kaushiki Singh, Yusen Zhang, Eugene Wu
bullets: Targets pre-attempt difficulty estimation for model routing, test-time compute allocation, and tool selection.
Uses a cheap LLM to convert problems into a Constraint Intermediate Representation, which deterministically compiles into a constraint graph.
A graph neural network encodes the constraint structure to predict LLM response correctness.
Evaluated across seven SAT, logic, and math reasoning benchmarks and four LLMs.
Improves prediction over the strongest baselines, lowering NLL from 0.465 to 0.423 and raising AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727.

papers.selection_reason: Predicts LLM task complexity from constraint structure to guide routing and test-time compute allocation, relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Security operations centers (SOCs) need to turn terabytes of alerts, logs and flows into trusted, affordable decisions to unveil hidden threats. We present LanG 2.0, an agentic system that detects threats, correlates evidence and writes rules, investigating whether small local models can replace frontier models affordably and safely when structural safeguards, not model accuracy, provide the guarantees. It incorporates entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger. Tests span eight flow datasets from five networks, real XDR alerts and multistage campaigns. Against its predecessor, campaign correlation precision rises from 18.75% to 51.81%, and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33%. Against Claude Opus 5.5, scoring flows against each network's normal traffic detects attacks on unseen networks at 73.42% F1 without false positives, versus 58.10% with 49.00% false positives, for at least 650 times less energy. Finetuned models statistically match it on alert classification and rule writing for 5.6 to 59 times less energy. The work demonstrates LanG's practical scalability, processing 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes, over 30 million hourly, and its safeguards resisted prompt injection, label poisoning and ledger tampering, so small local models can carry most SOC detection affordably and safely.
authors: Anes Abdennebi, Nadjia Kara, Laaziz Lahlou, Hakima Ould-Slimane
bullets: Correlates entities and evidence, detects campaigns, and proposes detection rules for semi-automated security operations.
Uses human approval for rule changes and a tamper-evident ledger to improve safety and accountability.
Improves campaign-correlation precision from 18.75% to 51.81% and rule acceptance from at most 60.00% to 98.33% over its predecessor.
Achieves 73.42% F1 on attacks from unseen networks without false positives, using at least 650× less energy than Claude Opus 5.5.
Scales to 3.33 million records in 6.4 minutes and resists prompt injection, label poisoning, and ledger tampering.

papers.abstract: Latent dynamics learning has emerged as a prominent approach for Model Order Reduction (MOR) of time-dependent, parameterized Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Traditional autoencoder-based approaches are intrinsically tied to fixed spatial discretizations during both training and inference, motivating the development of meshless methodologies. In this context, conditioning provides a natural mechanism for representing temporal evolution through spatially continuous functions, enabling mesh-agnostic Latent Dynamics Models (LDMs). In this work, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for mesh-agnostic LDMs based on conditioning in Neural Fields (NeFs). Leveraging a taxonomy of conditioning mechanisms (weak, strong, and pure), we formulate meshless LDMs as NeFs conditioned on a latent state. We establish a Universal Approximation Theorem (UAT) for this class of models and analyze their stability by deriving Lipschitz bounds for different conditioning mechanisms. Our analysis reveals an expressivity--stability trade-off, providing insight into why more expressive conditioning, despite its higher representational capacity, can potentially degrade performance during temporal extrapolation. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of meshless and mesh-based architectures in the continuous limit of the spatial discretization, showing that meshless models guarantee grid-independent Lipschitz bounds, unlike mesh-based counterparts. Our experiments across Burgers' equation, Navier--Stokes flow past a cylinder, and linear advection show that meshless LDMs can achieve predictive accuracy comparable to or better than their mesh-based counterparts while using only 2% of the trainable parameters and exhibiting nearly constant error across spatial discretizations.
authors: Lorenzo Tomada, Federico Pichi, Gianluigi Rozza
bullets: Recasts meshless latent dynamics models as neural fields conditioned on a latent state, enabling inference across spatial discretizations.
Introduces a unified framework covering weak, strong, and pure conditioning mechanisms.
Proves a universal approximation theorem and derives Lipschitz stability bounds for each conditioning type.
Identifies an expressivity–stability trade-off: more expressive conditioning can impair temporal extrapolation.

Experiments on Burgers’ equation, cylinder-flow Navier–Stokes, and linear advection show comparable or better accuracy than mesh-based models, with 2% of their trainable parameters and nearly discretization-independent error.

papers.selection_reason: Meshless latent dynamics models conditioned on latent states are transferable to learned environment dynamics and world-model prediction.
papers.title: Meshless Latent Dynamics Models for Model Order Reduction of time-dependent Partial Differential Equations
papers.tldr: This paper develops mesh-agnostic latent dynamics models for PDE model reduction, with theory and experiments showing grid-independent stability and competitive accuracy using far fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.
bullets: Frames continual world-model learning as a contextual MDP with behavioral and physical context components.
Organizes continual learning into knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition.
Studies direct reuse when behavioral rules stay fixed using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks.
Finds that physical-context changes can substantially degrade zero-shot reuse, depending strongly on observation representation.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies zero-shot generalization bottlenecks in continual world models, directly relevant to world-model reuse and continual RL.
papers.title: Before We Adapt: The Zero-Shot Generalization Bottleneck in Continual World Models
papers.tldr: Zero-shot reuse of learned world models can fail under physical changes, making representation generalization a key bottleneck in continual reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $\alpha^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $\alpha$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.
authors: Ka\u{g}an Akman, Jake Feldman Starosta, Naci Saldi, Serdar Y\"uksel
bullets: Develops theoretical error bounds using finite-model and finite-window approximations.

For finite-order hidden Markov sources, the error decays exponentially with context length under filter stability.

Shows near-lossless prediction in the limiting regime for general stationary ergodic sources and stable hidden Markov models; numerical studies support the theory.

papers.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.
authors: Zhixuan Xu, Yichen Li, Bingchen Wu, Rui Wang, Yiwen Hou, Zixuan Liu, Tianyu Qiu, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving natural human dexterity while creating robot-compatible, contact-grounded demonstrations.

Improves mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand–task pairs on LEAP and Wuji.
Hardware and software designs are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods. Across continuous-control tasks and Atari Pong, empirical evaluations show that dynamic boundary selection enhances sample efficiency and late-training performance over fixed-horizon and auxiliary-enabled baselines.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing a fixed imagination horizon when model predictions become unreliable.
Uses a score-informed relative-density proxy to estimate trajectory reliability and determine bootstrap depth.
Introduces hard boundaries that stop return expansion and soft boundaries that gradually shift toward critic bootstrapping.
Preserves boundary value estimates and applies survival weights to actor and critic losses.
Theory establishes contraction of the gated Bellman operator and reduced conditional target variance from earlier bootstrapping; experiments cover continuous control and Atari Pong.

papers.selection_reason: Improves latent world-model RL by adaptively bounding imagined rollout depth, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: Density-Guided Bootstrap Boundaries for Latent World-Model Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Density-guided boundaries adapt how far imagined trajectories are trusted, improving world-model RL’s sample efficiency and late-training performance.

papers.abstract: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.
authors: Armin Shafiee Sarvestani, Sheyang Tang, Jialu Xu, Zhou Wang
bullets: Addresses underconstrained HDR recovery and limited camera response function supervision from single-exposure LDR views.
Uses pseudo-HDR reconstructions as guidance while enforcing consistency with input LDR images through a closed reconstruction loop.
Learns a monotonic CRF prior to support plausible LDR re-exposure beyond the observed intensity range.
Factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and 3D gain field, reducing the impact of inconsistent pseudo-HDR targets and enabling HDR appearance editing.
Reports substantial superiority over baselines in extensive experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of PriorGS. Given single-exposure multi-view LDR captures of a scene, we reconstruct the 3D HDR scene as an LDR base extended by a 3D gain field. Input views supervise the LDR base, while pseudo-HDR targets generated by a 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction model impose LDR-to-HDR prior on HDR recovery. We then re-expose the HDR view by a priorconstrained learnable CRF to match the same input view, which closes the reconstruction loop.

Figure 1: Given the same single-exposure inputs, methods lacking learned LDR-to-HDR priors reconstruct the LDR novel view faithfully but fail at HDR radiance recovery. We leverage this prior to recover radiance much closer to the GT. HDR results are tone-mapped identically for visualization.

papers.abstract: In multi-task settings, combining multiple modalities allows task representations to draw on signals that a single modality alone would not capture. However, individual tasks may depend disproportionately on particular modalities, a structure that conventional fusion-based architectures do not model explicitly, instead enforcing a unified representation space. Consequently, a task's gradients can affect parameters tied to modalities it barely relies on, leaving features that compromise between competing demands. Although prior work has explored task-weighting and loss-balancing strategies, their effectiveness is limited by the absence of explicit modality separation, preventing models from optimising each modality according to its task-specific importance. To address these limitations, we propose MOSAIC (MOdality-Separated Architecture with Inter-modal Cross-attention), which preserves unimodal representations while enabling controlled interaction between them, and uses modality-specific losses to route gradients to their corresponding partitions. On the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation (CEJC), MOSAIC improves average macro-F1 by 7.4 points across four tasks with a 72% reduction in backbone parameters relative to a fusion-based baseline. Our results demonstrate that modality partitioning yields consistent gains across tasks while requiring far fewer backbone parameters than a fusion-based design.
authors: Aryan Chowdhury, Yizheng Sun, Thomas Carroll, Riza Batista-Navarro
bullets: Targets tasks that rely disproportionately on different modalities, which conventional fused representations do not explicitly model.
Preserves unimodal representations, enables controlled inter-modal interaction through cross-attention, and uses modality-specific losses for gradient routing.
On the CEJC benchmark across four tasks, it raises average macro-F1 by 7.4 points over a fusion-based baseline.
Uses 72% fewer backbone parameters than the baseline while achieving consistent gains across tasks.
Scope: results are reported on the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation and four tasks.

papers.abstract: A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.
authors: Jin-Cheng Rao, Zheng-Meng Zhai, Ying-Cheng Lai
bullets: Trains parameter-aware reservoir computers on time series collected across multiple parameter values.
Generates autonomous closed-loop trajectories at user-specified parameters not present in the training data.
Supports multi-parameter training, parameter scans, fixed-parameter echo state network forecasting, hyperparameter optimization, and optional PyTorch GPU acceleration.
Demonstrates applications on three benchmark dynamical systems, including predicting collapse and estimating critical transitions from pre-critical data.
Scope is data-driven prediction when governing equations are unknown; performance is illustrated through benchmark examples rather than a universal guarantee.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Structure of rc prediction. The model predicts the next state as a trained linear readout of the reservoir features, u(t+∆t) ≈Wout ϕ(r(t+∆t)); each factor of this equation corresponds to one part of the package, which supplies the data u, fits the readout Wout, or generates the reservoir features ϕ(r). The dashed box labeled “Parameter-aware extensions” collects the components added for the parameter-aware framework on top of a standard echo state network.

Figure 1: Parameter-aware reservoir computing as implemented in rc prediction, shown for the collapse-prediction setting. The reservoir, with state r(t), is fixed and randomly connected; only the linear readoutWout is trained, by a single ridge regression pooled over all training values pj . For prediction, the output is fed back as the next input, u(t+∆t)← v(t+∆t) (dashed loop), while the parameter input is held at a test value ptest. (3) Top: the closed-loop trajectory at one ptest > pc is the model’s prediction of whether and when the system collapses. Bottom: repeating this over a grid of parameter values gives the estimate p∗c , the first collapsing grid value.

(2) Training: the user configures collapse detection, hyperparameter tuning, and GPU acceleration, and then fits the model. papers.abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.
bullets: Addresses privacy and intellectual-property risks from large language models reproducing training sequences.
Zeros out task-redundant attention heads before inference, without retraining or changing training data.
On GPT-2-XL, pruning 729 heads reduced memorisation count by 91.5%.

papers.abstract: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.
authors: Abdul Wasi, Akhil Gorugantu, Mahesh Bhosale, Anjan Dutta, Junsong Yuan, Sauradip Nag, David Doermann
bullets: Addresses limitations of whole-object rigging and 2D part-level handles in geometry-intensive image editing.
Uses CS-ARAP deformation with neighborhood covariance smoothing to reduce rotation discontinuities at part boundaries.
Introduces inversion-free selective texture transfer to move source appearance onto edited geometry through semantic matching.
Experiments report state-of-the-art geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

Stage 2 (Global 3D Refinement): The Stage 1 Jacobian field is refined using Lrefine, combining handle constraints with SDS gradients from the diffusion model, producing a semantically plausible mesh for final rendering.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in deep learning has substantially advanced automated grading of ophthalmologic pathologies, supported by large annotated datasets and improved representation learning. However, a significant gap remains between state-of-the-art performance and clinical scalability. In particular, foundation models have reshaped image-based medical screening and diagnosis. These large-scale architectures trained on extensive datasets learn rich, generalizable feature representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In ophthalmology, RETFound, one of the most relevant foundation models for retinal images, performs strongly across classification, segmentation, and risk prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, foundation models are often computationally prohibitive, hindering their deployment in real-world clinical environments where hardware constraints and latency are critical. To bridge this gap, we introduce CAMEL (Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning), a novel cross-architecture distillation framework that uses an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning to effectively transfer knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact, lightweight student models. Our experimental evaluation across four datasets shows that CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity, enabling lightweight yet highly accurate models suitable for resource-limited clinical settings.
authors: Andre Guarnier De Mitri, Giovani Decico Lucafo, Miller Matheus Lima Anacleto Rocha, Diego Furtado Silva
bullets: Addresses the deployment barriers of large retinal foundation models, including hardware requirements and latency.

Targets resource-limited clinical screening and diagnosis settings.

papers.abstract: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of attention with increasing context length by compressing the KV cache.
Formulates attention in a kernel-associated Hilbert space, representing it as a ratio of linear maps whose interpolants can be compressed directly.
Proposes GAIM and Q-DAIM methods based on GEIM and Q-DEIM interpolation techniques.
Uses Taylor-series, Performer, and Random Fourier Features surrogates to reduce compression cost from quadratic to linear time, and extends the approach to streaming attention.

Numerical experiments evaluate residual and future-query output errors; preliminary LongBench-E results show performance comparable to existing methods, while suggesting Q-DAIM can reveal where KV-cache information is concentrated.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising way to oversee increasingly capable agents. It succeeds in part because current models appear limited in their ability to control what they verbalize in their reasoning traces. We investigate the source of this limitation and link it to an entropy collapse in the first few tokens following the opening thinking tag. We exploit this mechanism to recover CoT controllability through two inference-time interventions on initial tokens: prefilling, where even a single token can substantially increase controllability, and banning frequent opening tokens combined with in-context examples, which improves average compliance by 34-41 percentage points across models. These interventions recover mainly addition and style controllability (adding or transforming information), while suppression controllability (avoiding or removing information) exhibits more varied responses, suggesting distinct underlying mechanisms. Consistent with this, the two groups behave as separate capabilities: across models, performance correlates positively within these groups, while cross-group correlations are mostly negative. Importantly, we find that the relationship with monitorability depends on the evaluation: addition and style controllability more consistently positively correlate with monitorability, while suppression often shows negative associations. Our findings motivate the development of controllability evaluations that distinguish difficulty initiating a specific opening from general limitations of the ability to alter reasoning content, alongside separate reporting of control tasks and categories.
authors: Hugh Van Deventer, Dmitrii Troitskii, Laura Ruis
bullets: The study links limited CoT controllability to entropy collapse immediately after the opening thinking tag.

Addition and style control improve more consistently than suppression, indicating partly separate capabilities.
Monitorability is more positively associated with addition and style control, while suppression often shows negative associations.
