papers.abstract: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.
authors: Paul Lutkus, Lars Lindemann, Stephen Tu
bullets: Targets feedback control from learned latent dynamics while preserving stability of the original system.
For linear time-invariant systems, jointly learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with sufficiently long multi-step backward losses recovers stabilization-relevant structure.
A minimum H∞-norm controller designed in latent space can stabilize the original system through the learned encoder when the latent dimension is sufficient.
Forward prediction-only losses may discard unstable modes, and single-step reconstruction may produce controllers that fail to stabilize the original system.
Experiments on a nonlinear flexible-arm system demonstrate practical implications for nonlinear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model agents by sampling and selecting among multiple candidate trajectories, but common realizations assume that these trajectories can be executed in parallel. This assumption breaks in realistic deployments, where enterprise workspaces and cloud services are shared and persistent, costly or infeasible to replicate, and actions may introduce irreversible side effects or cross-trajectory interference. Existing generative world models avoid direct execution, but typically compress environment state into a single prompt, limiting their ability to reliably simulate transitions under partial observability. Instead, we introduce Agentic World Modeling (AWM), which reformulates next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task. For each hypothetical action, an agentic simulator adaptively queries the real environment through safe read-only interfaces, reasons over the returned evidence, and uses executable computation to construct the resulting observation without mutating shared state. Integrated with trajectory-level TTS, AWM enables parallel exploration over a single shared environment. Across $\tau$-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench, AWM outperforms a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07% on average, and surpasses a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% on average. These results establish interactive, read-grounded simulation as a practical foundation for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments.
authors: Wendi Li, Huseyin A. Inan, Wei-Ning Chen, Yanzhi Chen, Chetan Bansal, Saravan Rajmohan, Sharon Li
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of executing many agent trajectories in shared, persistent, or irreversible environments.
Uses multi-turn evidence acquisition: an agentic simulator queries safe read-only interfaces, reasons over evidence, and computes hypothetical observations without mutations.
Integrates the simulator with trajectory-level test-time scaling to explore multiple trajectories on one non-resettable environment.
Outperforms single-shot simulation by 40.07% on average and a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% across τ-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench.
Scope: relies on environments that provide sufficiently informative safe, read-only interfaces.

papers.title: Agentic World Modeling for Agent Test-time Scaling without Environment Replica
papers.tldr: Agentic World Modeling enables safe parallel test-time exploration by simulating action outcomes through adaptive, read-only interaction with a shared environment.

papers.abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.
bullets: Fixed-conservativeness filters trade performance inside their operational design domain (ODD) against safety margin outside it.
The proposed filter-agnostic pipeline uses policy confidence to modulate filtering at runtime.
High confidence permits better performance where filter assumptions are valid; low confidence adds margin beyond the ODD.
Preliminary F1TENTH simulations show the approach combines strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

(b) Zooms into a sharp corner. (c–d) Same corner for fixed γ = 0.55 (crashes) and fixed γ = 0.08 (completes).

Table 1: Outcomes for 60 laps per method, inside and outside of the ODD.

papers.selection_reason: Runtime confidence-modulated safety filtering for learned robot policies; relevant to embodied navigation and control.
papers.title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
papers.tldr: A runtime confidence-based safety filter adapts conservativeness to policy reliability, improving the balance between performance and safety across and beyond its certified operating domain.

papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.
bullets: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share spaces with companion animals, motivating welfare-informed navigation.
Researchers designed a laterally arcing pass-by maneuver triggered at the dog’s alert distance, based on canine communication and legible-motion theory.
In a naturalistic home evaluation with one companion dog, the maneuver produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline.
Repeated stopping and reorienting made the maneuver discontinuous and potentially less legible, becoming a stressor itself.
The pilot reframes cross-species navigation around animal legibility and the validity of proxy stimuli.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a pilot study on robot navigation behavior and canine welfare, highlighting challenges in cross-species legibility for embodied agents.
papers.title: Robot Navigation and Canine Welfare: A Pilot Study Surfacing Challenges for Cross-Species Legibility and Proxy Validity in Animal-Machine Interaction
papers.tldr: A pilot study found that a dog-oriented robot curve-out maneuver increased stress compared with a straight-line pass, revealing challenges in making robot behavior legible to animals and validating proxy stimuli.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents equipped with tools expose intermediate outputs for inspection and comparison with the model's reasoning, which may offer safety benefits over single-shot models. This paper tests that potential benefit when the sensor reading itself is untrusted, so that the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault. We consider a dermatology agent based on segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and an iterative vision-language reasoner and define a coupling taxonomy that distinguishes single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. On PAD-UFES-20, we show that typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval preserves the payload at a readable scale and produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases); full-image retrieval produces 35% (43%). Under a binary decision, if both channels are wrong, their predictions must agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect joint failures, limiting disagreement recall to 0.29 (crop-first) versus 0.57 (full-image). The direction of the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.
authors: Nishi Kanta Paul, Md Shihabul Islam Shovo, Md Mostafijur Rahman, Jamil Fayyad
bullets: Defines a fault-coupling taxonomy for separating single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree.
Evaluates a dermatology agent combining segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and iterative vision-language reasoning.
Typographic injection causes detectable directional retrieval capture, while physical corruption does not.
Crop-first retrieval yields more joint wrong agreement than full-image retrieval (55% vs. 35% across cases).
Hard-label comparison cannot detect agreeing joint failures; disagreement recall is 0.29 for crop-first and 0.57 for full-image retrieval, with the order effect reproduced on HIBA.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates fault coupling in vision-language agents, which are a form of embodied AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Coupled or Independent? Fault Coupling in Agentic Medical Vision Systems
papers.tldr: When tool and reasoning channels share visual faults, agreement between them can conceal failures, limiting the safety value of channel comparison in medical vision agents.

papers.abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.
authors: Lun Ai, Yu-Heng Wu, Jonathan Schaul, Leonie K\"uchenhoff, Denes Turei, Francesco Carli, Fabio Petroni, Aurelien Dugourd, Julio Saez-Rodriguez
bullets: Studies two recursive-agent design choices: what evidence state is built and how recursion is stopped.
Introduces ProClaim-eval, a dataset of 718 SUPPORT/REFUTE claims across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy.
ProClaim maintains evidence outside the model context, enabling controlled comparison of recursion components.
Evidence-state accumulation outperforms in-context accumulation, and the stored content affects performance.
A separately trained judge performs better than fixed-round stopping and achieves the highest gold-label agreement on three of five subsets.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Verdict prediction-label agreement (outlined segments) across three verification settings on the SIGNOR and ConnectomeDB subsets of ProClaim-eval (406 claims), using Claude Sonnet 4.6. Both document-guided and naive retrieval verification do not produce consensus reliably and overproduce REFUTE predictions due to insufficient or noisy information, a limitation that ProClaim addresses. This comparison with ProClaim highlights the benefit of recursive knowledge construction, driven by adaptive retrieval and evidence organisation before deciding the final verdict.
Figure 1: Document-guided vs. consensus scientific claim verification.

papers.tldr: Structured, externally maintained evidence states and trained stopping judges improve agents’ verification of scientific consensus claims.

papers.abstract: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting rich but opaque histopathology foundation-model embeddings in terms of tissue and cellular concepts.
Trains vanilla and Batch-TopK sparse autoencoders on NCT-CRC embeddings from CONCH, with UNI2-h used for robustness evaluation.
Evaluates reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, feature coherence, label enrichment, and preservation of downstream tissue-class information.
Sparse representations preserve most tissue-class signal and yield more coherent, label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components.

Introduces a WSI-level visualization workflow that places latent activations in broader tissue context; findings appear across two foundation models but do not automatically establish histopathological meaning.

papers.abstract: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,\mu\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of simulating fast flapping-wing aerodynamics efficiently for slower flight-control and reinforcement-learning tasks.
Combines robot and wing geometry descriptions with composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline.
A five-block model reaches 0.9646 mean fidelity at 65.19× speedup, while a streamlined four-block model reaches 0.9662 at 67.98×.
Stroke harmonics improve held-out frequency-step fidelity by 0.3176; explicit transient lag states add no benefit once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are used.
The benchmark covers 48 held-out scenarios, including wind, gusts, frequency transitions, and cross-robot flat-plate cases.

papers.selection_reason: Composable simulation platform and reduced-order aerodynamic models for flapping-wing robot learning and RL.
papers.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics
papers.tldr: FlapSim is a modular MuJoCo platform whose reduced-order aerodynamic models achieve near-reference wrench fidelity at roughly 65–68× lower computational cost, with phase-locked harmonics especially important during frequency changes.

papers.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.
bullets: The study introduces a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score by measuring text–audio distance in valence–arousal–dominance space.
The score is validated against human judgments and tested across acted, conversational, and spontaneous speech using three audio-capable models.
Audio-related incongruence increases prediction errors across all three corpora, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance.
Supervised classifiers show the opposite pattern, implicating how audio-language models combine evidence rather than the underlying signal.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates audio-capable large language models for speech emotion recognition, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Multimodal speech emotion recognition models are more error-prone when a speaker’s words and vocal delivery convey incongruent emotions, suggesting a fusion problem rather than a lack of emotional signal.

papers.abstract: High-dimensional tensors are ubiquitous in real-world applications but lead to massive storage overhead. Functional tensor decomposition addresses this by employing neural networks to map element coordinates to tensor cores, significantly reducing the parameters for data compression. However, existing functional methods typically flatten high-order tensors into 1D sequences. This folding operation causes highly overlapping local coordinate sequences and struggles to capture complex cross-mode spatial dependencies, severely limiting their expressiveness on diverse datasets. To tackle these challenges, we propose TensorSSM, a novel Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for functional decomposition method that memorizes spatial positions within a dynamic State Space Model (SSM). Specifically, TensorSSM first decomposes mode-wise coordinates into sequences spit by K-ary rule, encoding spatial tokens from coarse to fine, which effectively captures spatial variations. Furthermore, we extend the SSM's state space to explicitly map cross-mode spatial dependencies, allowing inter-mode interactions to enhance the updates of each mode. By integrating cross-mode information from previous hidden states into the current state transitions, TensorSSM effectively expands tensor representation along two dimensions: the sequence dimension for coarse-to-fine spatial tokens, and the state dimension for cross-mode memorization. This design effectively integrates spatial information into the state space and the tensor core, substantially advancing the state adaptability and enhancing the expressiveness of the data compression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TensorSSM achieves significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, exhibiting robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without relying on strict spatial assumptions.
authors: Sheng Zhang, Xinyi Wang, Maolin Wang, Xiangyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitations of flattening high-order tensors into 1D coordinate sequences, which can lose complex spatial relationships.
Decomposes mode-wise coordinates using a K-ary rule to encode spatial tokens from coarse to fine.
Extends the SSM state space to memorize cross-mode spatial dependencies and interactions.
Reports high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency across diverse tensor datasets without strict spatial assumptions.

papers.abstract: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/FARO.
authors: Xiaojun Wu, Cehao Yang, Xuhui Jiang, Chengjin Xu, Jia Li, Jian Guo
bullets: Targets hand-designed optimizer assignments and uniform global update budgets in large-language-model training.
Assigns each parameter block a geometry using realized counterfactual return, then reallocates frozen budgets via cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC).
On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, FARO-Adaptive matches NorMuonAndAdam, while FARO-ERC lowers loss by 0.0136 nats on average across 6 seeds.
The gain is consistent across all seeds, exceeds measured run-to-run noise, and persists under a corrupted data stream.
Budget changes trim riskiest blocks rather than expanding safest ones.

Figure 2: FARO. Lane 1 routes every parameter block by comparing candidate geometries on a held-out counterfactual probe, then freezes the routes. Lane 2 reallocates the frozen budgets: it measures each block’s update-to-weight ratio, winsorizes and caps it, and solves for the scale λ⋆ that preserves the total budget exactly. The frozen budgets flow down from the routing lane; the risk signal is refreshed upward from the applied step.

papers.selection_reason: New optimizer for GPT-style large language model training, relevant to LLM foundation model research.
papers.title: FARO: Function-Space Adaptive Return-to-Risk Optimization via Cross-Block Equal-Risk-Contribution Budget Allocation
papers.tldr: FARO automatically chooses optimizer geometry and reallocates update budgets across parameter blocks, improving language-model training loss over a strong hand-designed baseline without extra time or memory.

papers.abstract: Scientific foundation models (SciFMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of PDEs, including the ability to efficiently adapt to unseen data distributions with additional finetuning. As with all neural architectures, finetuning such models comes with the risk of catastrophic forgetting, whereby adapting to new tasks degrades prior knowledge of the model. We study catastrophic forgetting in Walrus-1.3B, a SciFM for continuum dynamics, over the course of a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation: first finetuning on simulated flow around a cylinder and then adapting to experimental data of the same system. We find that finetuning on the simulations rapidly degrades rollout performance on the original pretraining datasets, with one-step errors increasing up to 35x after just 20 epochs. Subsequent adaptation to real data further erodes performance on the simulated task. We characterize the potential drivers of forgetting, such as dataset dependence and task representation similarity. We then show that replaying as little as 1% simulated data during real-data finetuning recovers most of the lost simulation performance while retaining effective adaptation to the experimental dynamics. Our results identify catastrophic forgetting as a practical obstacle to sim-to-real adaptation of SciFMs and show that lightweight replay strategies significantly improve retention.
authors: Haaris Mian, Miles Cranmer, Alessandro Favero, Payel Mukhopadhyay
bullets: Studies forgetting across two stages: simulated cylinder-flow finetuning followed by experimental-data adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Examines catastrophic forgetting and replay during sim-to-real adaptation of foundation models, directly relevant to continual learning.
papers.title: Frozen in Time: How a Physics Foundation Model Forgets Under Sim-to-Real Adaptation
papers.tldr: Walrus-1.3B suffers severe catastrophic forgetting during sim-to-real adaptation, but replaying just 1% simulated data largely preserves prior simulation performance while enabling adaptation to experiments.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.
authors: Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu

More LangFlow denoising steps improve results at lengths 16 and 128, showing that inference refinement affects model comparisons.

papers.abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
bullets: An opponent’s group-level response can serve as a shared “tell,” revealing information unavailable to individual members.
Precommitting to response rules determines how much the opponent can hide and can prevent losses when the opponent prioritizes its own objectives.
In a solved Gaussian setting, deliberately limiting how much information the team uses can recover the truth while preserving the opponent’s concealment cost.
An exact test characterizes when this information-recovery result holds in finite games.
Trust allocation matters: private randomization, differentiated responses, or a small trust discount can protect against deception.

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.
authors: Mingzhi Pei, Zhangchen Ye, Ruoqu Chen, Liu Cao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified hand, camera, scene, and interaction reconstruction in existing methods.

Figure 3: Overview of EgoHSI3R. Each incoming egocentric frame is encoded by the scene encoder Es into image tokens, and each detected hand is processed by the pretrained hand encoder Eh. The decoder jointly processes scene tokens and hand prompts while reading from and updating a persistent scene state. The Scene Head predicts camera pose and world-space pointmaps, and the MANO Head reconstructs bilateral MANO parameters. The interaction-aware Contact Builder combines decoded hand tokens with local scene features, which are then used by the Contact Head to predict per-vertex contact and refine hand reconstruction. All outputs are produced online in a shared world space without test-time optimization.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
bullets: Evaluated 281 policies from seven families across about 1,700 trials of RJ45 grasping and insertion with a five-fingered hand.

Absolute actions improved vision-language-action insertion success by up to 70 percentage points; decomposition, multi-view sensing, and recovery data appeared beneficial but were not isolated.
Only five of 67 offline metrics correlated reliably with success, and only within one policy family, so real-robot evaluation remains necessary.

papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.
authors: Jiahe Wu, Bing Cao, Xingyue Guo, Ruipu Zhao, Beiming Yu, Jiekang Feng, Qinghua Hu, Pengfei Zhu
bullets: Targets incomplete visual observations involving small objects, subtle attributes, changing viewpoints, and multimodal inputs.

Finds persistent weaknesses in spatial judgment and cross-modal/cross-view reasoning, with stronger perception linked to better reasoning.
UAV-PUR models adapted from Qwen3-VL improve multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points for 4B and 8B variants, respectively.

papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.
authors: Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Yilei Jiang, Dongming Wu, Jiaxu Wang, Xiangyu Yue

papers.abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
authors: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
bullets: A human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models found 86.1% semantically plausible, but several models overused BLOCK and missed clarifiable ASK cases.
The paper defines safety sufficiency as preserving and exposing evidence needed for policy-conditioned authorisation decisions.
SafeWebWorld benchmarks safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains using action-conditioned futures, decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions.
Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning improved evidence preservation but could worsen authorisation-sensitive decisions.
Latent Authorisation Recovery recovered some performance through score recalibration, but fine-grained and matched-authorisation behaviour remained poor.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.
authors: Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, Dongsheng Luo

Explicitly stating the named-grouping convention improves accuracy by 14.5–16.5 points.
With GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet reach 78% accuracy and outperform raw-history baselines, indicating model-dependent rule learning.

papers.title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum

papers.abstract: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.
authors: Daniel Levine, David van Dijk, Kenneth Kay
bullets: Targets limitations of existing zero-shot inference and continual-learning models, especially weak inductive biases and externally controlled learning.
Uses internally generated activity and external feedback to create a neuromodulatory signal that gates a local three-factor Hebbian update.
Reports success on zero-shot tasks, emergent zero-shot and continual-learning abilities, and reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms.
The abstract states that AutoHebb outperforms modern learning models on zero-shot and continual-learning tasks.
Comparisons indicate that meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous learning control are all important components.

figures.caption: Figure 16: AutoHebb networks benchmarked in the present study: 1- and 2-neuromodulator AutoHebb (AH-1NM and AH-2NM). For both models, the main network was chosen to be a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with four hidden layers; the models differed by the number of neuromodulators (and corresponding control network; in the 2-neuromodulator network, the control networks were parallel, as diagrammed). AH-2N is loosely inspired by the existernce of multiple neuromodulatory systems in the brain, and was included in benchmarking to evaluate the possibility that parallel neuromodulated plastic architecture would enhance task performance. Note that each set of plastic weights at a given layer in the 2-neuromodulator network were summed (Eq. 18). Top, AH-1N, Bottom, AH-2NM. Note that additional AutoHebb networks were also investigated in this study, and are indicated accordingly were applicable. Implementation details can be found in Appendix E.

Figure 1: AutoHebb architecture. Network weights (W) are either fixed (black) or plastic (red). The architecture consists of a "main" network (here an MLP with hidden layers h) and an auxiliary "control" network (here an MLP with hidden layers c) that receives two inputs: (1) internally generated activity from the main network (here from last hidden layer hlast), and (2) external input reflecting environmental (external) feedback given an output (y) generated by the network. The control network generates a scalar-valued neuromodulatory signal (m, red circle) that gates changes to the plastic weights within network (here Wn∗). See Appendix E for further details; additional network variants in Figure 16.

Figure 13: Length generalization on TE with respect to numbers of groups. Top: Heatmaps show average model choices (1 for same group, 2 for different group, see Figure 5), from 3 groups of 3 items to 6 groups (left to right). AutoHebb shows successful ZI ability up to 6 groups. Notably, though ANML shows weaker generalization up to 5 groups, its overall accuracy outperforms the other two models after 6 groups. Generally, AutoHebb maintains its same-group ZI ability while its different-group accuracy decays, even for training trials. In contrast, ANML maintains its different group bias and loses its same group accuracy, even on training trials. These behaviors suggest different underlying inductive biases, as would be expected given the models’ different architecture and learning rules. OML has similar behavioral bias as ANML, though OML cannot infer on same-group trials at any group size. Bottom: accuracy (calculated the same way as in Section 4.1) and F1 plots, where F1 is computed for same-group ZI trials.

Figure 5: Transitive equivalence (TE) task and performance of representative models. TE tests 0-shot inference (ZI) of grouping. a, Task schematic. Items (A, B, C, etc.) belong to multiple unseen underlying groups (e.g. ABC and JKL), and pairs of items are presented in each trial. In training trials, particular item pairs are omitted both within- (e.g. AC and CA) and across- (AL and LA) group: these item pairs are testing trials, here equivalent to inferential (infer) trials. b, Average model output after training trials. c, Model performance across trial types. Trial types (item pairs) are separated based on same group (choice 1) or different group (choice 2). Example outputs across all models in Figure 19. Model performance across all models reported in Table 1.

Figure 4: Transitive inference (TI) task and performance of representative models. TI tests 0-shot inference (ZI) of ranking. a, Task schematic. Items (A to H) belong to an unseen underlying ranking, and a pair of items are presented in each trial. In training trials, only adjacent items are presented; in test trials, non-adjacent items are presented; inferential (infer) trials are test trials that do not contain the first or last item. b, Average model output after training trials. c, Model performance by trial type. Trial types (item pairs) are grouped based on the difference in rank between items ("symbolic distance" [57, 58]). Solid lines and shaded regions represent the mean and IQR, respectively. Example outputs across all models in Figures 17 and 18. Model performance across all models reported in Table 1.

Figure 7: Multi-task 0-shot continual learning: model setup, tasks, and performance. Left, schematic of meta-learning and learning modeling procedure. Models were meta-trained on episodes in which 2 to 4 TI and TE tasks (i.e. having different randomly generated items) were serially presented and with variable numbers of trials. Models were then presented with a random sequence of 10 TI and TE tasks at evaluation. Right, performance of models at testing (mean ± 2 s.e., n=100 task sequences). Full details are in Appendix F.4.

Figure 9: TI length generalization with 14 items. Plots follow the format based on Figure 4, where item pairs (on x-axis) are grouped and organized from left to right with increasing symbolic distance. Each model was meta-trained on 8 items (left) and subsequently evaluated (after meta-training) on 14 items (right). Note that ANML and OML show near-chance performance on many inferential trial types (item pairs) except for item pairs with larger symbolic distances. AutoHebb is the only method with above chance performance on all inferential trial types.

Figure 3: Task items and trial structure. In the present study, a given task involves a set of items (item panel) that correspond to arbitrary sensory stimuli, such as fractal images. Trials consist of four steps: (1) presentation of two items (input), (2) generation of a binary output (e.g. choose item 1 vs. 2) by the model or participant (output), (3) generation of a learning control signal by the model or participant upon receiving external feedback from the environment (e.g. cash reward) (control), and (4) a learning or plasticity update (update), as governed by the control signal.

Figure 6: Two continual learning (CL) tasks and performance of representative models. a and c, Task schematics. Each task (TI-L and TE-L) is based on the ZI tasks TI and TE, respectively, and tests 0-shot inference following presentation of a new item pair (new input; diagramed in green). In TI-L, also known as "list-linking" [66, 68, 48], the item pair is a "linking pair" (here DE or ED) that connects separate previously learned rankings (here A to D and E to H). In TE-L, the new input is an item pair (here CD/DC) containing a novel item (here D) and previously presented item (here C). Note that both tasks test the ability to perform structure-sensitive transfer to items beyond that of the new item pair. b and d, Average model output (across all item pairs) following presentation of the new item pair. See Figures 17 and 18 for example outputs across all models. Model performance across all models reported in Table 2.

Figure 10: TI length generalization with 20 items. Plots follow the format based on Figure 4, where item pairs grouped from left to right with increasing symbolic distance. All models are meta-trained on only 8 items (see Figure 9, left) and evaluated on 20 items. Note that ANML and OML show relatively weaker performance than AutoHebb on inferential trials, though on this more difficult task AutoHebb chance performance on some inferential trials, indicating limitation in length generalization and/or memory capacity (e.g. compare to 14 items Figure 9).

Figure 14: Performance of three representative models on TI before vs. after overexposure of a single trial type (item pair DE). Plot follows the format of Figure 4, where trial types are ordered by symbolic distance. (Left) Performance after the standard 20 training trials are shown, (Middle) Performance after an additional 40 trials of DE are shown, (Right) Performance after an additional (from standard training trials) 100 trials of DE are shown. Results are averaged over 100 episodes with 2 s.e. bands. Note that for OML and AMNL, several trial types approach (or reach) chance performance, indicating lack of robustness to the overexposure manipulation; in contrast, AutoHebb trials remain well above chance.

Figure 17: TI and TI-L tasks: model performance by trial type. Plots follow the convention in Figure 4c, where within each plot, trial types (item pairs) are organized by symbolic distance. Plotted are model outputs for an example model instance for each indicated model. Note that on TI-L, various models such as MAML, Reptile, OML, ANML show overtly inconsistent performance across trial types, in contrast to FLP, 2F-A, 2F-ABCD, AH-1NM, and AH-2NM.

Figure 2: Meta-learning in AutoHebb. In AutoHebb networks, fixed (non-plastic) network weights were identified through meta-learning optimization, which involves two levels of adaptation: an "inner" and "outer" loop. In the inner loop, corresponding to learning, (3-factor Hebbian) plastic updates to the network occur across an episode, i.e. a sequence of trials (where each trial involves input, output, control, and update steps; see main text). At the start of each episode, fixed weights are frozen and plastic weights are set to 0. In the outer loop, corresponding to metalearning (or meta-training), the network’s fixed weights are updated via optimization based on performance within the episode and/or testing following the episode.

papers.title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
papers.tldr: AutoHebb combines meta-learned fixed weights with autonomously controlled Hebbian plasticity to enable zero-shot inference and continual learning.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45{\deg} Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.
authors: Jingnan Zheng, Cheng Jin, Ming Zhang, Huan Sun, Zhongtian Ma, Kaisen Yang, Ziyuan Zhou, Tong Wu, Dongcheng Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiao Wang, Han Qi, Shu Yu, Ermo Hua, Zongji Yu, Chaozhuo Li, Xiaoyu Wen, Zhekai Chen, Jiawei Zhou, Sirui Chen, Ning Ding, An Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua, Xiangnan He, Xia Hu, Bowen Zhou, Qiaosheng Zhang, Youbang Sun, Xiang Wang, Zhongyu Huang, Chaochao Lu

Experiments report strong safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models; specific metrics and evaluation details are not provided in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 4 | The three-stage ReSI framework. In each round, ReSI applies red-teaming methods to identify vulnerabilities in the current target model 𝑀𝑟, develops training recipes through automated research, and promotes the eligible update with the largest safety gain as 𝑀𝑟+1, the target for the next round. Stage 1 collects successful attacks against 𝑀𝑟 (Section 3.2.1). Stage 2 screens attack sources and alignment methods through low-budget pilot trials and shortlists the most promising recipes (Section 3.2.3). Stage 3 conducts full-scale training and feedback-guided refinement, then selects the eligible checkpoint with the largest safety gain (Section 3.2.4).

Figure 3 | Overview of REX. (1) Expert expansion copies and scales the source experts of the base model 𝐵 to form removable experts (𝐹0), and joint training with selective gradient masking and routing differentiation relocates hazardous knowledge into them (𝐹1). (2) Excising the removable experts yields 𝐴1, and a light RMU cleanup yields the public base model 𝐴2, while the removable experts and their router rows are kept. (3) Recombining them with 𝐴2 gives the full structure 𝐹2, on which standard post-training produces the full model 𝐹3 for authorized users; excising its removable experts produces the public model 𝐴3.

Figure 2 | Overview of Safin-1.5. At the architectural level, MARCH and REX provide persistent safety memory and hazardous-knowledge disentanglement, respectively. At the training level, ReSI supports continual safety improvement through iterative red-teaming, pilot screening, and full-scale model updates. At the formal assurance level, the formal reasoning harness leverages POGB to address semantic gaps between natural-language problems and formal representations, enhancing the model’s logical reasoning capabilities.

papers.abstract: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.

papers.abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

papers.abstract: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.
bullets: Uses frozen historical anchor observations excluded from candidate optimization and compares old versus candidate policies via forward KL divergence.
Provides conditional off-anchor guarantees under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, plus bounds for interpolation, grid resolution, trajectories, and sequential updates.
In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition sensor-policy proxy, mean forgetting fell from 1.01% to 0.00% at ε=0.05, while final average accuracy decreased from 93.04% to 88.48%.
The study demonstrates a retention–plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance.
Deployment still requires separate evidence that the accepted update improves current-task utility.

papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $\tau$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

papers.abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
bullets: Supports waypoint, discrete local, pixel-based, and object-directed navigation actions.
Lets agents ask for clarification or assistance when facing ambiguity or difficulty.
Stores observations and dialogue by location to improve future visits.
Evaluated across eight benchmarks spanning four navigation task families and multi-day physical navigation.
Reports strong performance, including 100% first-visit SR across four 100-episode sets and improved R2R revisit SPL from 82.23% to 93.31%.

papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA
bullets: Targets the latency and memory costs of token-by-token VLM action generation for mobile GUI agents.
Uses a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabeled screenshots and an action- and region-conditioned predictor to produce one latent per candidate action.
Lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass without language decoding.
On AndroidControl, it is 2.8–4.0× faster than a comparable fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent and reaches 86–92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters.
The predictor’s decision-focused training is supported by similar performance from a randomly initialized predictor and one pretrained on screen dynamics.
