papers.abstract: Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach target objects in complex environments. Humans often rely on low-cost yet informative schematic maps, such as rough sketches or directional annotations. We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework. Our lightweight data-generation pipeline turns 2D floorplans into navigation training environments, yielding Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes and noise-controllable schematic maps. ScheNav turns rough schematic guidance into exploration and stopping decisions by using SchemaField, a learned spatial module that fuses the guidance with accumulated observations and predicts spatial value fields. The framework updates these fields as exploration proceeds, with trajectory-based training and a cross-frame consistency objective supporting coherent guidance across changing viewpoints. ScheNav learns to use schematic guidance entirely from simulated floorplans and transfers this ability to unseen embodied environments. Experiments show improved navigation success and path efficiency across schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, together with tolerance to the tested schematic perturbations and omissions. Together, these results demonstrate that rough schematic guidance offers a practical way to improve embodied navigation.
bullets: Addresses object-goal navigation in complex environments using low-cost schematic maps such as sketches, goal ellipses, and directional pointers.
Introduces Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with navigation episodes and controllable schematic-map noise.
Uses SchemaField to fuse schematic guidance with accumulated visual observations and predict spatial value fields for exploration and stopping.
Trains with trajectory-based learning and cross-frame consistency to maintain coherent guidance across viewpoints.
Experiments report improved navigation success and path efficiency, with tolerance to tested schematic perturbations and omissions.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The ScheNav framework. Schematic guidance at any level, a schematic map, ellipses, a pointed direction, or none, is encoded by SchemaField, the only learned component our framework introduces: a schematic-fusion transformer fuses the guidance with the observed map from the map memory, and a distance decoder and a corridor decoder predict the two value fields from the fused embedding in a single forward pass. Two rule-based components read the fields. The Goal Verification module compares the distance-field value at goal instances detected in the map memory against a threshold τstop, and the decision transformation scores frontier candidates with the corridor field and gates stopping, emitting a waypoint or a stop. Map memory, frontier extraction, and execution are supplied by the host navigation system, and each new observation closes the loop.

Figure 3. Furnished-RPLAN construction pipeline. Starting from an RPLAN vector floorplan, a vision-language pipeline proposes and extracts a machine-readable furniture layout. The resulting furnished environment is used to generate navigation episodes, paired schematic guidance, and the local observations consumed by ScheNav.

Figure 1. Overview of schematic-guided navigation. A human provides imperfect schematic guidance, such as a rough sketch or a pointed direction. ScheNav grounds the guidance in the agent’s observations and predicts a value field that rises toward the goal. Guided by the predicted field, the agent reaches the goal along an efficient route in an environment it has barely explored.

Figure 4. Closed-loop trajectories on one episode under decreasing guidance. The five panels show our four input conditions and unmodified UniGoal on the same episode, rendered on a textured top-down view of the scene. The dashed inset in each panel shows the schematic input the agent receives, and is blank for the no-guidance condition and the baseline; in the direction panel the floorplan behind the arrow is drawn only for illustration, and the model receives the direction vector alone. Orange curves trace the agent from start to stop, a green check marks a successful stop, and the red cross marks a failed stop. The path lengthens gracefully as guidance weakens, from the schematic map through the ellipse and direction conditions to no guidance at all, while the host stops incorrectly after prolonged, tangled exploration.

papers.abstract: A dexterous hand can change an object's pose without setting it down. This survey covers 113 learning-based methods that attempt it, the hands they run on, the simulators they train in, and how they report results. The field has largely converged on one recipe: reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, distilled into a vision-only student for transfer to hardware. Almost half the corpus trains that way, nearly all of it in one simulator, whose own successors are barely used. A second and faster-growing branch learns from teleoperated demonstration instead, through vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, and systems whose contribution is the collection rig itself. Published work has tripled since 2022. Grasping remains the largest task family and bimanual coordination the fastest-rising, and almost every experiment runs on one of four hands. What the survey adds comes from reading released code and vendor specifications beside the papers. Eight hands that can be bought or built from published designs appear in no method paper here. Where the depth a hand sinks into the object it holds is reported at all, it is not measured in the physics that produced the motion. Section VII proposes a protocol for the unreported quantities; the body gives the counts behind every claim above.
bullets: Reviews the hands, simulators, training paradigms, tasks, and evaluation practices used in 113 methods.
The prevailing pipeline trains reinforcement learning on privileged state in a GPU simulator, then distills it into a vision-only policy for hardware transfer.
A faster-growing alternative learns from teleoperated demonstrations using vision-language-action models, diffusion policies, or specialized data-collection rigs.
Research output has tripled since 2022; grasping is the largest task family, while bimanual coordination is growing fastest, and most studies use one of four hands.
The survey identifies underused available hands and missing physical measurements, including object penetration depth, and proposes a reporting protocol.

papers.abstract: Detailed image captioning is usually framed as an amount problem: a model should mention more visual facts while avoiding hallucination. However, autoregressive VLMs generate captions as ordered sequences, and later generations may be produced under weaker or noisier visual grounding. We therefore argue that long-form captioning should be studied not only by what facts are mentioned, but also by where they appear. We introduce a position-aware rubric representation that decomposes dense human references into atomic visual claims, verifies generated captions against those claims, and induces a quartile-wise composition of supported, hallucinated, and generic content. This lens reveals two qualitatively different failures in long captions: models tend to produce unsupported specificity in the middle, while the final portion often escapes into vague, non-evidential language rather than simply accumulating more hallucination. A same-reference human control does not exhibit these patterns; additional human audits examine the visual validity of the induced labels. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose PAGER (Position-Aware Grounded Evidence Reinforcement), a GRPO training objective with separate signals for supported fine-grained middle evidence, evidence-bearing tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length control. The result is a closed loop: the same ordered claim representation identifies where long captions fail and supplies the position-specific reward needed to repair those failures. Experiments on detailed-caption benchmarks show that PAGER improves position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while preserving competitive global caption quality.
bullets: Long captions often become unsupportedly specific in the middle and vague or non-evidential near the end.
A position-aware rubric decomposes references into atomic visual claims and evaluates supported, hallucinated, and generic content by caption quartile.
PAGER applies position-specific GRPO rewards for grounded middle evidence, evidential tail continuation, claim coverage, and content-aware length.
Experiments show improved position-wise grounding and pairwise caption preference while maintaining competitive overall caption quality.

papers.abstract: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
bullets: Problem: Vision-language encoders contain spatial information, but image generators often fail to use it for precise layout control.
Method: Evaluate spatial grounding on synthetic geometric primitives with a color-aware layout metric, then vary the training signal-to-noise-ratio distribution.
Key finding: Centered SNR training yields 25.9% layout adherence, while emphasizing high-noise stages raises it to 80.8%, near the 83.6% VAE reconstruction ceiling.
Scope: The required SNR shift grows with resolution and aspect-ratio variability; conservative schedules such as FLUX.1’s are insufficient for precise layouts.
Transfer: Distribution tuning also improves layout adherence on COCO, increasing Average Precision from 1.0 to 57.3 without architectural modifications.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Qualitative comparison of generated images across varying µ . We compare the ground truth (GT) and VAE baseline against our model for µ ∈ [0,3.0]. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic benchmark with controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean–perturbed rollouts, and simulator-grounded stage-aware failure analysis.
Evaluates GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts.
Robustness varies across tasks and perturbations, and greater severity does not always cause monotonic performance degradation.
Perturbations with identical end-to-end success degradation can produce different failure-depth profiles, revealing where execution breaks down.
Motivates reporting outcome degradation, paired-outcome sensitivity, and failure progression jointly; code is publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of RoboCasa-Shift. RoboCasa-Shift evaluates VLA robustness on selected long-horizon RoboCasa tasks under controlled single-factor distribution shifts with multiple frozen severity levels. Strictly matched clean-perturbed rollouts enable counterfactual comparison under shared task conditions, while robustness is characterized jointly through end-to-end task outcomes and stage-aware semantic execution diagnostics. Representative findings illustrate that aggregate success rates can mask substantial episode-level outcome changes, similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to different failure locations, and severe visual corruption can shift failures toward earlier stages of task execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of StageTracker. (a) A long-horizon task is represented as an ordered sequence of semantic subgoals, each associated with a simulator-state predicate. (b) During rollout, StageTracker evaluates the current predicate, records the completion step when it is first satisfied, and advances to the next subgoal. Completed subgoals are latched, allowing the tracker to report the deepest semantic progress reached and the first incomplete subgoal for failure localization.

Fig. 2: Pipeline of RoboCasa-Shift. (a) Task Suite. Candidate RoboCasa tasks are filtered through clean-competence screening to construct the formal evaluation suite. (b) Controlled Shifts. Selected tasks are evaluated under four singlefactor distribution shifts with calibrated and frozen severity levels. (c) Counterfactual Pairing. Clean and perturbed rollouts share the underlying task conditions and policy seed and differ only in the target shift. (d) Diagnosis. RoboCasa’s official task outcome is complemented by stage-aware semantic diagnostics of execution progress, first incomplete subgoal, and subgoal reach.

Fig. 8: Representative severity calibration examples. Rows correspond to the four perturbation factors, and columns show the clean condition (L0) and three calibrated severity levels (L1–L3). Illumination progressively darkens the scene, camera orientation changes the third-person viewpoint, robot base initialization perturbs the initial base position and yaw orientation, and Gaussian blur progressively reduces visual sharpness. For base initialization, the inset provides a schematic top-down view, where the black and orange markers represent the nominal and perturbed base poses, respectively, while the straight and curved arrows indicate planar displacement and yaw rotation. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor and are not assumed to be physically equivalent across factors.

Fig. 9: Task-wise distributions of first incomplete semantic milestones among perturbation-induced failures. Each subplot corresponds to one formal task. For each perturbation factor and severity level, the stacked bar shows the distribution of first incomplete milestones g1, . . . , gK among strictly matched S→F transitions, where K depends on the task. Trackercomplete official failures, in which all tracked milestones are reached but RoboCasa’s official task-success criterion remains unsatisfied, are reported separately without assigning a first incomplete milestone. The proportions are calculated over all S→F transitions in the corresponding task and condition. The annotation above each bar indicates the number of transitions n; conditions without such transitions are marked as n = 0.

Fig. 7: Representative matched replays at different semantic failure depths. Each case compares a strictly matched clean– perturbed rollout pair that shares the same task instance, initial simulator state, episode metadata, and episode-level policy seed, while differing only in the target perturbation. The two rows show the clean and perturbed executions, respectively, and the columns present selected frames spanning the execution process. Checkmarks and crosses indicate whether the corresponding tracked semantic subgoals are completed, while the final annotation reports the official task outcome. These examples provide a qualitative view of how perturbations can change execution depth and failure location, complementing the aggregate stage-aware statistics in Figure 6.

Fig. 5: Task-level robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Each cell reports the paired success-rate degradation ∆SR for one task and perturbation condition, computed from 20 matched episode pairs. Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition, while negative values indicate a higher success rate under the shifted condition for the corresponding finite paired sample. The task-level breakdown reveals heterogeneous severity responses that can be obscured by macro aggregation.

Fig. 10: Representative counterfactual outcome transitions under camera orientation at L1. Case A (StackBowlsCabinet) shows a success-to-failure (S→F) transition, whereas Case B (PreSoakPan) shows a failure-to-success (F→S) transition. Within each case, the clean and perturbed rollouts share the same task instance, initial simulator state, and episode-level policy seed, differing only in the target camera-orientation perturbation. Columns show selected frames from the initial, intermediate, and final stages of execution, with the final outcomes determined by RoboCasa’s official task-success criterion. These examples illustrate opposite episode-level outcome changes under the same perturbation condition, despite zero aggregate success-rate degradation at L1.

Fig. 4: End-to-end robustness under controlled distribution shifts. Macro-averaged paired success-rate degradation ∆SR is shown for the four distribution-shift factors, with each factor evaluated at three frozen severity levels (L1– L3). Positive values indicate degradation relative to the matched clean condition. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals obtained from paired bootstrap resampling. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor, and equal level indices across different factors do not imply physically equivalent perturbation magnitudes.

Fig. 6: Stage-aware execution depth of perturbationinduced failures. Each marker summarizes strictly matched clean-success-to-perturbed-failure (S→ F) transitions under one perturbation factor and severity level. The vertical position indicates the mean normalized subgoal progress of the corresponding S→F cohort, marker size represents the number of transition events, and marker color denotes the fraction of failures occurring before the first tracked semantic milestone. The annotated n gives the number of transitions in each condition. Gray lines connect L1–L3 within the same perturbation factor only to visualize the within-factor severity trend and do not encode an additional quantity. Severity levels are ordinal within each perturbation factor and are not assumed to be physically equivalent across factors.

papers.title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation
papers.tldr: RoboCasa-Shift shows that VLA robustness in long-horizon manipulation is multi-dimensional and cannot be captured by aggregate task success alone.

papers.abstract: For practical motion generation, it is essential to handle multimodality (multiple actions can be correct for the same observation) while maintaining low inference cost and strong generalization from limited demonstrations. We introduce an attentive mixture-density policy trained with the Energy Score that represents future visuomotor trajectories as explicit probability distributions with a single forward pass. Concretely, we output Gaussian mixture parameters for joint commands (and optionally attention points) and optimize them with the Energy Score (computed as a sum of 1D CRPS under a diagonal covariance assumption) instead of the negative log-likelihood (NLL) to avoid MDN singularities and gradient-scale instabilities. Our architecture couples explicit spatial attention with mixture-density outputs, enabling robust multimodal behavior selection under visual noise and small-data regimes. On an 8-DOF manipulator, the method generates distinct avoidance trajectories and stabilizes learning in obstacle avoidance. Moreover, in a randomized moving-object grasping task, where spatiotemporal multimodality and fast timing decisions are required, the proposed model outperforms Diffusion Policy by 15-25% under several unseen conditions, demonstrating superior generalization and real-time feasibility.
bullets: Represents future visuomotor trajectories as explicit Gaussian-mixture distributions in a single forward pass.
Uses Energy Score, implemented via 1D CRPS under diagonal covariance, instead of NLL to reduce MDN singularities and gradient-scale instability.
Combines spatial attention with mixture-density outputs for robust behavior selection under visual noise and limited demonstrations.
Produces distinct obstacle-avoidance trajectories and outperforms Diffusion Policy by 15–25% in several unseen moving-object grasping conditions.
Demonstrates real-time feasibility on an 8-DOF manipulator, with scope focused on the evaluated manipulation tasks and assumptions.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Architecture of the proposed model. The output layer (green box) represents the multimodality of future predictions by outputting joint angles and attention points as GMM parameters (π,µ,σ). The Energy Score (CRPS) is adopted as the loss function. The yellow box indicates the reconstruction process optimized for the modified prediction format.

Fig. 3: Comparison of Exp. 1 results. The left panel shows the success rate, and the right panel shows the failure rate and its breakdown. The left graph confirms that the proposed model achieves success rates equivalent to or higher than representative conventional models such as ACT and DP. In the right graph, the area enclosed by the crimson frame indicates the proportion of ”mode averaging” generated; it can be seen that this proportion is significantly reduced in the proposed model compared to SARNN without GMM.

Fig. 6: Comparison of success rates by input context length in Exp. 2. For ACT-based models with a 10-step context, inference was performed on an external PC because the inference speed on the robot’s built-in PC fell below 10 Hz.
Fig. 5: Success rates in Exp. 2: seen vs. unseen random patterns (1.0×, 1.5×, 2.0× speeds). Trials: 160 (seen), 40 per speed (unseen).
Fig. 4: PCA visualization of internal states in Exp. 1 using only successful grasping trials. We plot nine trajectories in total: three trials each at the three seen target positions.

Fig. 2: Left: Experimental setup for Exp. 1. The target object is positioned behind an obstacle. Right: Movement patterns of the moving object in Exp. 2. During training, four reciprocating patterns are used: vertical, horizontal, right-diagonal, and left-diagonal. During inference, an additional unlearned pattern with random turn-back angles is introduced.

papers.abstract: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io
bullets: Targets the difficulty of modeling contact mechanics, coupled dynamics, deformation, stiffness, and friction in robot-object interactions.
Lets users explicitly edit the solver, contact model, and physical parameters while iteratively matching observed behavior.
Built using the open Newton physics simulation system.
Evaluated through human-guided real2sim with visual assessment, force feedback, and agentic Real2Sim2Real.
The abstract does not report quantitative results or specific limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RoboSimStudio Architecture. RoboSimStudio integrates asset creation, robot interfaces, and multi-physics simulation through Newton and external physics solvers. It supports interactive task visualization, human-guided Real2Sim, and agentic Real2Sim through a shared simulation framework.

Figure 3: Multi-physics coupling in RoboSimStudio. Five manipulation tasks using different physics solvers and coupling methods. Top: rendered simulation scenes. Bottom: visualization of the physics solvers used for each object, including MuJoCo-Warp (violet), finite-element simulation (FEM, teal), and Vertex Block Descent (VBD, amber). All tasks use the same robot interface and scene description framework in RoboSimStudio.

Figure 7: Agentic Real2Sim2Real for sponge wiping. (a) A real-world bimanual manipulation task, where one arm holds a bar while the other wipes a marker stripe using a sponge. (b) Simulation challenges involving robot motion, object-object contact, and robot-object contact. (c) A coding agent constructs and iteratively refines the simulation through the interactive studio, completing a verified simulated wipe in 56 minutes. (d) A multi-physics simulation in RoboSimStudio. (e) Physical variation of sponge stiffness and spatial variation of the bar and sponge across 30 generated layouts (bottom). (f) GaP [5] improves the simulated wiped area from 0% to 100% over 14 iterations using spatial-temporal simulation feedback from rss. (g) The improved policy is deployed on the real robot to perform sponge wiping. (h) A real-world failure caused by displacement of a bar support that was fixed in the original simulation. (i) Given the observed failure, the coding agent revises the physical simulation to allow the bar and its supports to move under contact. papers.abstract: Reasoning models can benefit from test-time scaling, but continued reasoning may become ineffective or harmful, a phenomenon termed overthinking. Evaluations against full thinking compare accuracy and token usage but lack references for overthinking severity and strategies' theoretical mitigation potential. To characterize overthinking at the model-task level, we first introduce Step-wise Truncation Probing (STP), repeatedly generating answers from multiple retained prefixes along each fixed sampled reasoning trajectory. Using each trajectory's earliest measured position attaining maximum empirical accuracy as a reference, we define Overthinking Ratio and Accuracy Degradation as the fraction of thinking tokens generated afterward and the accuracy decrease from this reference to full thinking, respectively. Secondly, we then formulate dynamic routing, fixed budgets, and dynamic early exit within a unified framework to quantify the theoretical mitigation potential of different termination strategies. Based on this unified framework, we use the complete STP measurements to construct a token-accuracy Pareto frontier for each strategy under a common normalized thinking-token budget. We further develop OTBench, a reusable benchmark built from the STP process, which produced 70.5B reasoning tokens and the corresponding probing measurements across six models and four benchmark groups.
bullets: Overthinking occurs when continued test-time reasoning stops helping or harms accuracy, but existing evaluations lack severity references and theoretical comparisons.
Step-wise Truncation Probing (STP) evaluates answers from multiple prefixes of fixed reasoning trajectories.
It defines Overthinking Ratio and Accuracy Degradation relative to each trajectory’s earliest prefix achieving maximum measured accuracy.
A unified framework compares dynamic routing, fixed budgets, and dynamic early exit by constructing token–accuracy Pareto frontiers under a normalized budget.
OTBench provides STP-based measurements across six models and four benchmark groups, totaling 70.5B reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: Latent safety filters certify safety on a learned low-dimensional representation of the state, enabling constraints that resist analytic description. Because the encoder is lossy, a filter can report safe while the physical state is unsafe, with no detectable model error. Existing transfer conditions leave the effect of discarded safety information implicit. We ask when a lossy encoder admits a safety certificate that transfers to the physical system, and show the answer is governed by the detectability of the discarded safety-relevant dynamics. We construct a system whose latent model is exact and whose latent signals always report safe, while the physical state becomes arbitrarily unsafe. For this system no certificate exists and no monitor downstream of the encoder can detect the failure. When the discarded dynamics contract, a latent barrier certifies true safety up to two explicit margins, one for the latent-model error and one for the variation of safety across states the encoder cannot distinguish. In the linear case and under boundedness and non-degeneracy conditions, every calibrated barrier transfers with a finite margin when the safety-relevant subspace is detectable, and none does otherwise. On learned cartpole encoders, the model error does not indicate for which representations the estimated bound is non-vacuous, while the second margin does.
bullets: Lossy encoders can report safety while the physical state is arbitrarily unsafe, even when the latent model is exact.
No downstream monitor can detect failures hidden by the encoder when discarded dynamics are undetectable.
Contractive discarded dynamics yield latent safety certificates with separate margins for latent-model error and encoder-induced safety variation.
For linear systems, calibrated barriers transfer with finite margins exactly under detectability of the safety-relevant subspace; otherwise they do not.
In learned cartpole encoders, encoder-induced safety variation—not model error—indicates when the transfer bound is non-vacuous.

papers.abstract: Due to limited support for intra-tensor heterogeneous precision in conventional accelerators, neural network quantization remains largely restricted to per-tensor precision assignment. We present ShatterQuant, a hardware-software co-designed framework enabling mixed-precision quantization within each tensor by assigning independent bit-widths to blocks of a weight projection. ShatterQuant couples precision granularity with PE configuration, such that each precision determines an effective block height. We introduce (1) a hardware-aware post-training method that assigns intra-tensor precision based on block-level standard deviation and weight sensitivity; (2) the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator supporting 1/2/4/8-bit weight precision, precision-dependent PE configuration, block rescaling, and integrated softmax and piecewise-linear nonlinearities; and (3) an evaluation of model-hardware tradeoffs using an implementation in the TSMC 16nm PDK operating at 1 GHz, achieving 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/$mm^2$ area efficiency, and 2.8 TOPS/W energy efficiency. On DeiT and ImageNet-1K, ShatterQuant achieves accuracy within $3.3\%$ of state-of-the-art mixed-precision techniques while using a 2 bit lower effective bitwidth, while for PixelDiT demonstrates comparable generation quality. ShatterQuant demonstrates how fine-grained intra-tensor mixed-precision can be realized through hardware-software co-design.
bullets: Assigns independent 1/2/4/8-bit precisions to weight blocks based on block variability and sensitivity.
Links precision granularity to processing-element configuration and effective block height.
Introduces a systolic Transformer accelerator with block rescaling, integrated softmax, and piecewise-linear nonlinearities.
A 16nm, 1GHz implementation achieves 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/mm², and 2.8 TOPS/W.
On DeiT/ImageNet-1K and PixelDiT, it maintains comparable accuracy or generation quality with lower effective bitwidth than referenced mixed-precision approaches.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to solve complex scientific and practical problems via iterative optimization. However, dynamically coordinating diverse search mechanisms as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets evolve remains a critical open challenge. Targeted empirical diagnostics reveal that mechanism effectiveness is highly state-dependent. Motivated by this, we analyze how individual decisions drive final outcomes, decomposing the expected terminal improvement under a shared budget into cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses. Guided by this opportunity-loss theoretical foundation, we propose OptiCom, a unified framework that represents LLM-driven optimizers within a shared configuration space: C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S), corresponding to artifact, query, operator, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Operating within this space, a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller dynamically composes immediate mechanisms through structured Action Packages, while a slower Strategy Adapter refines long-term selection preferences, operator weights, and templates based on accumulated trajectory feedback. Comprehensive evaluations across 32 benchmark groups demonstrate the superiority of framework: OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 among 14 evaluated configurations, securing the top score in 23 groups. Ultimately, these results highlight the broad applicability and high extensibility of OptiCom as a general-purpose paradigm for robust LLM test-time scaling.
bullets: LLM-driven optimization mechanisms vary in effectiveness as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets change.
The framework analyzes terminal improvement as cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses.
OptiCom unifies optimizer components in a shared configuration space covering artifacts, queries, operators, evaluation, memory, and strategy.
A fast controller selects structured Action Packages, while a slower adapter updates preferences, operator weights, and templates from trajectory feedback.
Across 32 benchmark groups and 14 configurations, OptiCom ranked first on average and achieved the top score in 23 groups.

Composing optimization mechanisms. The analysis in Section 4 identifies two factors governing adaptive optimization: the opportunities provided by available actions, ∆t, and the loss incurred when selecting among them, ℓt. Guided by this decomposition, OptiCom dynamically combines complementary mechanisms within the shared configuration space. To maximize opportunities while mitigating selection loss, the framework operates through a continuous, state-conditioned execution loop driven by two core components: an Optimization Controller for immediate mechanism composition, and a slower Strategy Adapter for long-term guidance revision. Both components operate through LLM API calls with fixed model parameters (see Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1).

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for natural-language logical reasoning, where the final answer is easy to check but the proof behind it is not. In natural-language logical reasoning, an intermediate conclusion should follow from its premises, and the resulting derivation should support the final answer. Existing methods lack machine-checkable verification of intermediate conclusions and answer-supporting proof dependencies, so they may assign credit to invalid or answer-irrelevant steps. We propose Proof-R1, an RL framework from formal verification that trains LLMs to construct verifiable proofs for natural-language logical reasoning. Proof-R1 admits a generated conclusion into the verified proof state only when the corresponding reasoning action satisfies the proof obligations through UNSAT-based machine-checkable formal verification. Proof-R1 also recovers the answer-supporting dependency closure to trace the proof structure of the final answer and align outcome credit with the proof dependencies. Experiments demonstrate that Proof-R1 improves answer accuracy across three logical reasoning benchmarks and four backbone models and outperforms training-free agents and training-based methods in terms of reasoning-process verifiability.
bullets: Existing approaches may reward invalid intermediate steps or reasoning that does not support the final answer.
The framework admits conclusions into the proof only when UNSAT-based verification confirms their proof obligations.
It traces the dependency closure supporting the final answer and aligns training credit with those proof dependencies.
Experiments across three benchmarks and four backbone models improve answer accuracy and reasoning-process verifiability.
The approach targets natural-language logical reasoning and depends on formal verification of generated proof steps.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents require reinforcement learning methods that can assign credit to intermediate decisions under sparse and delayed rewards. Existing group-based methods such as GRPO and GiGPO alleviate this issue by comparing rollout returns or repeated anchor states, but they still fail when the compared returns have no variation. We identify this failure mode as zero-credit failure: during early training, many failed rollouts contain useful prefixes, yet existing methods assign them no task-discriminative advantage. To address this issue, we propose Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm that learns from viable failure prefixes. MVPO estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions, repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages, and attenuates the potential branch according to relative performance progress. Experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct show that MVPO outperforms eight strong baselines, including GRPO and GiGPO. Under the same training length, MVPO improves over the GiGPO baseline by +4.4 success points on ALFWorld and +5.3 on WebShop, while adding only 0.16%-0.20% advantage-construction overhead.
bullets: Targets sparse, delayed rewards where early decisions are difficult to credit.
Identifies zero-credit failure: failed rollouts with useful prefixes may receive no task-discriminative advantage when returns lack variation.
Uses Union-Find viability regions to estimate prefix potential and construct potential-difference advantages for zero-credit groups.
Attenuates the potential-based learning branch according to relative performance progress.
On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, improves over GiGPO by 4.4 success points on ALFWorld and 5.3 on WebShop, with 0.16%–0.20% advantage-construction overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MVPO. MVPO first estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions using future success, loop statistics, and adaptive milestone progress (§4.1). It then routes step-level credit according to anchor-group availability: informative anchor groups use anchor-based comparative credit, while zero-credit groups are repaired with prefix-potential advantages (§4.2). Finally, the routed step-level credit is combined with the episode-level group advantage for critic-free policy optimization (§4.3).

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of MVPO. Top: an ALFWorld case of zero-credit failure: all rollouts fail, making GRPO/GiGPO assign no task-discriminative advantage, while MVPO identifies viable prefixes using prefix potential. Bottom (a): zero-advantage steps affect over 90% of GRPO steps and about 65% of GiGPO steps in early WebShop training. Bottom (b): higher prefix potential predicts higher future success on ALFWorld. Bottom (c): MVPO reaches 40% success earlier during training. Bottom (d): MVPO improves final success over GiGPO on both benchmarks.

Figure 3: Training dynamics of MVPO. (a) The performance-progress attenuation mechanism works as intended. At the beginning of training, the EMA success rate is low and κt stays close to 1, allowing prefix-potential credit to repair zero-credit groups with full strength. As the policy improves, the EMA success rate increases and κt decreases accordingly, causing the potential branch to fade and leaving more gradient space to anchor-based comparative credit. (b) The learned prefix potential remains directionally meaningful throughout training. Successful trajectories maintain higher mean potential than failed trajectories, while the Union-Find region statistics remain stable. This supports the central assumption of MVPO: potential can distinguish viable failure prefixes from unproductive prefixes before final rewards become frequent.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-infrastructure cooperation can complement onboard sensing with broader and more informative observations of the traffic environment, providing valuable support for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing cooperative driving methods mainly exploit roadside information to enhance the representation of the current scene, while the future consequences of prospective driving actions are rarely modeled explicitly. This limits the ability of the planner to anticipate how its decisions may interact with the evolving traffic environment. To address this issue, we propose V2X-WAM, a cooperative world action model that tightly couples cooperative scene understanding, action generation, and future-world reasoning. V2X-WAM constructs a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle- and infrastructure-side observations, while compressing infrastructure information into a compact quantized message for efficient communication. Based on the resulting cooperative representation, a multimodal planner generates prospective trajectories, which explicitly condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow prediction. The predicted world consequences are then fed back to refine the planned trajectory, forming a closed interaction between action and future-world evolution. Experiments on a large-scale real-world cooperative driving dataset demonstrate that V2X-WAM consistently improves planning accuracy and safety over representative end-to-end cooperative driving methods, while achieving stronger future-world prediction and substantially lower communication overhead. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing V2X methods mainly represent the current scene without explicitly modeling action consequences.
Builds a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle and infrastructure observations, with infrastructure data compressed into a quantized message.
Uses a multimodal planner whose candidate trajectories condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow predictions.
Feeds predicted future-world consequences back into trajectory planning, creating a closed action–world interaction loop.
Experiments show improved planning accuracy and safety, stronger future-world prediction, and substantially lower communication overhead; ablations support the design.

papers.abstract: Rare but consequential failures can persist in learned locomotion policies for legged robots even when average task performance is high, in part because standard curricula primarily adapt task difficulty rather than the distribution of safety-critical experience. We introduce Predictive Safety Curricula (PSC), a framework for allocating locomotion training experience using learned predictions of future safety cost. PSC trains a distributional safety critic from policy rollouts and uses its predictions to prioritize both terrain contexts and previously encountered randomized events. The resulting curriculum modifies the training distribution while leaving the task reward and policy-optimization loss unchanged. We evaluate PSC in controlled rough-terrain locomotion and in production locomotion systems. PSC improves reliability relative to standard terrain progression, advantage-based replay, and learning-progress curricula, with the largest gains on difficult terrain and under degraded observations. The same allocation principle transfers to two production locomotion stacks. On ANYmal-D hardware, PSC reduces shank-collision incidence by $63\%$ relative to the learning-progress curriculum across three matched training seeds, with a reduction in every seed. On a production stair-climbing platform, PSC eliminates observed shank collisions in the evaluated hardware trials. These results show that learned predictions of future safety cost can provide an effective signal for allocating training experience toward rare failure modes and improving locomotion reliability.
bullets: Targets rare, consequential failures that standard task-difficulty curricula may overlook.
Trains a distributional safety critic from rollouts to prioritize terrain contexts and previously seen randomized events.
Changes the training distribution without modifying the task reward or policy-optimization loss.
Improves reliability over several curriculum baselines, especially on difficult terrain and with degraded observations.
Reduces shank collisions by 63% on ANYmal-D across three matched seeds and eliminated observed collisions in evaluated stair-climbing trials.

papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.
bullets: Addresses jailbreaks in non-high-resource languages where models recognize risks in reasoning but still produce unsafe responses.
Introduces Think Gap Score and reasoning-trace substitution to measure cross-lingual gaps in how safety reasoning influences outputs.
Identifies safety-relevant neurons by comparing neuron importance with reasoning enabled versus disabled.
Uses neuron-selective consistency optimization with a frozen judge, without human-annotated responses or preference data.
Across two reasoning models, reduces attack success on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, generalizes to unseen languages, and preserves multilingual task performance while limiting false refusals.

papers.abstract: Streaming video assistance requires models to answer asynchronous questions from an observed prefix under a fixed context budget. Existing approaches model response timing or compress history, but an online state formed before future questions are known can omit visual details before later questions reveal their relevance; the retained state alone cannot recover them. We introduce Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning. WTI maintains compact natural-language memory entries tagged with source-video time ranges; these entries support direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchor selective recall of finer visual evidence. For each question, WTI answers when current context and memory suffice, continues watching when required evidence has not appeared, or recalls a relevant past interval and decides again after incorporating the returned chunks, without replaying the full observed history. To train this behavior, we construct WTI-82K, comprising 82,335 timed questions across 4,812 causally aligned trajectories, and develop Stream-GDPO to optimize complete multi-question streaming rollouts using trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates. WTI achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance among the compared open-source streaming baselines, reaching 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench.
bullets: Addresses the problem that early online summaries may omit visual details needed by later questions under a fixed context budget.
Stores compact natural-language memories linked to source-video time ranges, enabling targeted recall without replaying the full history.
Uses a closed-loop policy that decides whether to answer, continue watching, or retrieve past visual evidence before answering.
Trains with Stream-GDPO on WTI-82K, optimizing response timing, video recall, and memory updates across complete question trajectories.
Reports 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted accuracy on OVO-Bench, achieving state-of-the-art performance among compared open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Watch-Think-Interact. For each arriving chunk, WTI updates a short thinking state and chooses to remain silent, answer, or recall. Recall returns visual evidence and loops back to the decision at the same time step; controller-triggered memory updates separately compress elapsed observations into a bounded temporal index. Stream-GDPO optimizes the resulting complete interaction trajectories.

Figure 3: WTI-82K construction pipeline. WTI-82K converts videos into streaming-causal trajectories by standardizing clips, aligning chunk-level evidence chains, generating QAs from aligned evidence, placing query and answerable times, and checking timestamp bounds, answer availability, action grammar, and evidence-interval fields. The resulting samples cover Real-Time, Backward Tracing, and Proactive interactions under the same visibility constraints as inference.

Figure 1: Motivation for Watch-Think-Interact. In causal streaming video, asynchronous questions may require current, past, or not-yet-observed evidence. WTI uses a bounded active window for current perception, compact time-indexed memory for direct reasoning and temporal localization, and selective recall to reload a past visual interval.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid skills from videos typically requires a successful human demonstration, which often demands custom data collection. Although failures have traditionally been treated only as negative examples in robot learning, they can still reveal a usable trajectory prefix before the task fails, as well as the intended outcome. To leverage this information from a failed-attempt video, we propose TRACC, a pipeline that imitates the useful portion of the motion trajectory and then completes the task based on the inferred task outcome. The usable motion prefix serves as prior knowledge until the failure occurs, after which the task-completion reward guides the policy to learn the intended task goal without requiring a successful task trajectory. We evaluate our method on six in-the-wild failed human tasks from the Oops! dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for learning from failed attempts when no successful demonstration is available. Thus, these findings establish failed human videos as a viable source of supervision for humanoid skill learning.
bullets: Failed demonstrations provide both a usable trajectory prefix and clues about the intended outcome.
TRACC imitates the motion before failure, then uses task-completion rewards to learn the remaining behavior.
The method targets settings without any successful task demonstration.
Evaluated on six in-the-wild failed human tasks from the Oops! dataset.
Results support failed human videos as a viable supervision source for humanoid skill learning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of the TRACC pipeline. Human motion is reconstructed from the failed video, retargeted to the humanoid, and aligned with the simulated scene to train the prefix tracker. A VLM infers the intended goal, proposes task-reward candidates, and estimates a PoNR window. The tracker is then fine-tuned to complete the intended task.
